teile.einleitung: A ball bearing is a component that lets turning parts run easily and almost without friction. Instead of rubbing, small steel balls roll between two rings inside it. Ball bearings are found in bikes, inline skates, cars, washing machines and countless other machines.
wichtigste: In a ball bearing, balls roll between an inner ring and an outer ring.
A cage keeps the balls evenly spaced.
Rolling produces much less friction than sliding.
Ball bearings and roller bearings belong to the group of rolling bearings.
The balls are usually made of hardened steel.
Grease makes friction and wear even smaller.
On a bike you find ball bearings in the wheel hubs, for example.

abschnitte.titel: How a ball bearing is built
abschnitte.text: A ball bearing consists of an **inner ring**, an **outer ring** and a row of balls between them. The inner ring sits on an axle or shaft, and the outer ring fits into the housing. A **cage** made of sheet metal or plastic keeps the balls apart so that they do not touch each other. Seals at the sides often protect the bearing from dust and water.

When two surfaces slide over each other, a lot of **friction** is produced, which slows things down and creates heat. Rolling balls, on the other hand, touch the rings only at tiny points and roll along easily. You know this from the difference between pushing a heavy box and rolling a wheeled suitcase. That is why such bearings are also called **rolling bearings**: the balls roll along. A good grease makes friction and wear even smaller.

On a bike there are ball bearings in the wheel hubs, the bottom bracket and the headset. Every wheel of an **inline skate** or skateboard contains two small ball bearings, which is why they keep rolling for so long. Cars, trains, fans, hard disks and washing machines also need ball bearings. Even a fidget spinner spins for so long thanks to a ball bearing in the middle.

The balls are usually made of **hardened steel**, which is very hard and smooth. For special uses there are also ceramic balls, which are lighter and hardly rust. Besides balls, cylinders, cones or needles are also used as rolling elements; these are then called **roller bearings**. Roller bearings can usually carry heavier loads, while ball bearings often turn faster and more quietly.

Leonardo da Vinci already sketched ideas for bearings with balls around 1500. But ball bearings only became widespread in the 19th century, when machines could grind balls to exactly the same roundness. In Germany, Friedrich Fischer in Schweinfurt developed a **ball grinding machine** for this around 1883. The invention of the bicycle created a great demand for smooth-running bearings at the time.

begriffe.erklaerung: Bearing in which balls or rollers roll between two rings.
Part that keeps the balls in the bearing evenly spaced.
Force that slows down a movement when surfaces rub against each other.
Middle part of a wheel in which the axle turns.
The wearing away of parts through use.

gewusst: The balls in good ball bearings are made so precisely that they differ from a perfect sphere by only fractions of a thousandth of a millimetre.
Every car contains dozens of ball bearings, from the wheels to the alternator.
For inline skates and skateboards, the precision of the bearings is often given with an ABEC number.

teile.einleitung: Metals are substances such as iron, copper, gold or aluminium that shine, conduct electricity and heat well and can be shaped. Most chemical elements are metals. Without them there would be no cars, no mobile phones and no steel bridges.
wichtigste: Metals shine, conduct electric current and heat well and can be bent, rolled or forged.
Most of the chemical elements are metals.
At room temperature almost all metals are solid; only mercury is liquid.
The density of metals varies widely, from lithium with about 0.5 g/cm³ to osmium with about 22.6 g/cm³.
At about 2.7 g/cm³ aluminium is a light metal and is therefore used in aircraft construction.
Mixtures of metals are called alloys, for example bronze, brass or steel.
Metals can be recycled well.

abschnitte.text: **Metals** are chemical elements or substances with typical properties: they have a metallic **lustre**, conduct electricity and heat well and can be shaped without breaking. This is due to their inner structure. The atoms sit in a lattice, and some electrons can move freely between them like an electron gas. These free electrons carry the current. Of the more than 100 known elements, the great majority are metals.

Metals differ greatly in their **density**, that is in how heavy a cube of 1 cm³ is. Lithium is so light that it floats on water. Aluminium has about 2.7 g/cm³, iron 7.9 g/cm³, copper 8.96 g/cm³ and silver about 10.5 g/cm³. Gold and tungsten have almost exactly the same density of about 19.3 g/cm³, and **osmium** is the densest element of all. A copper cube of 10 cm³ therefore weighs 89.6 g, and 54 g of aluminium have a volume of 20 cm³.

Because aluminium is light, it is used in **aircraft construction**, for bike frames and drinks cans. As steel, iron is the most important building metal for bridges, rails and cars. Copper conducts electricity very well and is found in almost every cable. Lead has a high density and is cheap, which is why it was used for example for weights on fishing lines; today it is often replaced because it is poisonous. Gold and silver are **precious metals** that hardly corrode and are used for jewellery and electronics.

Many metals are mixed to obtain better properties; such mixtures are called **alloys**. **Bronze** consists of copper and tin, brass of copper and zinc. Steel is iron with a little carbon; stainless steel also contains chromium and nickel. People already learned to melt and cast metals in the Bronze Age. Later came the Iron Age, in which tools and weapons were made of iron.

Whether a metal floats depends on the density of the liquid. An iron cube even floats on liquid **mercury**, because at about 13.5 g/cm³ mercury is denser than iron. In Switzerland aluminium was produced from 1888 in Neuhausen at the Rhine Falls, with electricity from hydropower. Today aluminium cans, sheet steel and electronic waste are collected and **recycled** in Switzerland. This saves a lot of energy, because scrap metal can be melted down almost any number of times.

begriffe.erklaerung: The mass of a substance per volume, given for example in g/cm³.
A mixture of a metal with other metals or substances.
A valuable metal such as gold or platinum that hardly corrodes.
A metal with a low density, such as aluminium or magnesium.
Reusing waste as a new raw material.

gewusst: Gold can be hammered so thin that gold leaf becomes translucent and lets light through with a greenish tint.
The metal gallium melts at only about 30 °C and can turn liquid in a warm hand.
A cube of osmium with 10 cm sides would weigh around 22.6 kg.

teile.einleitung: A tape measure is a long, flexible band with numbers and lines, used for measuring lengths. Because it can bend, you can also measure round things with it. In Switzerland the best-known kind is the “Rollmeter”, a tape measure with a steel band.
wichtigste: A tape measure is a flexible band with numbers and lines.
Because it is flexible, you can measure round a head or a tree trunk with it.
A usual tape measure for sewing is 150 centimetres long.
On a steel tape measure the band rolls back when you press the button.
On sports day the distance in the long jump is measured with a long tape measure.
At the paediatrician's, height is often measured with a measuring rod on the wall.
In experiments lengths are measured with a tape measure.

abschnitte.text: A **tape measure** is a band made of fabric, plastic, fibreglass or steel. **Centimetres** are printed on it with numbers and **millimetres** with small lines. Unlike a ruler it is flexible and long. You can roll it up and take it with you easily.

For **sewing** people use a soft tailor's tape measure of 150 centimetres. Craftspeople need a **steel tape measure**, a steel band in a case that is pulled back by a spring. For very long distances, for example on the sports field, there are tape measures of 20 or 50 metres on a reel with a crank. Many tape measures have a second scale in inches on the back.

You cannot measure round a head with a ruler, but you can with a tape measure. That is how you measure, for example, your **head size** for a bike helmet or a cap. Foresters measure the circumference of tree trunks to estimate how thick a tree is. Dressmakers also measure the chest, waist and arm length with the soft band.

On sports day a long tape measure lies next to the sandpit for the long jump. It is measured from the take-off line to the mark that is closest to the line. At school, in experiments, you measure for example how far a toy car rolls. For height it is better to use a **measuring rod** on the wall, because you can stand up straight against it.

The band must start exactly at the zero point and be taut, but not stretched. When reading it, you look straight down onto the scale, not at an angle. Long distances are best measured by two people. If you press the button on a steel tape measure, keep your fingers away from the band, because it snaps back quickly.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tape measure made of steel in a case that rolls itself up.
The row of lines and numbers on a measuring device.
The length all the way round an object.
Vertical scale on the wall for measuring height.

gewusst: The small metal hook at the front of a steel tape measure is deliberately a little loose, so that you measure inside and outside equally accurately.
A steel tape measure gets a tiny bit longer in heat than in cold.

teile.einleitung: A minute is a unit of time and lasts exactly 60 seconds. Sixty minutes make an hour. We use minutes every day to read the clock, catch the bus or brush our teeth for long enough.
wichtigste: A minute has 60 seconds, and an hour has 60 minutes.
The symbol for minute is min.
A quarter of an hour has 15 minutes, three quarters of an hour have 45 minutes.
An hour and a half is 90 minutes.
A day has 1440 minutes.
You should brush your teeth for about 2 to 3 minutes.
Dividing into 60 comes from the ancient Babylonians.

abschnitte.text: The **minute** is a unit of time. It lasts exactly 60 **seconds**, and 60 minutes make an **hour**. So a whole day with 24 hours has 24 times 60, which is 1440 minutes. It is written in short as min, for example 5 min. The word comes from the Latin pars minuta prima, which means “first small part”.

On a clock with hands, the long hand shows the minutes. It takes one hour to go all the way round, and each small mark on the clock face stands for one minute. There are 5 minutes between two numbers. A **quarter of an hour** has 15 minutes, half an hour has 30 minutes. On a digital clock, the minutes come after the colon or, in Switzerland, often after a full stop, such as 10.50.

When you calculate with time, remember that a new hour begins after 59 minutes. For example, it is 10.50, and 20 minutes later it is 11.10, because 10 minutes are missing until the full hour and then another 10 are added. An hour and a half is 60 plus 30, so 90 minutes. A football match lasts two halves of 45 minutes, which is also 90 minutes. You need calculations like these when reading timetables, for example.

The fact that an hour has 60 minutes goes back to the **Babylonians** in ancient Mesopotamia. They used a number system based on the number 60, the **sexagesimal system**. The number 60 can be divided by many numbers: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30. That is why an hour can easily be split into halves, thirds or quarters. However, clocks with minute hands only became common in the 17th century, when clocks became more accurate.

A famous example of the minute is the **Swiss railway clock**, which Hans Hilfiker designed for the SBB in 1944. Its red second hand with the round disc goes round a little faster than one minute. At the top, at the 12, it stops briefly until a signal arrives. Then the minute hand jumps forward one minute, and all the clocks in the country show the new minute at the same time. This way the trains leave on time to the minute.

The word minute is also used when measuring **angles**. A degree is divided into 60 minutes of arc, just like an hour. This is needed, for example, for coordinates on maps and at sea. The minute of time and the minute of arc have the same origin in the Babylonian number system. For angles, you write a small dash, for example 30 degrees and 15 minutes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The 60th part of a minute.
15 minutes, a quarter of an hour.
A number system based on the number 60.
The surface of a clock with the numbers and marks.

gewusst: Because of the leap second, a minute has already had 61 seconds several times.
A child's heart beats about 80 to 100 times in a minute.
The SBB railway clock is so well known that its design has also been used for wristwatches.

teile.einleitung: The eyepiece is the lens of a microscope or telescope that you look into with your eye. It works like a magnifying glass and enlarges the image formed by the objective. Without an eyepiece, you could hardly see anything through a telescope.
wichtigste: The eyepiece is the lens on the side of the eye.
Its German name, Okular, comes from the Latin word “oculus”, which means eye.
The eyepiece works like a magnifying glass for the intermediate image of the objective.
Around 1660, Christiaan Huygens developed an eyepiece made of two lenses.
A telescope's magnification is the focal length of the objective divided by the focal length of the eyepiece.
A telescope with a focal length of 1200 millimetres magnifies 120 times with a 10-millimetre eyepiece.
People who wear glasses need eyepieces with a long eye relief.

abschnitte.text: Telescopes and microscopes have two important lens systems. The **objective** points towards the object and forms a small image inside, the **intermediate image**. The **eyepiece** sits at the other end, right in front of the eye. It works like a magnifying glass with which you look at this intermediate image enlarged. Its German name, Okular, comes from the Latin “oculus”, which means eye.

For a telescope, the magnification is easy to work out. You divide the **focal length** of the objective by the focal length of the eyepiece. If a telescope has a focal length of 1200 millimetres and the eyepiece 10 millimetres, it magnifies 120 times. So an eyepiece with a short focal length magnifies more. That is why amateur astronomers often have several **interchangeable eyepieces** to choose between low and high magnification.

On a microscope, the eyepiece usually has a number on it such as 10x. You get the **total magnification** by multiplying this number by the magnification of the objective, for example 10 times 40 equals 400 times. Many microscopes have two eyepieces so that you can look in with both eyes. A **measuring eyepiece** has a built-in scale with which you can read off the size of cells or other things in the specimen. Microscopes like these are found in many Swiss schools.

The first telescopes were made in the Netherlands at the beginning of the 17th century. Galileo Galilei used a diverging lens as an eyepiece; Johannes Kepler suggested a converging lens. Around 1660, the Dutch physicist **Christiaan Huygens** developed an eyepiece made of two lenses, which is named after him. Later many other designs were added, such as the eyepiece by Jesse Ramsden. Modern eyepieces often consist of five or more lenses and give a large, sharp field of view.

If you wear glasses, you need an eyepiece with a long **eye relief** so that you can see the whole field of view despite your glasses. Some eyepieces have a rubber eyecup for this that you can fold down. On binoculars, one eyepiece lets you adjust the focus for each eye separately. You should never touch the glass surfaces with your fingers and should only clean them with a soft cloth. Important: never look at the **Sun** through a telescope without a special filter, as this can seriously injure your eye immediately.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lens of an optical instrument that you look through with your eye.
The image the objective forms inside the instrument.
A converging lens through which you see things enlarged.
How far your eye can be from the eyepiece and still see everything.

gewusst: With his telescopes, Christiaan Huygens also discovered Titan, the large moon of the planet Saturn.
If you magnify too much, the image gets bigger but also darker and blurrier.
On a microscope with a camera, a screen sometimes replaces the eyepiece completely.

teile.einleitung: A maglev train is a train that does not roll on wheels but floats above its track with magnets. Because the vehicle and the rail do not touch, there is no rolling resistance and hardly any wear. Such trains can travel faster than almost all other trains.
wichtigste: A maglev train floats above the track without touching it.
It is driven by a linear motor, a kind of unrolled electric motor.
The maglev train developed in Germany is called the Transrapid.
The Transrapid floats only about 1 centimetre above its track.
In Shanghai a Transrapid runs in regular service to the airport.
In 2015 Japan set a record of over 600 km/h with a maglev train.
The Swiss project Swissmetro planned a maglev train in tubes under the ground.

abschnitte.text: A **maglev train** is a rail vehicle without wheels. Strong magnets lift the train and keep it on track. Because nothing touches, there is no **rolling resistance** and hardly any wear. The ride is therefore very quiet and smooth; at high speed you mainly hear the rush of air.

On the German **Transrapid**, electromagnets reach under the track and pull themselves up towards it from below. A computer regulates the current thousands of times per second so that the gap is always about 1 centimetre. The Japanese train works differently, with **superconducting** magnets that push the train away. As a result it floats about 10 centimetres up, but needs wheels at low speed.

The train moves forwards with a **linear motor**. You can picture it as an electric motor that has been cut open and rolled out flat. In the track, coils produce a travelling magnetic field that pulls the train along. To brake, the field is simply reversed.

Since the early 2000s a Transrapid in **Shanghai** has linked the airport with the city over a distance of around 30 kilometres. In Japan a maglev line is being built between Tokyo and Nagoya, the Chuo Shinkansen. On its test track a Japanese maglev train travelled at over 600 km/h in 2015, a world record for rail vehicles. In Germany itself the Transrapid was only used on a test track in the Emsland region.

In Switzerland the idea of the **Swissmetro** emerged from the 1970s onwards. Maglev trains were to run in underground tubes with little air, so that air resistance would stay small. That way you could have travelled from Geneva to St. Gallen, for example, in a short time. However, the project was never built; the idea lives on in concepts such as the Hyperloop.

Because nothing touches, the vehicle and track hardly wear, and the train can climb steep gradients. A big disadvantage is the high cost of building the special **track**. A maglev train cannot run on normal rails and cannot enter existing stations. That is why there are still only a few lines worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: Electric motor that does not turn but pulls in a straight line.
Braking force that arises when a wheel rolls on the ground.
Material that conducts current without loss when very cold.
The special route on which a maglev train runs.

gewusst: A maglev train actually cannot derail, because the Transrapid wraps around its track from below.
At over 600 km/h you would get from Geneva to Lake Constance in less than an hour.

teile.einleitung: The money of Switzerland is the Swiss franc, which is divided into 100 centimes (Rappen). There are seven coins and six different banknotes. The coins are minted by Swissmint in Bern, and the banknotes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
wichtigste: The currency of Switzerland is the Swiss franc, abbreviated CHF.
One franc has 100 centimes (Rappen).
There are coins worth 5, 10 and 20 centimes and ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs.
The five-franc piece is the largest Swiss coin; the most drops of water fit on it.
The banknotes come in 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs.
The coins are minted by Swissmint in Bern; the banknotes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
The franc has been the common currency of the whole of Switzerland since 1850.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland has seven **coins**: 5, 10 and 20 centimes and ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs. The 5-centime piece is gold-coloured; the other coins are silvery. The centime coins show the head of the goddess of liberty, Libertas. The ½, 1 and 2-franc pieces show Helvetia, a female figure who represents Switzerland. The five-franc piece shows the head of an alpine herdsman and is popularly called the **Fünfliber**.

You can do an exciting experiment with coins: how many drops of water fit on a coin? Using a pipette, you carefully drip water onto it. The water bulges upwards like a dome before it overflows. The reason is **surface tension**: the water particles hold on to each other like a thin skin. The most drops fit on the five-franc piece, because it has the largest surface.

The banknotes come in 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. The current ninth series was introduced between 2016 and 2019. Each note has a theme that shows the many sides of Switzerland, for example time, light, wind, water, matter and communication. A hand and a globe can be found on all the notes. The 1000-franc note is one of the banknotes with the highest value in the world.

Banknotes have many **security features** so that they are hard to forge. These include a security thread, shiny elements that change colour when you tilt them, and raised printing you can feel. If you hold a note up to the light, you can see a Swiss cross. The coins also have features on the edge. The edge of the Fünfliber bears the inscription “Dominus providebit”, which means “The Lord will provide”.

The coins are made by **Swissmint**, the federal mint in Bern. The banknotes are issued by the **Swiss National Bank** and printed in Zurich. Before the Swiss franc existed in 1850, many cantons had their own money. That made paying complicated, because you constantly had to convert. The 1-centime coin was abolished in 2007 because it was hardly used any more.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hundredth part of a franc.
The everyday name for the five-franc piece.
The force with which water particles hold together at the surface.
The federal mint in Bern, which strikes the Swiss coins.
The state's bank, which issues the money and keeps the franc stable.

gewusst: Swiss coins have looked almost the same for over a hundred years.
The abbreviation CHF comes from “Confoederatio Helvetica” and franc.

teile.einleitung: A bed of nails is a board with a great many sharp nails sticking out of it close together. Amazingly, you can lie down on it without getting hurt. The bed of nails is a well-known example of how pressure depends on the size of the area.
wichtigste: On a bed of nails, the body's weight is spread over a great many points.
Pressure is force divided by area.
The more nails carry the weight, the smaller the force on each single nail.
All the nails must be exactly the same height, or a few nails carry the whole weight.
When standing, the pressure on the soles of the feet is greater than when lying down.
The bed of nails is known as a trick performed by fakirs.
The word fakir comes from Arabic and means “poor”.

abschnitte.titel: What is a bed of nails
abschnitte.text: A bed of nails is a wooden board with hundreds or even thousands of nails whose points face upwards. The nails are only a few centimetres apart and all the same length. Anyone who carefully lies down on it feels many small points but does not get hurt. It is often shown in shows, museums and physics lessons.

abschnitte.titel: Pressure is force divided by area
abschnitte.text: **Pressure** tells you how strongly a force presses on a certain area. It is calculated as force divided by area, and the unit is the **pascal**. If the area is small, the pressure becomes large; if it is large, the pressure becomes small. A single nail has a tiny point and so easily pierces the skin.

If a person with a weight of 600 newtons lies evenly on 600 nails, each nail carries only 1 newton. That is about the weight of a bar of chocolate. If 500 newtons are spread over 1000 points, each with an area of 1 mm², the pressure is **500,000 pascals**. That is not enough to pierce the skin, but a single nail carrying the whole weight would go in deep.

On a board with only a few nails, each nail would have to carry much more weight, which would be dangerous. The height must be right too: if one nail sticks out further, it carries a large part of the load on its own. If you stand on the board instead of lying, the whole weight rests on the small soles of your feet and the pressure becomes greater. That is why you should never try such experiments without guidance from experts.

Lying on beds of nails is often linked with **fakirs**. The word comes from the Arabic word for “poor” and originally meant religious begging monks. In India, some ascetics showed how they could bear pain. Later, the bed of nails became a popular trick in the circus and at fairs.

abschnitte.titel: The same principle in everyday life
abschnitte.text: Stepping barefoot on a small toy brick hurts a lot, because the whole weight presses on a tiny area. **Snowshoes**, on the other hand, spread the weight over a large area so that you do not sink into the snow. Wide tyres on tractors protect the ground for the same reason. Knives and needles work the other way round: their fine edge or point creates enormous pressure.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on a certain area.
The unit of pressure, one newton per square metre.
Originally a poor, religious begging monk; today also a performer who lies on nails.
The force with which the Earth pulls an object downwards.

gewusst: Because the weight is spread over many points, usually only small red dots are left on the skin after getting up.
A bed with only a few nails is more dangerous than one with many nails.
There are mats with many small plastic spikes that people lie on to relax.

teile.einleitung: A multimeter is a measuring device that can measure several electrical quantities. You use it to check voltage, current and resistance. Electricians, hobbyists and physics classes use it every day.
wichtigste: A multimeter measures several electrical quantities, mainly voltage, current and resistance.
The black test lead usually goes into the COM socket.
A straight line next to the symbol stands for direct current, a wavy line for alternating current.
If you do not know how big a value is, you first choose the largest measuring range.
Resistance is only measured with the circuit switched off, because the device itself produces a measuring current.
A minus sign for direct voltage shows that the leads are swapped.
For large currents, you put the red lead into the 10A socket.
In a continuity test, the device beeps if a wire is connected all the way through.

abschnitte.text: The word **multimeter** means something like multiple meter. In the past, you needed a separate device each for voltage, current and resistance. Today, all the functions are in one handy box with a rotary switch. Most devices show the value as a number on a display; older ones have a pointer.

The black lead goes into the **COM** socket, which stands for common. Depending on the measurement, the red lead goes into the socket for volts and ohms or for amperes. There is a separate 10A socket for large currents. On the rotary switch, V stands for voltage, A for current and the omega sign for resistance, with a straight line for direct current and a wavy line for alternating current.

**Voltage** is measured in parallel, so you hold the tips to two points, for example to the terminals of a battery. **Current** is measured in series: the current must flow through the device. Resistance is only measured without current, because the multimeter sends a small measuring current through itself. If you do not know the value, you start in the largest range and then switch down.

In a **continuity test**, the device beeps if there is a connection between two points. This lets you quickly find a broken cable or a blown fuse. A minus sign in front of the value shows that the leads are swapped, but with direct voltage this does no harm. Some devices also measure temperature or test diodes.

The units of the measured quantities are named after scientists. The volt recalls the Italian Alessandro Volta, who built the first battery. The ampere honours the Frenchman André-Marie Ampère, and the ohm the German Georg Simon **Ohm**. A fresh AA battery shows about 1.5 volts, a flat one clearly less.

A socket in Switzerland carries 230 volts of alternating voltage, which is life-threatening. Such measurements should only be made by experts with suitable devices. At school, you measure with batteries and small power supplies. Before every measurement, you check that the leads and tips are undamaged.

begriffe.erklaerung: The electrical pressure that drives the current, measured in volts.
How much electric charge flows per second, measured in amperes.
How strongly a component slows down the current, measured in ohms.
The range of values the device can measure at one setting.
A test to see whether a cable or wire is connected all the way through.

gewusst: For measuring voltage, a good multimeter has a very high internal resistance so that it hardly changes the circuit.
Devices set to measure current, on the other hand, have almost no resistance, which is why a wrong setting can destroy the built-in fuse.

teile.einleitung: An overhead line is a power cable stretched above railway tracks or streets that supplies trains, trams and trolleybuses with electricity. The vehicles pick up the current with a pantograph on the roof. In Switzerland, almost the entire railway runs on electricity from overhead lines.
wichtigste: Trains, trams and trolleybuses get their electricity from the overhead line.
The current is picked up by a pantograph on the roof of the locomotive.
On the railway, the current flows back through the rails.
The SBB's railway power has a frequency of 16.7 hertz.
Many Swiss trams run on around 600 volts direct voltage.
An overhead line is practically always live, even when no train is running.
Even getting close is life-threatening, because the current can jump across as an electric arc.
That is why you never climb onto parked goods wagons or fly kites near power lines.

abschnitte.text: The **overhead line**, also called the contact line on the railway, is a copper wire hanging above the tracks. It is held up by a carrier cable fixed to masts. The wire runs in a slight zigzag so that the pantograph wears evenly. Weights at the ends keep the wire taut in both heat and cold.

On the roof of the locomotive, a **pantograph** presses against the wire from below. The current flows through the motors and back through the wheels and **rails** to the substation. A trolleybus has no rails and so needs two wires and two poles. The SBB use alternating current at 15,000 volts and 16.7 hertz; trams mostly use around 600 volts direct current.

Switzerland has one of the densest **electrified** railway networks in the world. Because it had hardly any coal, it turned early on to electricity from hydropower. The SBB even run their own power stations and their own grid for railway power. Cities such as Zurich, Bern, Basel and Geneva also have tram and trolleybus lines with overhead lines.

An overhead line is practically always at **high voltage**, even when no train is running. At 15,000 volts you do not even have to touch the wire: the current can jump through the air as an **electric arc**. That is why climbing onto parked goods wagons or masts is life-threatening. A kite string or a long branch can also carry the current to a person.

A bird often sits on a single power line without coming to harm. There is almost no **voltage** between its two feet, so hardly any current flows through it. But if it touches something at a different voltage at the same time, such as an earthed mast, it is dangerous. For people, the rule is always: keep your distance.

begriffe.erklaerung: A frame on the roof of a vehicle that picks up current from the wire.
A hot, glowing flow of current through the air between two conductors.
How often alternating current changes direction per second, measured in hertz.
A facility that provides the current for the overhead line.
A bus with an electric motor that draws current from two overhead wires.

gewusst: At 16.7 hertz, the SBB's railway power has a different frequency from household power at 50 hertz, which is why the railway needs its own power grid.
When braking, modern locomotives can produce electricity and feed it back through the overhead line to other trains.

teile.einleitung: When you climb stairs, you lift your whole body against gravity and do work as you do so. How quickly you do it is described by power, measured in watts. With scales, a tape measure and a stopwatch you can easily work out your own power.
wichtigste: To work out your own power when climbing stairs, you need body mass, height and time.
The lifting work is weight times height, in other words mass times g times height.
Power is work divided by time and is measured in watts.
For lifting work only the height counts, not the length of the stairs.
A person weighing 50 kg does 1500 J of lifting work over a height of 3 m.
If they need 5 s for it, they produce 300 W.
A light child and a heavy adult can produce the same power if the child is faster.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who climbs stairs lifts their body weight. This needs **lifting work**, which is calculated like this: mass times gravitational field strength g times height. With g equal to 10 N/kg, a person weighing 50 kg does 1500 joules of work on stairs 3 m high. Only the height counts, because only lifting against **gravity** costs lifting work. Whether the stairs are steep or flat and long makes no difference to this.

**Power** tells you how much work is done per second. You calculate work divided by time, and the unit is called the **watt**, named after the Scottish inventor James Watt. If the person weighing 50 kg needs exactly 5 s for their 1500 J, they produce 300 W. Leo, who weighs 60 kg, runs up stairs 4 m high in 8 s: 2400 J divided by 8 s also gives 300 W.

First weigh yourself and then measure the height of one step with the tape measure. Multiply it by the number of steps to get the total height. Ask a second person to time you with a **stopwatch** while you walk or run up the stairs. A pupil weighing 50 kg who manages four floors of 3 m each in 30 s produces 6000 J divided by 30 s, or 200 W. Compare your results when walking at a relaxed pace and when running.

Mia weighs 40 kg and needs 6 s for stairs 3 m high; her father weighs 80 kg and needs 12 s. Both produce exactly 200 W, because the father lifts twice as much mass but takes twice as long. You can also turn the formula round: a man weighing 70 kg who produces 420 W needs 2100 J divided by 420 W, or 5 s, for a height of 3 m. What always matters is the ratio of work to **time**.

A person can produce about 100 to 200 W for a long time, and much more for a few seconds. An old unit of power is **horsepower**; 1 metric horsepower equals about 735 W. The staircase next to the Niesen funicular in the Bernese Oberland, with 11,674 steps, is regarded as the longest staircase in the world. In the annual Niesen stair race, runners climb about 1700 metres in height there.

begriffe.erklaerung: Work needed to lift something against gravity.
Work per unit of time, in other words how quickly work is done.
Unit of power; 1 watt is 1 joule per second.
Unit of work and energy.
The number g, about 10 N per kilogram on Earth.

gewusst: An old 60 W light bulb needs about as much power as a person produces over a long time when climbing stairs at a relaxed pace.
Our muscles turn only about a quarter of the energy from food into movement; the rest becomes heat, which is why you get warm climbing stairs.

teile.einleitung: Optics is the branch of physics that deals with light. It explains how light travels, is reflected and refracted, and how lenses form images. Without optics there would be no glasses, cameras, microscopes or fibre-optic cables.
wichtigste: Optics is the study of light.
In a vacuum, light travels at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second.
When it passes into another material, light is refracted.
In a prism, violet light is refracted the most.
Converging lenses form images that can be calculated with the lens equation.
The power of a lens is measured in dioptres.
Short-sightedness is corrected with a diverging lens.

abschnitte.text: **Optics** studies light and how it behaves. **Geometric optics** represents light as straight rays and explains mirrors, lenses and shadows. Wave optics describes light as a wave and explains colours and interference. In a vacuum, light travels at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second.

When light passes at an angle from air into glass, it is refracted. Snell's **law of refraction** says n₁ · sin α = n₂ · sin β. If light hits glass with n = 1.5 at 30°, the angle of refraction is around 19.5°. Because different colours are refracted by different amounts, a **prism** splits white light, with violet being bent the most.

When light passes from glass into air, beyond a certain angle it cannot get out at all. It is then completely reflected back; this is called **total internal reflection**. For glass with n = 1.5, this **critical angle** is around 41.8°. Fibre-optic cables use total internal reflection to carry light and data over long distances.

A **converging lens** brings light together at the focal point. Where the image forms is calculated with the **lens equation** 1/f = 1/g + 1/b. If an object is 30 cm in front of a lens with a focal length of 10 cm, the image forms 15 cm behind the lens. The **power** of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres, so a lens with a focal length of 50 cm has 2 dioptres.

Our **eye** is an optical system with a cornea and a lens. In short-sightedness, the image forms in front of the retina, and a diverging lens corrects this. Cameras, binoculars, microscopes and telescopes are made of several lenses. In Switzerland, companies such as Leica in Heerbrugg have long been known for precision optical instruments.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number n that tells you how strongly a material bends light.
When light is completely reflected back at a boundary.
The distance between the lens and the focal point.
The unit of the power of a lens.

gewusst: The sparkle of diamonds comes from total internal reflection inside the stone.
Much of the internet runs through glass fibres, in which light signals travel.
Light takes only a little over a second to travel from the Moon to the Earth.

teile.einleitung: No measurement is completely exact; every result has a certain measurement uncertainty. It tells you in which range the true value probably lies. Anyone who measures should therefore give not only a value but also its uncertainty, for example (50.0 ± 0.5) cm.
wichtigste: Every measurement comes with an uncertainty.
It is written with a plus-minus sign, for example (50.0 ± 0.5) cm.
The relative uncertainty here is 0.5 divided by 50, that is 1 per cent.
Random deviations can be reduced by repeating often and taking the average.
Systematic deviations, for example from a wrongly calibrated scale, do not disappear through repetition.
Four times as many measurements halve the uncertainty of the mean.
The international guide to stating measurement uncertainty is called the GUM.

abschnitte.text: If you measure the length of your desk, you might get 50.0 cm. But the ruler only has millimetre lines, and reading it is never perfect. The **measurement uncertainty** describes by how much the true value probably differs from the measured value. You write (50.0 ± 0.5) cm; the **relative uncertainty** is then 1 per cent.

If you measure several times, you get slightly different values, because, for example, you press the stopwatch sometimes earlier and sometimes later. Such **random deviations** scatter upwards and downwards. If you take the mean of many measurements, they partly cancel out. The uncertainty of the mean falls with the square root of the number of measurements, so with four times as many measurements it falls to half.

A wrongly calibrated scale always shows too much or always too little. This is a **systematic deviation**, and it does not disappear even with a hundred repetitions. You can only find it by checking the measuring device against an accurate reference standard. Measured values can therefore be precise, that is scatter little, and still not be correct, because they all lie away from the true value.

If you calculate something new from measured values, the uncertainty is passed on too. For an area from length times width, you add the relative uncertainties according to the **maximum error estimate**. If length and width have uncertainties of 2 and 3 per cent, the area has up to 5 per cent. More precise methods take into account that deviations partly balance out.

So that researchers all over the world proceed in the same way, there is the **GUM**, the guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement. It was published by international organisations in the 1990s. It distinguishes two ways: Type A determines the uncertainty statistically from series of measurements, Type B from other sources such as manufacturers' data or calibration certificates. In Switzerland the Federal Institute of Metrology METAS in Bern-Wabern takes care of accurate measurements.

begriffe.erklaerung: The difference between the measured value and the true value.
The sum of all measured values divided by their number.
Check and adjust a measuring device against an accurate reference value.
How close repeated measurements lie to each other.

gewusst: Even the most accurate atomic clocks have a measurement uncertainty, but it is so small that it would amount to only about one second in millions of years.
Many decimal places in a result do not mean that the measurement was accurate.
In sport, times in ski races are measured to hundredths of a second so that the uncertainty is smaller than the gap between the racers.

teile.einleitung: Latent heat is energy that a substance takes up or gives off when it changes its state without its temperature changing. “Latent” means hidden: the heat is in the substance, but you cannot see it on the thermometer. It explains why ice cubes cool so well and why sweating is refreshing.
wichtigste: Latent heat is energy for a change of state without a change in temperature.
While ice melts, its temperature stays at 0 °C, and the heating curve is flat.
An ice cube cools more than the same amount of water at 0 °C, because it also takes up the heat of melting.
When sweat evaporates, it takes heat from the skin and so cools the body.
When something freezes or condenses, the stored heat is released again.
The Scottish scientist Joseph Black introduced the term in the 18th century.
The heat released when water vapour condenses is the most important source of energy for tropical cyclones.

abschnitte.text: Substances can be solid, liquid or gas. The change between these states is called a **change of state**. To melt ice or turn water into vapour, energy is needed to pull the particles apart instead of making them faster. This energy is called **latent heat**. Depending on the change, we speak of the heat of melting, the heat of vaporisation or the heat of condensation.

If you heat ice evenly, its temperature first rises to 0 °C. Then it stops, and the curve stays flat until all the ice has melted. Only then does the water get warmer, until it boils at 100 °C, and again the temperature stays the same as long as water is turning into vapour. To melt 1 kg of ice needs about 334 kilojoules, roughly as much as is needed to warm 1 kg of water by 80 °C. To turn 1 kg of water into vapour even needs about 2260 kilojoules.

Around 1760 in Glasgow the Scottish doctor and chemist **Joseph Black** studied why ice takes so long to melt. He noticed that heat flows into the substance without the thermometer rising. That is why he called it “latent”, meaning hidden. His findings later helped James Watt to improve the steam engine.

An ice cube in a glass cools the drink much more than the same amount of ice-cold water, because it also swallows heat as it melts. When we sweat, the sweat evaporates on the skin and takes heat with it; this is called **evaporative cooling**. The other way round, steam scalds the skin more than hot water, because it gives off a lot of heat when it condenses. A hand warmer filled with a salt solution gets warm when you bend the metal disc and the liquid turns solid.

When there is a risk of frost in spring, fruit growers and winegrowers spray their blossoms with water. As the water freezes it gives off heat, and the blossoms under the coat of ice stay protected at about 0 °C. In technology **latent heat stores** using paraffin wax or salt hydrate are used; they take up a lot of energy when they melt and give it off again when they solidify. Such stores are found, for example, in ice packs and in some heating systems.

Over warm seas a lot of water evaporates and takes up energy as it does so. When the moist air rises and condenses into clouds, this energy is released again as **heat of condensation**. It is the main driving force of tropical cyclones such as hurricanes. In thunderstorms in the Alps, too, the heat released by condensation makes the clouds tower high into the sky.

begriffe.erklaerung: The form of a substance: solid, liquid or gas.
Energy needed to melt a solid substance.
Energy needed to turn a liquid into a gas.
Cooling because an evaporating liquid takes heat with it.

gewusst: An iceberg can float in warm seas for months, because so much energy is needed to melt ice.
Dogs hardly sweat; they pant so that water evaporates on their tongue and cools them.

teile.einleitung: Noise protection covers all the measures that protect people from too much or too loud noise. Noise disturbs sleep, causes stress and, when very loud, can permanently damage hearing. In Switzerland laws lay down precisely how loud it may get next to roads, railway lines and airports.
wichtigste: Noise is unwanted sound that disturbs or can make people ill.
In Switzerland the Noise Abatement Ordinance sets limits for road, rail and aircraft noise.
The highest of these exposure limits is the alarm value.
In Switzerland events may be no louder than 100 dB(A) averaged over an hour (as of 2026).
Noise protection is most effective right at the source, for example with low-noise road surfaces.
Noise barriers keep out high sounds better than low ones.
Heavy walls and floating floors insulate against sound in buildings.

abschnitte.text: How loud a sound is is measured as a sound level in **decibels**, abbreviated dB. The scale is logarithmic: we feel 10 dB more as roughly twice as loud. Whispering is about 30 dB, a conversation about 60 dB, and a pneumatic drill close by more than 100 dB. Anyone exposed to very loud noise for a long time can suffer permanent hearing damage.

The basis is the Environmental Protection Act, and the details are in the **Noise Abatement Ordinance** of 1986. It has three levels: the planning value, the immission limit value and the highest, the **alarm value**. If the alarm value is exceeded, houses must be protected with particular urgency, for example with soundproof windows. A separate ordinance applies to concerts and parties, allowing no more than 100 dB(A) averaged over an hour. The biggest source of noise in Switzerland is road traffic.

It is best if noise does not arise in the first place. That is why Swiss authorities are increasingly laying **low-noise road surfaces**, which reduce the rolling noise of tyres. Other measures are 30 km/h zones in residential areas, quieter goods wagons on the railways and night flight bans at airports. Quiet tyres and electric vehicles also help, especially at low speeds.

Along motorways and railway lines there are often **noise barriers**. They cast a sound shadow, much as a house casts a shadow in sunlight. But low sounds have long waves, which bend more strongly over the top edge. That is why such barriers protect less well against low rumbling than against high sounds. The higher the barrier and the closer to the source, the better it works.

Heavy walls insulate against sound better than light ones. According to the mass law, a single-layer wall twice as heavy gives in theory about 6 dB more insulation. Against footstep noise between flats, a **floating floor** helps, that is a floor laid on a soft insulating layer. Porous materials such as foam or acoustic panels turn sound energy into heat; this is called sound absorption.

At concerts and in noisy surroundings **earplugs** protect your hearing. Do not turn headphones up too loud, and take breaks. If your ears whistle or hiss after a loud event, that is a warning sign. Being considerate also helps: in many Swiss municipalities there is a quiet period at night, usually from 10 pm.

begriffe.erklaerung: Unit for the loudness of a sound.
The highest noise limit in Switzerland. Above it, it is urgently too loud.
Keeping sound out, for example with a thick wall.
Turning sound energy into heat, for example in foam.
Sound of footsteps that passes through ceilings into other rooms.

gewusst: Noise barriers are sometimes made of glass so that residents do not have to look at a wall; then bird silhouettes or stripes are stuck on them so that birds do not fly into them.
Because the decibel scale is logarithmic, two equally loud machines together give only about 3 dB more, not twice as much.

teile.einleitung: Metres per second, abbreviated m/s, is the unit of speed in the international system of units. It tells you how many metres something covers in one second. In everyday life kilometres per hour are better known, but in physics and for the weather m/s is often used.
wichtigste: Metres per second is the SI unit of speed.
1 m/s means that 1 metre is covered every second.
Speed is calculated as distance divided by time.
1 m/s corresponds to exactly 3.6 kilometres per hour.
A person walks at about 1 to 1.5 m/s.
In 2009 Usain Bolt ran the 100 metres at an average of around 10.4 m/s.
Sound travels at around 340 m/s in air.

abschnitte.text: **Speed** tells you how fast something is moving. In metres per second you state how many metres a body manages in one second. If something moves at 1 m/s, it covers one metre every second. The unit belongs to the **International System of Units** (SI), which researchers all over the world use.

Speed is **distance divided by time**. A cyclist who rides 1000 metres in 200 seconds is therefore going at 5 m/s. The other way round: distance is speed times time. A ball rolling at 4 m/s gets 2 metres in half a second; a conveyor belt at 3 m/s carries a parcel 180 metres in one minute. And 0.5 m/s means 50 centimetres every second.

An hour has 3600 seconds and a kilometre 1000 metres. That is why 1 m/s corresponds to exactly **3.6 km/h**. To convert from m/s to km/h you therefore multiply by 3.6; the other way round you divide by 3.6. A car at 36 km/h travels 10 m/s, one at 108 km/h already 30 m/s. This shows well how many metres a car covers before you have even reacted.

A snail crawls only about one millimetre per second. A person walks at about 1 to 1.5 m/s; a bike in town often goes at 4 to 6 m/s. In 2009 **Usain Bolt** ran the 100 metres in 9.58 seconds, which is an average of around 10.4 m/s and, as of 2026, still the world record. **Sound** travels at about 340 m/s in air, light at as much as around 300 million m/s.

**Wind speed** is also often given in m/s, especially in science and aviation. A light wind blows at a few m/s, a strong storm at over 20 m/s. In the Swiss weather report you usually hear km/h, for example for foehn storms with gusts of over 100 km/h, which is almost 28 m/s. For sailors, paraglider pilots and wind power stations it is important to know the wind strength precisely.

begriffe.erklaerung: How fast something moves, that is distance per time.
Unit from the international system that applies in science worldwide.
Total distance divided by the total time.
Kilometres per hour, the measure of speed used in road traffic.

gewusst: A cheetah can run at over 25 m/s for a short time, that is over 90 km/h.
The Earth races round the Sun at around 30 000 m/s without us feeling it.
A car at 50 km/h travels almost 14 metres every second.

teile.einleitung: The lens equation is a simple formula from optics. It tells you where a sharp image forms behind a lens. Photographers, opticians and camera makers use it every day.
wichtigste: For thin lenses: 1/f equals 1/g plus 1/b.
f is the focal length, g the object distance and b the image distance.
If the object is exactly at the focal point, the rays run parallel and the image is at infinity.
If an object outside the focal length moves closer to a converging lens, the image distance becomes larger.
A negative image distance means a virtual image on the same side as the object, as with a magnifying glass.
The power of a lens is 1 divided by the focal length in metres and is given in dioptres.
A lens with a focal length of 25 cm has a power of 4 dioptres.

abschnitte.text: A **converging lens** brings light together at one point, the **focal point**. The distance from the lens to the focal point is the **focal length** f. The lens equation links the focal length with two other distances. These are the object distance g, the distance of the object in front of the lens, and the image distance b behind the lens.

The formula is 1/f equals 1/g plus 1/b. An example: a lens has f equal to 10 cm, and the object stands 30 cm in front of it. Then 1/b equals 1/10 minus 1/30, or 2/30, and the **image distance** is 15 cm. With f equal to 20 cm and g equal to 25 cm, the image is even 100 cm behind the lens.

If the object is exactly at the focal point, the rays run **parallel** behind the lens and no image forms on a screen. If it is even closer, the formula gives a negative image distance. This means a **virtual image**, which you can only see by looking through the lens. This is exactly how a magnifying glass works, showing things enlarged.

How large the image is is shown by the **magnification**. It is the ratio of image distance to object distance. If b is greater than g, the image is larger than the object, as with a projector. If b is smaller than g, it is smaller, as with a camera that fits a whole house onto a small image sensor.

Opticians give the strength of spectacle lenses in **dioptres**. The power is 1 divided by the focal length in metres. So a lens with a focal length of 50 cm has 2 dioptres. Long-sighted people need converging lenses with plus values, short-sighted people diverging lenses with minus values.

Our **eye** is also a lens system that projects images onto the retina. Because the image distance there is fixed, the lens of the eye changes its shape and so its focal length. A camera does it the other way round and moves the lens to focus. Strictly speaking the lens equation only applies to thin lenses, but it is a very good approximation.

begriffe.erklaerung: Distance between the lens and the focal point.
Distance between the object and the lens.
Distance between the lens and the sharp image.
Unit for the strength of a lens: 1 divided by the focal length in metres.
An image that you see through the lens but cannot catch on a screen.

gewusst: If an object is at twice the focal length, the image also forms at twice the focal length and is exactly the same size.
A child's eye lens can change its focal length much more than that of an older person, which is why many adults later need reading glasses.

teile.einleitung: A light source is something that shines by itself and gives out light. The most important light source for us is the Sun, but a candle, a lamp or a glow-worm are also light sources. Many things that look bright, on the other hand, do not shine by themselves at all; they only reflect light.
wichtigste: A light source is something that shines by itself.
There are natural light sources such as the Sun, the stars, lightning or hot lava.
Artificial light sources are made by people, for example a light bulb, an LED or a candle.
The Moon is not a light source; it only reflects the light of the Sun.
A bike reflector is not a light source either; it only reflects light.
In the Stone Age people made light at night with fire.
We see things because light from them reaches our eyes.

abschnitte.text: A **light source** produces light itself. Often the light comes from something being very hot, as with the Sun, a candle flame or glowing lava from a volcano. Everything else we see is lit up by a light source and reflects part of the light. Without a light source it would be pitch dark and we could not see anything at all.

The **Sun** is a huge, hot star and our most important light source. The stars twinkling in the sky on a clear night are distant suns too. In a thunderstorm you see **lightning**, a huge electrical discharge. Glow-worms and some animals in the deep sea even glow by themselves; this is called bioluminescence.

Artificial light sources were invented by people. In the Stone Age they used **fire**, and later oil lamps, candles and gas lamps. From about 1880 the electric light bulb came along, which Thomas Edison improved decisively. Today mostly **LED lamps** shine, which use much less electricity than old light bulbs and last much longer.

The **Moon** looks bright at night, but it is not a light source. It is lit by the Sun and reflects its light back to the Earth. In the same way a bike **reflector** is not a light source: it only lights up when light, for example from a car headlight, falls on it. A mirror, a white sheet of paper or snow do not shine by themselves either; they reflect light.

Anyone out and about in the dark should be easy to see. That is why in Switzerland a bike needs a white light at the front and a red light at the back at night, as well as reflectors. Bright clothing and high-visibility vests help children on the way to school in winter. In this way light sources and reflected light work together and make road traffic safer.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that gives out light itself.
The throwing back of light by a surface.
Light that living things such as glow-worms produce themselves.
A small, economical electric lamp made of a semiconductor.

gewusst: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us on Earth.
Some stars you see in the sky are so far away that their light has been travelling for thousands of years.

teile.einleitung: A mesoscaphe is a submarine that dives to medium ocean depths. The Swiss Jacques Piccard built the world's first passenger submarine for the national exhibition Expo 64 in Lausanne. Later he explored the Gulf Stream with another mesoscaphe.
wichtigste: The prefix “meso” means middle.
A mesoscaphe dives only to medium depths, whereas a bathyscaphe goes into the deep sea.
Jacques Piccard built the mesoscaphe “Auguste Piccard” for Expo 64.
During Expo 64 around 33 000 passengers travelled in it in Lake Geneva.
In 1969 Piccard explored the Gulf Stream with the mesoscaphe “Ben Franklin”.
The underwater drift voyage of the “Ben Franklin” lasted about a month.
NASA used the voyage to study life in confined spaces.

abschnitte.text: The word is made up of the Greek **meso** for middle and **skaphos** for ship. So a mesoscaphe is a ship for medium depths. In contrast, a **bathyscaphe** is a deep-sea submersible that can go down to the deepest places in the oceans. Both terms come from the Swiss family of explorers, the Piccards.

In 1931 Auguste Piccard became one of the first people to rise into the stratosphere in a balloon. After that he developed the bathyscaphe. In 1960 his son **Jacques Piccard** dived in the bathyscaphe Trieste into the Mariana Trench, the deepest point of the world's oceans. Jacques' son Bertrand later went round the Earth in a balloon and in a solar-powered aircraft.

For the Swiss national exhibition **Expo 64** in Lausanne, Jacques Piccard built the mesoscaphe “Auguste Piccard”, named after his father. It was the world's first submarine built specifically for tourists. Around 33 000 passengers dived in it into Lake Geneva and looked into the depths through portholes. Today the boat is on display at the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne.

In 1969 Piccard dived with the mesoscaphe **“Ben Franklin”** into the Gulf Stream off the coast of Florida. With five companions he let himself drift north with the current under water for around a month. During this time they measured temperature, currents and marine life. Without engine power they glided over 2000 kilometres along the American east coast.

**NASA** observed the crew of the “Ben Franklin” closely. It wanted to know how people live together for weeks in a small, closed space. These findings were important for later space stations. The voyage took place in the same summer in which the first people landed on the Moon.

begriffe.erklaerung: A submersible for medium ocean depths.
A deep-sea submersible that can reach very great depths.
A warm ocean current in the Atlantic that reaches as far as Europe.
A large exhibition in which Switzerland presents itself, such as Expo 64.

gewusst: The mesoscaphe of Expo 64 was the world's first tourist submarine.
While the “Ben Franklin” was drifting under water in July 1969, the astronauts of Apollo 11 landed on the Moon.
Three generations of the Piccard family have set records in the air, in the deep sea and in going round the world.

teile.einleitung: The mains frequency tells you how often the alternating current in the power grid changes direction back and forth each second. In Switzerland and almost all of Europe it is 50 hertz, in the USA 60 hertz. It has to be kept very precisely, otherwise there is a risk of a power cut.
wichtigste: In Switzerland and Europe, the mains frequency is 50 hertz.
In the USA, 60 hertz is usual; Japan has both frequencies.
In the European interconnected grid, all large generators turn in sync, so the frequency is the same everywhere.
If more electricity is used than produced, the frequency falls.
The spinning mass of the rotating generators softens rapid changes in frequency.
Primary control power reacts automatically within seconds.
If the frequency drops sharply, load is shed in stages to prevent a major blackout.

abschnitte.text: What comes out of the socket is **alternating current**, in which the direction of the current changes all the time. At 50 hertz, a full oscillation happens 50 times a second. The unit **hertz** is named after the German physicist Heinrich Hertz. The angular frequency of the 50 Hz grid is 2 · π · 50, around 314 per second.

Europe, Africa and large parts of Asia use 50 hertz, North and Central America mostly 60 hertz. Japan has a special situation: in the east of the country it is 50 hertz, in the west 60 hertz. This is because in the 19th century generators were bought there from Germany and from the USA. By the way, the Swiss railways use their own grid with 16.7 hertz.

The grid of continental Europe is a huge **interconnected grid** stretching from Portugal to Turkey. All the large generators in the power stations turn in exactly the same rhythm, that is **in sync**. That is why the mains frequency is the same everywhere, in Basel just as in Madrid. As early as 1958, the grids of Switzerland, Germany and France were connected at the “Star of Laufenburg” in Aargau.

The frequency shows whether exactly as much electricity is being produced as used. If suddenly more is used, the generators slow down a little and the frequency **falls**. If too much is produced, it rises. In the first moment after a power station fails, the **spinning mass** of the rotating generators softens the drop, like a heavy wheel that does not stop at once.

To keep the frequency at 50 hertz, power stations hold reserve power ready. **Primary control power** reacts automatically within seconds to any deviation. After that, secondary and tertiary control take over and balance out the deviation completely. In Switzerland, the national grid company Swissgrid coordinates these tasks.

If the frequency still drops sharply, a staged **load shedding** is triggered automatically. Individual areas or large users are briefly cut off from the grid. This prevents the whole grid from collapsing and causing a widespread blackout. Normally the frequency only varies by a few hundredths of a hertz.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of frequency, one oscillation per second.
Current that regularly changes direction.
At the same time and in the same rhythm.
Reserve power that power stations use to balance out fluctuations in the grid.
Deliberately switching off users in order to save the grid.

gewusst: Some alarm clocks and clocks count the oscillations of the grid and go wrong if the frequency is too low for a long time.
From the faint mains hum in sound recordings, experts can sometimes work out when a recording was made.
A generator with a single pair of poles has to turn 3000 times a minute to produce 50 hertz.

teile.einleitung: A laminar flow is a very calm, orderly flow of liquids or gases. The individual layers slide neatly past each other without mixing, almost like the pages of a book when you push it at a slant. The opposite is swirling, turbulent flow.
wichtigste: In laminar flow the layers of fluid slide past each other in an orderly way without mixing.
Right at a stationary wall the speed of a viscous fluid is zero.
In a round pipe the speed profile is parabolic, and the flow is fastest in the middle.
The top speed in the middle of the pipe is twice the average speed.
Whether a flow is laminar or turbulent is shown by the Reynolds number.
According to the Hagen-Poiseuille law, 16 times as much flows through when the pipe radius is doubled.
Laminar flows produce less friction than turbulent ones.

abschnitte.text: The word **laminar** comes from the Latin “lamina”, which means layer or plate. In a laminar flow each thin layer of the fluid moves along its own path. The layers hardly exchange any particles, so they do not mix. You can see this nicely when honey flows slowly off a spoon or when smoke from a candle first rises as a straight thread.

Every liquid and every gas has internal friction, its **viscosity**. Right at a stationary wall the fluid sticks, and its speed there is zero. Further from the wall each layer is a little faster than the one before. Between a stationary plate and a plate moving parallel to it, this creates a linear speed profile.

In a round pipe the flow is zero at the wall and fastest in the middle. The speed profile therefore has the shape of a **parabola**. The top speed is exactly twice the average speed. The **Hagen-Poiseuille law** says that the volume flow rate grows with the fourth power of the radius, so a pipe twice as thick lets 16 times as much through.

Whether a flow stays calm depends on its speed, the diameter of the pipe and the viscosity. These quantities are combined in the **Reynolds number**. In a pipe the flow usually stays laminar as long as the Reynolds number is below about 2300. Above that, eddies form and the flow becomes **turbulent**. The British physicist Osborne Reynolds showed this in 1883 with a coloured thread of water in a glass tube.

A laminar boundary layer produces less frictional drag than a turbulent one. That is why the wings of gliders are shaped so that the flow stays laminar for as long as possible. In the fine blood vessels and in the micro-channels of lab chips, everything also flows in a laminar way. For a small sphere with fluid flowing slowly round it, **Stokes' law** applies: the frictional force is proportional to the speed, which can be used, for example, to calculate how fog droplets sink.

begriffe.erklaerung: General word for anything that can flow, in other words liquids and gases.
How thick and sticky a fluid is. Honey is much more viscous than water.
Swirling, disorderly flow in which everything mixes.
A number that shows whether a flow tends to be calm or swirling.
The thin layer of fluid right at a surface, in which the flow is slowed down.

gewusst: A thin, calm stream of water from the tap looks as clear as glass, like a rod, because it flows in a laminar way.
If you slowly stir drops of colour into a very viscous liquid and then turn back just as slowly, the drops almost reappear, because in laminar flow nothing really mixes.

teile.einleitung: A fridge magnet is a small, often decorated magnet used to fix notes, photos and drawings to the fridge door. Many people collect fridge magnets as souvenirs of their travels. Behind it lies the physics of magnetism, which explains why the magnet holds and when it does not.
wichtigste: A fridge magnet holds because the fridge door is made of steel.
Magnets attract iron, nickel and cobalt and steels made from them.
Only the back of the magnet sticks to the door.
The more sheets you put under it, the less well the magnet holds.
A fridge magnet also sticks to a steel radiator.
The rubber seal of the fridge door often contains a magnetic strip.
Small, strong magnets should be kept away from children, because they can be swallowed.

abschnitte.text: A fridge magnet consists of a **permanent magnet** and a front with a picture, a figure or some lettering. It sticks to the fridge door because the door is made of **steel**, which contains iron. It does not stick to aluminium, wood, glass or plastic. People use them to hold shopping lists, timetables, photos and children's drawings.

A magnet creates a **magnetic field** around itself. When it comes near iron, the iron itself briefly becomes magnetic and attracts the magnet. Many flat fridge magnets are made of magnetic rubber containing tiny magnetic grains. Their back is magnetised in narrow strips, alternately as **north pole** and south pole, which is why only that side holds.

The pull of a magnet drops very quickly with **distance**. If you put a sheet of paper under it, it still holds well. With many sheets the distance to the steel is greater, and the notes slide off. Strong **neodymium magnets** hold even thick piles, but they are dangerous if children swallow them.

The door itself also uses magnetism. Its **rubber seal** contains a long magnetic strip. It pulls the seal tightly against the steel frame all the way round, so that no warm air gets in. Fridges used to have a latch from which a child could not free themselves from the inside, whereas the magnetic seal can be pushed open from inside.

Fridge magnets are popular **souvenirs**. In Switzerland you can get them with the Matterhorn, cows, chocolate or the Chapel Bridge. Some people collect hundreds of them from all over the world. Fridge magnets became popular from the middle of the 20th century, when magnetic rubber and cheap magnets came along.

begriffe.erklaerung: Magnet that keeps its force permanently without electricity.
Invisible space around a magnet in which it exerts forces.
Materials such as iron, nickel and cobalt that are attracted by magnets.
Particularly strong magnet made of a metal mixture containing neodymium.

gewusst: If you put two flat fridge magnets back to back and slide them against each other, you feel a juddering, because the poles change strip by strip.
Some fridge doors today are made of stainless steel that is not magnetic, and then no magnet will stick.
If a child swallows two strong magnets, they can attract each other through the wall of the gut and cause serious injuries.

teile.einleitung: A refracting telescope is a telescope that uses glass lenses to make distant things look closer and brighter. Its technical name is refractor. With a telescope like this, Galileo Galilei discovered the moons of Jupiter more than 400 years ago.
wichtigste: A refracting telescope is technically called a refractor.
A Keplerian telescope has two converging lenses; in a Galilean telescope the eyepiece is a diverging lens.
The objective lens must have a much longer focal length than the eyepiece for the telescope to magnify.
An objective lens twice as wide collects four times as much light.
The first telescope was submitted for a patent in the Netherlands in 1608.
The Yerkes telescope in the USA has an objective lens about 1 metre across.
Much larger refracting telescopes are not built, because large lenses bend under their own weight.

abschnitte.text: A **refractor** collects light with a large lens at the front, the **objective**. This lens bends the light and produces an image of the distant object. At the back you look at this image through a small magnifying lens, the **eyepiece**. The magnification is the focal length of the objective divided by that of the eyepiece, which is why the objective must have a much longer focal length.

In the **Galilean telescope** the eyepiece is a diverging lens; the image is upright, but the field of view is small. Small opera glasses still work like this today. In the **Keplerian telescope** both lenses are converging lenses; the image is upside down, but you see more. For astronomy the upside-down image does not matter, and most astronomical refractors are Keplerian telescopes.

In 1608 the spectacle maker Hans Lipperhey in the Netherlands applied for a patent for a telescope. As early as 1609 **Galileo Galilei** in Italy built his own telescopes and pointed them at the sky. He saw craters on the Moon, the phases of Venus and, in 1610, four moons of Jupiter. In 1611 Johannes Kepler described the better design with two converging lenses.

A simple lens bends different colours by different amounts, which is why coloured fringes appear. This fault is called **chromatic aberration**. In the 18th century people learnt to reduce it with two different kinds of glass, which gives an achromatic lens. Large lenses also bend under their own weight, because they can only be held at the edge. That is why all large modern telescopes are reflecting telescopes.

The largest refractor in the world has stood at the **Yerkes Observatory** in the USA since 1897; its lens measures about one metre. The amount of light grows with the area of the lens: a lens 10 cm across collects four times as much light as one of 5 cm. In Switzerland you can look through a large historic refracting telescope at public observatories such as the Urania Observatory in Zurich. Small refractors are also very popular with amateur astronomers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The large front lens that collects the light.
The small lens through which you look into the telescope.
Distance from the lens to the point where the rays of light meet.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and brings light together.
A telescope that collects light with a concave mirror instead of a lens.

gewusst: The four large moons of Jupiter that Galileo discovered are still called the Galilean moons today.
You must never look at the Sun through a telescope without a special solar filter; it can blind you instantly.

teile.einleitung: A megaphone is a funnel-shaped device with which you make your voice louder and audible further away. In German it is jokingly also called a “Flüstertüte”, a whispering bag. There are simple megaphones without electricity and electric ones with a microphone and loudspeaker.
wichtigste: With a megaphone you make your voice louder.
A megaphone has the shape of a funnel.
In German it is jokingly called a “Flüstertüte”.
Fire brigades, police and mountain rescuers often use megaphones.
Electric megaphones need batteries.
A megaphone is especially loud above all towards the front.
You can form a simple megaphone with your hands round your mouth.

abschnitte.text: The word **megaphone** comes from Greek and means something like big voice. It is a funnel into whose narrow end you speak. The sound comes out of the wide end. That way many people can understand what is said, even at a great distance.

Without a megaphone the voice spreads out in all directions and quickly gets quieter. The **funnel** bundles the sound and directs it mainly forwards. In addition, the slowly widening shape lets the sound pass out into the air better. That is why it is much louder in front of the megaphone than beside or behind it.

Modern megaphones have a **microphone**, an amplifier and a loudspeaker. They need batteries or a rechargeable battery as their energy source. Many also have a siren or can play recordings. They are so loud that you should never hold them right at someone's ear.

The **fire brigade** and the police use megaphones to give instructions during operations. At sports events, demonstrations or school trips they help to reach a large group. Cheerleaders and coaches often use simple funnels without electricity. Umpires at sailing regattas or lifeguards also sometimes need a megaphone.

You can make a simple megaphone from a **rolled-up piece of card** that is wide at the front and narrow at the back. It is even easier with your hands: you hold them in a funnel shape round your mouth. Anyone who wants to call something to a friend in the mountains does this quite automatically. Try it out and compare how far away you can be heard with and without a funnel.

Funnels for making the voice louder were known centuries ago, for example on ships as a **speaking trumpet**. In the 17th century the Englishman Samuel Morland described a large speaking tube with which you could call over long distances. Later Thomas Edison also studied such funnels. Electric megaphones with an amplifier appeared in the 20th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: Vibrations of the air that we hear as tones and noises.
An object that is narrow at one end and wide at the other.
An electrical device that makes weak signals stronger.
A device that turns electrical signals into audible sound.

gewusst: A megaphone not only makes the voice louder but also changes its sound a little.
The ears of some animals also work like a reversed megaphone that catches sound.
Old gramophones had a large horn that worked on the same principle.

teile.einleitung: Optical density describes how strongly a transparent substance slows down and bends light. The optically denser a substance is, the more slowly light travels through it. That is why a stick in water looks bent and a swimming pool looks shallower than it really is.
wichtigste: Of two substances, the one with the higher refractive index is optically denser.
In the optically denser substance, light is slower than in the optically less dense one.
When light passes at an angle into an optically denser substance, it is bent towards the normal.
When light passes at an angle into an optically less dense substance, for example from glass into air, it is bent away from the normal.
Optical density and mass density are not the same: cooking oil floats on water but is optically denser.
Because of refraction, water looks shallower when seen from above.
