Mirages over hot roads appear because hot air is optically less dense than cooler air.

abschnitte.text: Optical density tells you how strongly a substance slows down light. It is measured with the **refractive index** n. This tells you how much slower light is in the substance than in empty space, where it travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second. Air has a refractive index of almost exactly 1, water about 1.33, ordinary glass about 1.5 and diamond about 2.4.

When light hits the boundary between two substances at an angle, it changes direction. This is called **refraction**. As a helping line, you draw the **normal**, a line at right angles to the boundary surface. If the light enters the optically denser substance, it bends towards the normal; in the optically less dense substance, it bends away from it. If the light hits exactly at right angles, it carries straight on without bending.

If you hold a stick at an angle in water, it seems to bend at the surface. The light from the stick is refracted as it leaves the water, and our brain traces the light rays back in a straight line. That is why we see the stick in the wrong place. For the same reason, a pool 2 metres deep looks only about 1.5 metres deep from above, because the apparent depth is roughly the real depth divided by 1.33. So take care when swimming in a lake, because the water is deeper than it looks.

Many children think that a heavy substance is also optically dense, but that is not true. Cooking oil has a lower **mass density** than water and so floats on top. But its refractive index is about 1.47, which is greater than that of water. You can tell whether a substance is optically denser from the speed of light: if light is slower in substance A, at 200,000 kilometres per second, than in substance B, then A is optically denser.

Air can also have different optical densities, because warm air is optically slightly less dense than cold air. Over a hot road, light from the sky is therefore bent upwards, and it looks as if there were a puddle of water on the tarmac. This is called a **mirage**, or Fata Morgana. If light leaves an optically denser substance at a very shallow angle, it cannot get out at all and is completely reflected back. This **total internal reflection** is used in fibre-optic cables for the internet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that tells you how strongly a substance slows down and bends light.
An imaginary line at right angles to a boundary surface.
The change of direction of light when it passes from one substance into another.
Light is completely reflected at a boundary instead of passing out.
An apparent reflection caused by layers of air at different temperatures.

gewusst: Diamonds sparkle so much because their high refractive index makes light bounce back and forth inside them many times.
From under water, fish see the whole world above the lake through a circular window at the surface.
The Earth's atmosphere also bends light, which is why we can still see the Sun at sunset even though it is already just below the horizon.

teile.einleitung: A p-n junction is the boundary between two differently prepared regions of a semiconductor, for example made of silicon. It lets electric current through almost only in one direction. This makes it the heart of diodes, light-emitting diodes, solar cells and transistors in every mobile phone and computer.
wichtigste: A p-n junction forms where a p-doped and an n-doped semiconductor region meet.
At the boundary, a depletion region forms with hardly any free charge carriers.
The fixed ions at the boundary create the built-in voltage.
In the forward direction (positive terminal to p, negative terminal to n), the junction conducts.
In the reverse direction, the depletion region gets wider and only a tiny reverse current flows.
Above a threshold voltage, about 0.7 volts for silicon, the current in the forward direction rises sharply.
Diodes, LEDs, solar cells and varactor diodes are based on the p-n junction.

abschnitte.text: Pure **silicon** conducts electricity only poorly. Deliberately adding tiny amounts of foreign atoms to it is called **doping**. With phosphorus, you get an n-region with extra mobile electrons, that is negative charge carriers. With boron, you get a p-region with “holes”: missing electrons that behave like positive charges.

If you join a p-region and an n-region, electrons move across the boundary into the p-region because of the difference in concentration. This process is called **diffusion**. There they fill holes, and fixed, charged atoms are left behind on both sides. This creates a thin layer with almost no free charge carriers, the **depletion region**. The charges in it create the built-in voltage, which slows down any further movement.

If you connect the positive terminal to the p-region and the negative terminal to the n-region, the barrier layer is broken down and current flows. This is the **forward direction**. If you connect it the other way round, the depletion region gets wider and the junction blocks. Only a very small **reverse current** of minority carriers still flows. The characteristic curve shows that in the forward direction almost nothing flows until the threshold is reached, after which the current rises steeply.

The simplest use is the **diode**, a kind of one-way street for current, which rectifies alternating current in chargers, for example. In a light-emitting diode (LED), the electrons give off light as they cross. A solar cell does the opposite: light hits the junction and produces current. The varactor diode uses the fact that the width of the blocking zone, and so its capacitance, changes with the voltage, for example in radio receivers.

The American researcher Russell Ohl discovered the p-n junction in 1940 rather by chance on a silicon crystal. Shortly afterwards, William Shockley explained exactly what happens. Two p-n junctions one after the other led to the **transistor**, for which Shockley and colleagues received the Nobel Prize in 1956. Today a single computer chip contains billions of such junctions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that sometimes conducts electricity well and sometimes badly, for example silicon.
Deliberately adding foreign atoms to change conductivity.
The boundary layer in a p-n junction where there are hardly any mobile charges.
A component that lets current through in one direction only.
A missing electron that moves like a positive charge.

gewusst: The colour of an LED depends on which semiconductor material its p-n junction is made of.
A solar panel on a Swiss roof is basically a huge, flat p-n junction.
The depletion region is often thinner than a thousandth of a millimetre.

teile.einleitung: Magnetic declination is the angle between the direction a compass needle points and the direction to the geographic North Pole. It exists because the magnetic North Pole is not in the same place as the geographic one. Another name for it is magnetic variation.
wichtigste: Magnetic declination is the angle between magnetic north and geographic north.
Another technical term for it is variation.
It changes over the years, because the Earth's magnetic poles move.
In Switzerland it is only a few degrees today.
Lines of equal declination on a map are called isogonic lines.
Sailors and pilots have to take it into account carefully when navigating.
Close to a magnetic pole, the declination can become very large.

abschnitte.text: A **compass needle** is a small magnet and lines itself up with the Earth's magnetic field. So it points to the magnetic North Pole, not exactly to the geographic North Pole around which the Earth turns. The angle between these two directions is called **magnetic declination** or variation. If the needle points east of geographic north, it is called easterly declination, otherwise westerly.

The Earth's magnetic field is created by currents of liquid iron deep inside the Earth. These currents change slowly, so the magnetic North Pole moves. For a long time it was in northern Canada, and for decades it has been moving towards Siberia. That is why the declination is different in every place and changes over time.

In Switzerland today, the compass needle points only a few degrees east of geographic north. For a hike with map and compass, this error is usually small. On accurate national maps, the declination is given at the edge of the map. About a hundred years ago, it was still westerly in Switzerland and clearly larger.

Lines connecting places with the same declination are called **isogonic lines**. The line on which the declination is zero is called the agonic line. Worldwide maps of declination are recalculated regularly because the magnetic field changes. Navigation devices and mobile phones use such models to work out true north from the compass direction.

Sailors and pilots must know the declination precisely, or they would drift far off course on long journeys. In addition, iron parts and electrical devices in the ship or aircraft deflect the needle. This deflection is called **deviation**. Both errors are added together when the course is calculated.

The closer you get to a magnetic pole, the larger the declination can become. In the Arctic, a compass needle can even point almost south or west. Right at the magnetic pole, the needle points steeply down into the ground. There, an ordinary compass is hardly usable for navigation.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another technical word for magnetic declination.
A line on a map connecting places with the same declination.
Deflection of the compass needle by iron or devices in the vehicle.
The place in the north that compass needles point to.

gewusst: At times the magnetic North Pole has moved several dozen kilometres a year.
Centuries ago, sailors already noticed that the compass does not point exactly north.
Runway numbers at airports are based on the magnetic direction and therefore sometimes have to be changed.

teile.einleitung: Instantaneous speed is the speed an object has at one particular moment. This is exactly the number that the speedometer in a car shows. It is often different from the average speed that you calculate for a whole journey.
wichtigste: Instantaneous speed is the speed at a particular moment.
A car's speedometer shows the instantaneous speed.
You measure it by dividing a very short distance by a very short time.
On a distance-time graph, it is the gradient of the curve at one point.
In uniform motion, it is always equal to the average speed.
A ball thrown upwards has an instantaneous speed of zero at its highest point.
A pendulum is fastest at its lowest point.

abschnitte.text: If a car travels 60 kilometres in 1 hour, its **average speed** is 60 km/h. But on the way it was sometimes faster, sometimes slower, and it stood still at traffic lights. The speed at a single moment is called the **instantaneous speed**. The speedometer shows it all the time.

You measure the distance an object travels in a very short time and divide it by that time. The shorter the time span, the more precisely you get the speed at that moment. An example: a car covers a 4-metre measuring section in 0.2 seconds, which is 20 m/s or 72 km/h. Some speed checks work this way too, with **light barriers** or sensors in the road.

On a distance-time graph, you record how far an object has travelled at each point in time. If the curve is steep, the object is fast; if it is flat, it is slow. You can see the instantaneous speed from the **gradient** of the curve at a particular point. In maths this is called the derivative, which Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed in the 17th century.

Without air resistance, a falling stone becomes about 9.8 m/s faster every second. After 3 seconds, its instantaneous speed is 29.4 m/s, which is over 100 km/h. If you throw a ball straight up, it gets slower and slower. At its highest point, its instantaneous speed is exactly **zero** for a moment, and then it falls back down.

On a pendulum or a swing, the speed changes all the time. At the turning points right at the edges, it is briefly zero. At the lowest point, the instantaneous speed is greatest, because there most of the potential energy has been turned into kinetic energy. You can feel this on any swing as a brief tingle in your tummy.

On the road, it is always the instantaneous speed that counts, for example at a **speed camera**. Anyone caught doing 70 km/h in town cannot argue that they were only driving at 50 km/h on average. When skiing, cycling or in space travel, the speed at the moment is also important. Sports watches and mobile phones work it out, for example, with the help of GPS.

begriffe.erklaerung: Total distance divided by total time.
A display in a vehicle that shows the current speed.
Movement at an unchanging speed in the same direction.
How steeply a curve on a graph rises at one point.

gewusst: When a ball briefly stops at its highest point, gravity is still acting on it.
A speedometer usually shows a little more than you are actually doing, because it must never show too little.
A cheetah can run at over 90 km/h for a short moment, but can only keep up this speed for a few seconds.

teile.einleitung: A run-of-river power station is a hydroelectric power station on a river that uses the water constantly flowing past to produce electricity. It holds back the river only a little and therefore has a small head, but a very large amount of water. In Switzerland such power stations supply electricity reliably day and night.
wichtigste: A run-of-river power station uses the water of a river.
The head is typically small, but a lot of water flows through the turbines.
A weir holds back the river a little.
Turbines and generators are in the machine house.
Electricity is produced around the clock.
Because it has hardly any storage, a run-of-river power station can hardly shift its production.
In Switzerland run-of-river power stations supply most electricity in summer, when the snow melts.

abschnitte.text: A **run-of-river power station**, also called a river power station, stands across a river. It uses the water that flows downstream anyway. Unlike a **storage power station** in the mountains, it has no large reservoir. The head is usually only a few metres, but hundreds of cubic metres of water often flow through the plant every second.

A **weir** holds back the river a little, so that the water level above it is higher. The water flows through the **machine house** and drives large turbines there, often so-called Kaplan turbines with adjustable blades like a ship's propeller. The turbines turn generators, which convert kinetic energy into electrical energy. Then the water flows on downstream unchanged.

Because the river flows all the time, a run-of-river power station produces electricity day and night. This is called **baseload power**, a steady basic supply. But it can hardly store the water and has to use whatever arrives. In Switzerland these power stations supply most in summer, when snow and glaciers melt and the rivers carry a lot of water. In winter the rivers carry less water, and production falls.

Hydropower is Switzerland's most important source of electricity, and about half of it comes from run-of-river power stations. Many stand on the Aare, Reuss, Limmat, Rhône and the **High Rhine**, where the Rhine forms the border with Germany. Well-known examples are the Rheinfelden, Laufenburg and Eglisau power stations. The old Rheinfelden power station started up in 1898 and was one of the first large river power stations in Europe.

Run-of-river power stations produce electricity without exhaust gases and are regarded as renewable. However, they interrupt the river, and fish can no longer migrate freely. That is why **fish ladders** or near-natural bypass channels are built, so that salmon, grayling and other fish can get past the plant. In addition, power stations have to pass on sediment such as gravel so that the river below does not become impoverished.

begriffe.erklaerung: A barrier in a river that holds back the water a little.
A wheel with blades that is turned by the water.
A machine that turns a rotating movement into electricity.
The difference in height that the water falls through in the power station.
A staircase of small pools that fish use to swim round a power station.

gewusst: As early as the Middle Ages, water mills on Swiss streams and rivers used the same idea to grind grain.
Because the High Rhine forms the border, many power stations there are run jointly by Swiss and German companies, and the electricity is shared.

teile.einleitung: In magnet fishing you catch things made of iron with a magnet on a string. As a children's game you fish colourful fish out of a tank; as a hobby people pull real metal objects out of rivers. Along the way you learn in a playful way how magnets work.
wichtigste: In the magnetic fishing game a magnet hangs on a string.
The string is fixed to a stick, as on a real fishing rod.
Inside the fish there is something made of iron, such as a paper clip or a screw.
A paper fish without metal does not stick to the magnet.
If there is a magnet in the fish, like poles can repel each other.
Lighter fish are easier to catch.
In magnet fishing people often pull old metal objects out of waters.

abschnitte.text: Magnetic fishing is a popular game for children. You have a small **stick** with a string and a magnet hanging from it. With it you try to fish fish made of cardboard, wood or plastic out of a pond or a box. Whoever catches the most fish wins, and you practise skill and patience along the way.

A magnet mainly attracts objects made of **iron**, nickel or cobalt. That is why there is a paper clip, a screw or a metal ring in the fish. So a wooden fish with an iron screw in its head can be caught, but a paper fish without metal cannot. Aluminium, copper and most coins are hardly attracted either.

Some games have small magnets in the fish themselves. If two like **poles** meet, that is north to north or south to south, they repel each other. The fish is then pushed away instead of sticking. If you turn the fish round, the unlike poles attract each other again.

The pulling force of a magnet is limited. If two fish have the same paper clip, the **lighter** fish is easier to pull up. The closer the magnet is to the iron, the more strongly it pulls. Even a thin piece of paper in between can noticeably weaken the force.

Adults do **magnet fishing** with very strong neodymium magnets on a rope. They throw the magnet into rivers, lakes or canals and pull out nails, bicycle parts, keys or tools. In the process rubbish is also removed from the water. Because dangerous finds such as old ammunition sometimes turn up and a permit is needed in some places, you should find out properly beforehand.

begriffe.erklaerung: An object that attracts iron and has two poles.
One of the two ends of a magnet, where it is especially strong.
The name for substances such as iron, nickel and cobalt that are attracted by a magnet.
An especially strong permanent magnet made of a mixture containing the metal neodymium.

gewusst: A strong neodymium magnet can hold many times its own weight.
Most coins are hardly attracted by magnets, because they consist mainly of copper and nickel alloys.
Magnets even work through water, which is why magnetic fishing also works in a real paddling pool.

teile.einleitung: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and is known as the Red Planet because of its rusty red colour. It is smaller and lighter than the Earth, which is why gravity there is much weaker too. No other planet has been visited so often by space probes and robots.
wichtigste: Mars is the fourth planet in the solar system.
Its diameter is about half that of the Earth.
It has about a tenth of the Earth's mass.
Gravity on Mars is a little more than a third of the Earth's gravity.
The gravitational field strength on Mars is about 3.7 N/kg.
Gravity on Mars is a good twice as strong as on the Moon.
Mars has two small moons called Phobos and Deimos.

abschnitte.text: Mars is named after the Roman god of war. Its red colour comes from **iron oxide**, that is rust, in the dust and rock of its surface. With a diameter of around 6800 km it is about half the size of the Earth. But it has only about a tenth of its mass.

On Mars the **gravitational field strength** is about 3.7 N/kg, on Earth about 9.8 N/kg. So a person of 50 kg has a weight of 185 N there, a rover of 1000 kg one of 3700 N. A bathroom scale that shows 30 kg on Earth would show only about 11 kg on Mars. The **mass** stays the same, though; only the weight changes.

Because gravity is only a little more than a third as strong, an astronaut on Mars could jump about two and a half times as high with the same take-off. Compared with the Moon, however, gravity on Mars is a good twice as strong. For future space travellers, walking would therefore be easier than on Earth, but not as bouncy as on the Moon. At about **24 hours and 37 minutes**, a day on Mars lasts almost as long as a day on Earth.

On Mars stands **Olympus Mons**, one of the highest volcanoes in the solar system, more than twice as high as Mount Everest. The huge canyon system Valles Marineris is thousands of kilometres long. The atmosphere is very thin and consists mainly of carbon dioxide. On average it is icy cold at about minus 60 degrees Celsius, and there are caps of ice at the poles.

Since the 1960s space agencies have been sending probes to Mars. The NASA rovers **Curiosity** (landed 2012) and **Perseverance** (landed 2021) look for traces of past water and life. Perseverance even brought along the small helicopter Ingenuity, which was the first aircraft to fly on another planet. The University of Bern is also involved: its camera CaSSIS photographs Mars from orbit.

A year on Mars lasts about 687 Earth days, that is almost two Earth years. Mars has seasons because its axis is tilted similarly to the Earth's. Its two moons **Phobos** and **Deimos** are small and irregularly shaped. From Mars the Earth would shine in the sky like a bright blue star.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tells you how strongly a celestial body pulls on every kilogram, on Mars about 3.7 N/kg.
The force with which a body is attracted by a planet.
The amount of matter in a body; it is the same everywhere.
A remote-controlled vehicle that explores the surface of a celestial body.

gewusst: On Mars there are dust storms that sometimes cover almost the whole planet.
Sunset on Mars looks bluish, the opposite of on Earth.
Meteorites have been found on Earth that have been proven to come from Mars.

teile.einleitung: The ohm is the unit of electrical resistance. It tells you how strongly a component or a wire slows down the electric current. Its symbol is the Greek letter omega, Ω, and it is named after the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm.
wichtigste: The ohm is the unit of electrical resistance.
Its symbol is the Greek letter omega, Ω.
It is named after the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm.
If exactly 1 ampere flows at 1 volt, the resistance is 1 Ω.
4.7 kilohms are 4700 Ω, 2 megohms are 2,000,000 Ω.
Resistance can be measured with a multimeter.
Coloured bands on small resistors show their value in ohms.

abschnitte.text: **Georg Simon Ohm** lived from 1789 to 1854 and came from Erlangen in Germany. For a long time he was a teacher of maths and physics and experimented with wires and electricity on the side. In 1826 and 1827 he published the law named after him, **Ohm's law**. At first his work was hardly noticed; later he became a professor in Munich.

When current flows through a wire, the electrons keep bumping into the atoms of the material and are slowed down. This braking effect is called **electrical resistance**. Copper has a low resistance and is good for cables. Rubber and plastic have an enormous resistance and are used as insulators.

Ohm's law links voltage, current and resistance: resistance equals voltage divided by current, in short R = U / I. A component through which exactly 1 ampere flows at 1 volt has a resistance of **1 ohm**. If only 1 ampere flows at 10 volts, it is 10 ohms. The greater the resistance, the smaller the current at the same voltage.

In electronics, large values are often needed, so there are multiples. A **kilohm** is 1000 Ω, so 4.7 kΩ is 4700 Ω. A megohm is a million ohms, so 2 MΩ is 2,000,000 Ω. Very small resistances, for example of thick cables, are given in milliohms.

Small components with a fixed resistance value are simply called **resistors**. They limit, for example, the current through a light-emitting diode so that it does not burn out. Their value is marked on them with coloured bands, the so-called colour code. Each colour stands for a digit, for example black for 0, brown for 1 and red for 2.

With a **multimeter** you can measure voltage, current and resistance. To measure resistance, you set the device to Ω and hold the two probe tips to the ends of the component. The device sends a small current through it and works out the resistance. This also lets you find out whether a cable is broken.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly a material or component slows down the current.
The rule that resistance equals voltage divided by current.
A measuring device for voltage, current and resistance.
A material that hardly conducts electricity at all.

gewusst: At very low temperatures, superconductors have no electrical resistance at all.
The human body also has an electrical resistance, which is much lower when the skin is wet than when it is dry.
The reciprocal of resistance is called conductance, and its unit used to be jokingly called the “mho”, ohm backwards.

teile.einleitung: A cooling fin is a thin metal plate or strip that increases the surface area of a component so that it can get rid of its heat better. Many fins together form a heat sink. You find them on computer processors, motorbike engines and old radiators.
wichtigste: Cooling fins increase the surface area so that more heat is given off.
Heat sinks are often made of aluminium, because it is light and conducts heat well.
Typical cooling fins are found on a computer's processor.
Thermal paste between the processor and the heat sink improves the transfer of heat.
A fan blows the warmed air away from between the fins.
Dusty cooling fins cool less well.
Without a fan, cooling fins should stand upright so that warm air can rise.

abschnitte.text: Many devices produce **heat** while working, and it has to be carried away. Cooling fins are thin metal plates or pins arranged side by side. They greatly increase the **surface area** without taking up much space. The larger the area in contact with the air, the more heat can be given off.

First the heat travels by **conduction** from the hot component into the metal of the fins. There the metal passes it on to the air flowing past. The warmed air rises and cooler air flows in; this is called **convection**. That is why, without a fan, cooling fins should stand upright, so that the warm air can rise freely.

A computer's **processor** gets very hot while calculating. On top of it sits a heat sink made of aluminium or copper with many thin fins. Between them goes **thermal paste**, which fills tiny air gaps, because air conducts heat poorly. A fan blows the warmed air away. If dust builds up between the fins, the heat sink cools less well and the computer becomes noisy or slow.

Air-cooled motorbike engines have clearly visible cooling fins on the outside of the cylinder. Radiators in flats often have fins too, only there they are meant to give heat to the room. On the back of many older fridges there is a grille that gives off the heat from inside to the kitchen. Powerful amplifiers and LED lamps also have cooling fins.

Animals also use the principle of a large surface area. The **African elephant** has huge ears with a good blood supply. When it flaps them, the blood in them gives off heat to the air. Some dinosaurs such as Stegosaurus had large plates on their backs, which, according to one theory, may also have helped to control their temperature.

begriffe.erklaerung: Metal part with many fins that carries heat away from a component.
Passing on of heat within a material.
Paste that fills air gaps so that heat passes across better.
Computing chip, the brain of the computer.

gewusst: Copper conducts heat even better than aluminium, but it is heavier and more expensive.
The fennec, a desert fox, has particularly large ears for the size of its head, which help it cool down.
Some high-performance computers are cooled with water instead of air, because water can take up much more heat.

teile.einleitung: A laser is a device that produces a particularly narrow, single-coloured and very even beam of light. Today lasers are found in barcode scanners, fibre optic cables, eye operations and machine tools. They are based on an idea that Albert Einstein had as early as 1917.
wichtigste: Laser stands for “Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation”.
It is based on stimulated emission, which Albert Einstein described in theory in 1917.
In the active medium there must be a population inversion for light to be amplified.
A resonator, usually made of two mirrors, sends the light through the active medium many times.
Laser light is coherent and almost single-coloured.
The first working laser was built in 1960 by Theodore Maiman.
The forerunner of the laser, which amplifies microwaves, is called a maser.

abschnitte.text: The word **laser** is an abbreviation from English: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Unlike a light bulb, which gives off light in all directions and in many colours, a laser produces a narrow beam of almost only one colour. The light waves vibrate in step; we say the light is **coherent**. That is why laser light can be focused very tightly and sent over great distances.

Inside is an **active medium**, for example a gas, a crystal or a semiconductor. By supplying energy, known as pumping, more atoms are brought into an excited state than are in the ground state; this is the **population inversion**. When a particle of light then hits an excited atom, it triggers a second, identical particle of light; this is stimulated emission. Two mirrors, the **resonator**, send the light back and forth so that it is amplified like an avalanche. One of the mirrors lets a little light through: that is the laser beam.

Albert Einstein described stimulated emission in theory in 1917. In 1954 Charles Townes in the USA built the **maser**, which amplifies microwaves on the same principle. On 16 May 1960 Theodore Maiman made the first laser shine with a ruby crystal. In 1964 Townes received the Nobel Prize in Physics together with the Soviet researchers Nikolay Basov and Alexander Prokhorov.

There are a great many types of laser. The classic **helium-neon laser** shines red at a wavelength of 632.8 nanometres. Green laser pointers work at 532 nanometres, and one photon of this light carries about 2.33 electronvolts of energy. The most common today are tiny **laser diodes** made of semiconductors, found for example in Blu-ray players and fibre optic networks. Powerful carbon dioxide lasers can even cut sheet steel.

At the supermarket checkout a laser reads the barcode. In medicine eye doctors correct sight problems with laser light, and skin doctors use it to remove tattoos. Surveyors measure distances to within a millimetre with lasers. Lasers carry internet data through optical fibres.

Laser light can damage the retina in a fraction of a second, because it is so tightly focused. That is why lasers are divided into **laser classes**, from harmless to very dangerous. In Switzerland strong laser pointers have been banned since 2019. You must never point a laser at people, animals, cars or aircraft.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle of light makes an excited atom send out an identical particle of light.
All the light waves vibrate in step.
Two mirrors between which the light travels back and forth and is amplified.
More atoms are excited than not excited, which is needed for amplification.
Distance between two wave crests; it decides the colour of the light.

gewusst: Astronauts on the Apollo missions placed mirrors on the Moon, and researchers still use laser beams to measure the distance to the Moon to within a few centimetres.
When the laser was invented in 1960, it was jokingly called “a solution looking for a problem”, because nobody yet knew what it could be used for.

teile.einleitung: Food energy is the energy contained in what we eat and drink. Our body needs it to grow, move and think, and even while sleeping to breathe and keep warm. Food packaging shows how much energy a product contains, usually in kilocalories and kilojoules.
wichtigste: The body needs energy for everything it does, even during sleep.
On packaging, energy is given in kilocalories and kilojoules.
Carbohydrates, fats and proteins provide energy.
Fat contains more than twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates.
Nuts are particularly rich in energy.
Pure water contains no energy at all.
People who move a lot need more energy from their food.

abschnitte.text: Plants store the energy of sunlight in sugar and starch. When we eat plants or animals, our body takes in this stored energy. In the cells, it is released slowly with the help of oxygen, a bit like a very gentle burning. This is how muscles, brain and heart get the energy they need.

Energy is provided by three groups of nutrients. **Carbohydrates** are found in bread, pasta, rice and potatoes and give the body energy for everyday life. **Fats** in butter, oil and nuts provide about 9 kilocalories per gram, more than twice as much as carbohydrates or proteins with about 4 kilocalories. Water, vitamins and minerals are important but provide no energy.

On food packaging, the **nutrition table** shows how much energy there is in 100 grams. It is given in kilocalories, abbreviated kcal, and in kilojoules, abbreviated kJ. One kilocalorie is about 4.2 kilojoules. 100 grams of nuts often have over 600 kilocalories, 100 grams of apples only about 50.

abschnitte.titel: What the body needs energy for
abschnitte.text: Even when we sleep, the body needs energy for breathing, heartbeat and **body heat**; this is called the basal metabolic rate. On top of that comes energy for movement, sport and thinking, because the brain uses a lot of energy. Children also need extra energy to grow. A child playing football needs more energy than one sitting still.

Sweets give energy quickly but harm your teeth in large amounts and do not keep you full for long. Wholemeal bread, potatoes, vegetables and pulses release their energy more slowly and keep you full for longer. If you go a long time without eating, you feel tired and weak and find it hard to concentrate. The Swiss **food pyramid** shows how to eat a varied and balanced diet.

If you eat more energy than you use over a long time, the body stores it as fat. If you eat too little, you lack the strength to grow and learn. The best thing is a balance between eating and exercise. How much energy you need depends on your age, size and how much you move.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit for the energy in food, abbreviated kcal.
The physical unit of energy, abbreviated kJ.
The energy the body needs when completely at rest.
Nutrients such as sugar and starch that provide energy quickly.
The table on the packet showing energy and nutrients.

gewusst: The brain makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight but uses around 20 per cent of the energy at rest.
You can measure the energy content of a food by burning it completely in a calorimeter and measuring the heat produced.
The body also uses extra energy when you are cold, because the shivering of the muscles produces heat.

teile.einleitung: Air resistance is the force that slows down an object when it moves through the air. You feel it as a headwind when you ride your bike fast, even when there is no wind outside. The faster you go, the stronger it becomes.
wichtigste: Air resistance slows down everything that moves through the air.
It gets bigger the faster you move.
A large surface facing the wind also increases air resistance.
Streamlined shapes have little air resistance.
Parachutes use air resistance to land slowly.
Without air resistance a feather and a stone would fall equally fast.

abschnitte.text: Air consists of tiny particles. When you move, you have to push these particles aside. You feel this as **resistance**, as if wind were blowing against you. This braking force is called **air resistance**.

Air resistance depends above all on **speed**. If you ride twice as fast, it becomes about four times as big. The **frontal area** also matters, that is, how much surface you hold up against the wind. Finally the shape plays a part: a drop glides through the air better than a flat board.

Engineers test cars, trains and aircraft in a **wind tunnel**. There they measure how strongly the air slows them down. A **streamlined** shape saves energy and fuel. That is why high-speed trains have a long, pointed nose.

Sometimes air resistance is very welcome. A **parachute** has a large surface and slows the fall down strongly. Birds and paragliders also use the air to float. Dandelion seeds fly far on the wind thanks to their little umbrellas.

In sport people usually want to keep air resistance small. Ski racers go into a **crouch** so that they present less surface. Racing cyclists ride close behind one another in a group; in the slipstream you save a lot of strength. Tight-fitting racing suits also help you to be faster.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that slows down a movement.
A smooth, drop-like shape that air flows past easily.
A facility in which people test how air flows past an object.
The sheltered area behind a body where less wind blows.

gewusst: A skydiver without an open parachute reaches about 200 kilometres per hour and does not get faster because of air resistance.
There is no air on the Moon, which is why in an experiment on the Apollo 15 mission a hammer and a feather fell equally fast there.
On the motorway a car uses most of its energy to overcome air resistance.

teile.einleitung: The mass defect means that an atomic nucleus is slightly lighter than all its building blocks put together. The missing mass is hidden in the nucleus as binding energy. This puzzle explains why the Sun shines and why nuclear power stations supply energy.
wichtigste: An atomic nucleus is lighter than the sum of its individual protons and neutrons.
According to Einstein the missing mass corresponds to the binding energy, E = m · c².
One atomic mass unit corresponds to about 931.5 MeV.
The atomic mass unit u is a twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
In nuclear physics masses are often given in MeV/c².
The neutron is slightly heavier than the proton.
Through nuclear fusion the Sun loses around 4 million tonnes of mass every second.

abschnitte.text: An atomic nucleus consists of **nucleons**, that is protons and neutrons. If you weigh the finished nucleus very precisely, it is slightly lighter than all the nucleons on their own put together. This difference is called the **mass defect**. In the helium nucleus made of two protons and two neutrons, for example, just under 1 per cent of the mass is missing.

In 1905 Albert Einstein showed that mass and energy belong together: **E = m · c²**. Because the speed of light c is huge, even a tiny mass contains a great deal of energy. A mass defect of 1.0 · 10⁻²⁹ kg corresponds to about 9.0 · 10⁻¹³ joules. So the missing mass has not disappeared; it was given off as energy when the nucleus was built.

Because atoms are so light, the **atomic mass unit** u is used. It is defined as a twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. One mass unit corresponds to an energy of around 931.5 MeV, which is why masses are often given directly in MeV/c². A proton has about 938.3 MeV/c²; at about 939.6 MeV/c² the neutron is a little heavier.

In the Sun hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium; this is called **nuclear fusion**. The resulting helium nucleus is lighter than the four protons it is formed from. The difference is radiated as energy and reaches us as light and heat. In this way the Sun loses around 4 million tonnes of mass every second.

Energy is also released in the **nuclear fission** of heavy nuclei such as uranium. The fission products together are lighter than the uranium nucleus and the neutron that split it. Nuclear power stations use this energy, in Switzerland for example Gösgen, Leibstadt and Beznau. The nuclei around iron and nickel are the most strongly bound, which is why light nuclei release energy when they fuse and heavy ones when they split.

begriffe.erklaerung: A building block of the atomic nucleus, that is a proton or a neutron.
The energy that would be needed to break a nucleus down into its building blocks.
A very small unit of mass for atoms, abbreviated u.
The fusing of light atomic nuclei into heavier ones.

gewusst: Although the Sun loses millions of tonnes per second, in its whole life so far it has lost only a tiny fraction of its mass.
There is also a mass defect in a chemical reaction such as a fire, but it is far too small to weigh.
In France, not far from Switzerland, the major project ITER is researching how nuclear fusion can be used on Earth.

teile.einleitung: Mechanics is the oldest branch of physics. It describes how bodies move and which forces act as they do. Falling apples, rolling cars, levers and the orbits of planets all belong to mechanics.
wichtigste: Mechanics describes motion and forces.
Important quantities are distance, time, velocity, acceleration, force and energy.
In free fall without air resistance a body falls around 44.1 metres in 3 seconds.
Kinetic energy is calculated as one half times mass times velocity squared.
Power is work per unit of time.
For a lever: effort times effort arm equals load times load arm.
Without air resistance a throw at 45 degrees goes furthest.

abschnitte.text: **Mechanics** is the study of motion and forces. It is divided into **kinematics**, which describes motion, and dynamics, which asks about the causes. Modern mechanics was founded by Galileo Galilei and Isaac Newton in the 17th century. Newton published his famous laws of motion in 1687.

Without air resistance all bodies fall equally fast. The distance in **free fall** is calculated with s = ½ · g · t². In the first 3 seconds a body thus falls around 44.1 metres. In an oblique throw without air resistance the greatest distance is reached at a **launch angle** of 45 degrees.

Lifting 50 kilograms by 10 metres takes **work against gravity** of 4905 joules. A car of 1000 kilograms at 72 km/h, that is 20 m/s, has a **kinetic energy** of 200 kilojoules. Energy is never lost; it is only converted. If a motor does 6000 joules of work in 30 seconds, its average power is 200 watts.

A **lever** helps to move large loads with a small force. The **law of the lever** applies: effort times effort arm equals load times load arm. If a load of 300 N hangs on an arm of 0.5 m, 100 N on an effort arm 1.5 m long is enough. Seesaws, pliers, wheelbarrows and bottle openers use this principle.

When a car drives round a bend, it needs a force towards the centre of the bend. This is called the **centripetal force** and is calculated with F = m · v² : r. A car of 800 kg at 10 m/s in a bend with a radius of 50 m needs 1600 N. The tyres supply this force through friction on the road.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of mechanics that describes motion.
The energy a body has because of its motion.
Effort times effort arm equals load times load arm.
The force that keeps a body on a circular path.

gewusst: The Greek scientist Archimedes is said to have claimed he could move the Earth with a long lever.
Galileo Galilei studied falling motion with balls on inclined planes.
The formulas of mechanics are enough to send space probes precisely to other planets.

teile.einleitung: A microscope is a device with which you can look at tiny things greatly magnified. With it you can see cells, bacteria or the fine hairs on an insect's leg, which are invisible to the naked eye. The word comes from Greek and means something like “looking at small things”.
wichtigste: A microscope makes very small objects visible in large size.
In a light microscope two lens systems magnify, the objective and the eyepiece.
The total magnification is the objective magnification times the eyepiece magnification, for example 40 times 10 equals 400 times.
The specimen lies on a slide and must be very thin so that light shines through it.
A light microscope can only separate two points if they are about 0.2 micrometres apart.
In the 17th century Antoni van Leeuwenhoek was the first to see bacteria.
Electron microscopes reach much greater magnifications than light microscopes.

abschnitte.titel: How a light microscope is built
abschnitte.text: A school microscope consists of a foot, a stand, a stage and a tube. At the top you look through the **eyepiece**; at the bottom, close to the specimen, sits the **objective**. Usually several objectives are fitted on a turning nosepiece, for example with 4, 10 and 40 times magnification. With the coarse and fine focus knobs you make the image sharp.

In an ordinary school microscope the light comes from below, from a lamp or via a mirror. It shines through the specimen and then through the lenses into the eye. That is why a specimen must be wafer-thin, for example a thin skin from an onion. The objective produces a magnified intermediate image, which the eyepiece magnifies again like a magnifying glass.

You put the piece to be examined on a glass **slide**, often with a drop of water. A very thin **cover slip** goes on top so that the specimen lies flat. Some specimens are stained with dyes so that the cell nucleus or cell wall can be seen better. In this way you can examine onion cells, the lining of the mouth or pond water at school.

The first microscopes with several lenses were made around 1600 in the Netherlands. In 1665 the Englishman **Robert Hooke** looked at cork and called the small chambers he saw “cells”. The Dutch cloth merchant **Antoni van Leeuwenhoek** built tiny microscopes with only one lens and used them to discover bacteria and other tiny living things. These discoveries fundamentally changed biology and medicine.

A **stereo microscope** has two separate light paths and therefore shows a three-dimensional image, ideal for insects, stones or parts of plants. The electron microscope uses electrons instead of light and was developed from 1931 by Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll. With it you can even see viruses. In Rüschlikon near Zurich, Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at IBM invented the **scanning tunnelling microscope**, which makes individual atoms visible, and received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1986.

In hospitals and laboratories microscopes are used to examine blood, tissue and pathogens. Researchers in biology use them to watch how cells live and divide. In technology the finest structures on computer chips are checked with them. Forensic scientists also compare fibres, hairs or marks on bullets under the microscope.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lens at the bottom, close to the specimen, that produces the first magnified image.
The lens at the top that you look into and that magnifies the image again.
A small glass plate on which the specimen is placed.
The prepared piece to be examined, for example a thin skin from a plant.
How finely a microscope can still show two close points separately.

gewusst: Leeuwenhoek's microscopes were hardly bigger than a postage stamp and had only a single tiny lens.
A light microscope cannot magnify as much as you like, because the wavelength of light sets a limit.
The scanning tunnelling microscope, with which you can see atoms, was invented in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Light is what lets us see. Without light it would be completely dark and we could not make out anything at all. The most important source of light for the Earth is the Sun.
wichtigste: Without light you cannot see anything.
The Sun is the most important source of light for the Earth.
Light travels in straight lines if nothing is in the way.
Light is much faster than sound.
The Moon does not shine by itself; it reflects sunlight.
A mirror reflects almost all of the light.
White light is made up of all the colours of the rainbow.

abschnitte.text: We see something when light from an object enters our **eye**. That is why in a completely dark room you see nothing at all, because there is no light. Most things do not shine by themselves. They are lit up and reflect part of the light.

Objects that give out light themselves are called **light sources**. The most important one is the **Sun**; without it there would be no life on Earth. Other sources of light are candles, lamps, lightning and glow-worms. The Moon is not a source of light, because it only reflects sunlight.

Light travels straight on as long as nothing is in the way. That is why **shadows** form behind objects. Light is incredibly fast: it covers almost 300,000 kilometres in one second. That is why in a thunderstorm you see the lightning before you hear the thunder, because sound is much slower.

A **mirror** reflects almost all of the light, which is why you can see yourself in it. Light surfaces such as snow reflect a lot of light, while dark surfaces absorb it. Glass and water let light through but bend it. A **magnifying glass** uses this to make a small ant look much bigger.

White sunlight is made up of many **colours**. A rainbow forms when sunlight is split up in raindrops. You then see red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet. A red bike looks red because it reflects mainly red light.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that gives out light itself, such as the Sun or a lamp.
A dark area behind an object where no light reaches.
When light is thrown back by a surface.
The speed of light, almost 300,000 kilometres per second.

gewusst: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us on Earth.
In one second light could travel about seven times round the whole Earth.
Plants need light to make food by photosynthesis.

teile.einleitung: Copper is a shiny reddish metal that people have been using for thousands of years. It conducts electricity and heat extremely well and is therefore found in almost every cable. Over time copper turns green in the air, as you can see on old church towers and on the Statue of Liberty.
wichtigste: Copper has the chemical symbol Cu and the atomic number 29.
Freshly polished copper is reddish brown; after many years outdoors it turns green.
Copper conducts electricity very well; only silver is better, but it is much more expensive.
Because copper conducts heat well, some saucepans have a copper base.
Brass is a mixture of copper and zinc, bronze a mixture of copper and tin.
The outside of the Statue of Liberty in New York is made of copper, which is why it is green.
Copper is obtained in mines from rock that contains copper.

abschnitte.text: **Copper** is a soft metal that is easy to shape and has a reddish-brown colour. It has the chemical symbol Cu, which comes from the Latin word cuprum. Copper melts at about 1085 °C and, with a density of almost 9 grams per cubic centimetre, is noticeably heavier than iron. It can be drawn into very thin wires or rolled into sheets.

Copper is one of the best **electrical conductors**. Only silver conducts electricity a little better, but it is far too expensive for cables. That is why the wires in power cables, electric motors and generators are usually made of copper. Copper also conducts heat very well, which is why some saucepans have a copper base and heat sinks in computers are often made of copper.

In the air copper slowly reacts with oxygen, water and other substances. First it turns dark brown, and after many years a green layer forms, the **patina**. This layer protects the metal underneath from further damage. The **Statue of Liberty** in New York was copper-coloured when it was unveiled in 1886 and is green today, as are many church roofs in Switzerland.

Copper mixes well with other metals; such mixtures are called **alloys**. **Brass** consists of copper and zinc, is golden yellow and is used for trumpets, door handles and screws. **Bronze** is a mixture of copper and tin and has been used for a long time for bells and statues. A whole age is even named after it, the Bronze Age.

Copper is one of the first metals people worked, more than 7000 years ago. The glacier mummy **Ötzi**, found in the Ötztal Alps, carried an axe with a copper blade. The Latin name goes back to the island of Cyprus, where a lot of copper was mined in ancient times. Today copper is obtained in large mines from rock that contains copper, most of all in Chile.

Copper is becoming more and more important, because electric cars, wind turbines and solar panels need a lot of it. An electric car contains several dozen kilograms of copper. Copper can be melted down and **recycled** again and again with almost no loss of quality. Copper also kills many bacteria on its surface, which is why it is sometimes used for door handles in hospitals.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mixture of two or more metals, for example brass or bronze.
Green protective layer that forms on copper in the air.
Material through which electricity or heat can flow well.
Rock from which a metal can be obtained.

gewusst: The copper skin of the Statue of Liberty is only about 2.4 millimetres thick, roughly as thick as a coin.
Humans need small amounts of copper to live; it is found, for example, in nuts and cocoa.
A large part of all the copper ever mined is still in use today, because it can be recycled so well.

teile.einleitung: An optical fibre, often called a glass fibre, is a hair-thin fibre of glass or plastic in which light is carried over long distances. Today almost all internet data races round the world through such fibres. The light stays trapped in the fibre because it is completely reflected back again and again at its edge.
wichtigste: Light is carried in an optical fibre by total internal reflection at the boundary between core and cladding.
The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding.
Optical fibres are not affected by electromagnetic interference.
For long distances infrared light with a wavelength of about 1550 nm is often used.
In a single-mode fibre the core is only about 9 µm thin, so only one light path travels along it.
A light signal takes about 0.5 milliseconds to pass through 100 km of fibre with n equal to 1.5.
As early as the 19th century the Geneva physicist Daniel Colladon showed that light can be guided in a jet of water.

abschnitte.titel: How an optical fibre is built
abschnitte.text: An optical fibre consists of an inner **core** and a surrounding **cladding**, both made of very pure quartz glass. At about 0.125 millimetres, the cladding is about as thick as a human hair. Around it is a protective plastic layer. Many such fibres are bundled together in a cable that is laid in the ground or even on the sea floor.

The core has a slightly higher **refractive index** than the cladding, so light is a little slower in it. If light hits the boundary with the cladding at a very shallow angle, it cannot get out and is reflected back completely. This is called **total internal reflection**. With a core of n equal to 1.48 and a cladding of n equal to 1.46, the critical angle is about 80.6 degrees and the numerical aperture is about 0.24. In this way light zigzags along the fibre, even when it is bent.

To transmit data, a laser switches the light on and off billions of times a second, producing noughts and ones. Over long distances invisible infrared light of about 1550 nanometres is usually used, because glass absorbs very little of this light. In a **single-mode fibre** with a core only about 9 micrometres across, just one light path travels along it, so the signal stays sharp. In glass with n equal to 1.5 light travels at about 200,000 km per second, so it needs 0.5 milliseconds for 100 km.

Around 1842 the Geneva physicist **Daniel Colladon** showed that light follows a curved jet of water. In 1966 Charles Kao suggested using glass fibres for telecommunications, as long as the glass could be made pure enough. In 1970 the first low-loss fibre was achieved in the USA. Kao received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009, and since the 1980s submarine fibre optic cables have linked the continents.

Optical fibres carry much more data than copper cables and are not affected by **electromagnetic interference**, for example from motors or lightning. In Switzerland Swisscom and many municipal utilities are extending fibre connections right into people's homes. In medicine doctors look into the stomach with an **endoscope** made of bundles of glass fibres. Lamps, decorative lights and sensors also use optical fibres.

begriffe.erklaerung: Number that shows how strongly a material slows light down.
Complete reflection of light at the boundary with another material.
Light with a longer wavelength than red, invisible to us.
Very thin optical fibre in which only one light path travels.
A device used to look inside the body.

gewusst: The glass of modern optical fibres is so clear that you could still see through a window of it a kilometre thick.
Millions of videos can run at the same time through a single submarine fibre optic cable.

teile.einleitung: Michel Mayor is a Swiss astrophysicist from Geneva who in 1995, together with Didier Queloz, discovered the first planet around a Sun-like star outside our solar system. For this the two received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019. Their discovery opened up a whole new field of research, the search for exoplanets.
wichtigste: Michel Mayor was born in Lausanne in 1942.
He did research as a professor at the University of Geneva.
In 1995 he discovered the planet 51 Pegasi b with Didier Queloz.
The discovery was made with the ELODIE spectrograph at the Observatoire de Haute-Provence in France.
He used the radial velocity method, which gives only a minimum mass for the planet.
In 2019 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics together with Queloz.
The Geneva group later built high-precision spectrographs such as HARPS and ESPRESSO.

abschnitte.text: Michel **Mayor** was born in Lausanne in 1942 and studied physics at the University of Lausanne. After that he did research at the observatory of the **University of Geneva** and became professor and director there. At first he studied how stars move in our Milky Way. For this he developed instruments that measure the speed of stars very precisely.

In October 1995 Mayor and his doctoral student Didier Queloz announced that they had found a planet around the star **51 Pegasi** in the constellation Pegasus. They used the **ELODIE** spectrograph at the Observatoire de Haute-Provence in southern France. The planet is about half as heavy as Jupiter but orbits its star in only about 4 days. Nobody had expected such a hot giant planet so close to its star.

A planet pulls on its star and makes it wobble slightly. If the star comes towards us, its light becomes a little bluer; if it moves away, it becomes redder. This is the **Doppler effect**. Our Sun is moved by Jupiter at around 13 m/s, and at 60 m/s a line at 500 nm shifts by only about 0.0001 nm. Because the tilt of the orbit is not known, this **radial velocity method** on its own gives only a minimum mass.

The Geneva group searched for more planets with the Swiss **Leonhard Euler Telescope** at the La Silla Observatory in Chile. The HARPS spectrograph, with which dozens of planets were found, is also there. Its successor ESPRESSO works at ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile. It is so precise that it can measure speeds of less than one metre per second.

In 2019 Mayor and Queloz received one half of the **Nobel Prize in Physics**; the other went to the cosmologist James Peebles. Since their discovery several thousand exoplanets have been found. If companions are heavier than around 13 Jupiter masses, they no longer count as planets but as brown dwarfs. Thanks to this research, the big question of whether there is life on another planet somewhere has come closer to an answer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planet that orbits a star other than our Sun.
A measuring device that splits light into its colours.
The shift in wavelength when a source comes closer or moves away.
A celestial body between a planet and a star, too light to shine like a star.

gewusst: Since 2015 the planet 51 Pegasi b has also had the official name Dimidium, Latin for half, because of its half Jupiter mass.
A radial velocity curve in pure sine shape reveals that the planet moves on an almost circular orbit.
Before 1995 it was not certain whether there were any planets at all around other Sun-like stars.

teile.einleitung: Gravitational potential energy is the energy an object has because it is at a certain height. If you lift a stone, you put energy into it; if you let it fall, the energy is released again. This energy is used, for example, by hydroelectric power stations, pendulum clocks and roller coasters.
wichtigste: Gravitational potential energy is energy an object has because of its height.
It is also called potential energy or energy of position.
It is calculated as mass times gravitational acceleration times height.
The unit of energy is the joule.
The value depends on where you set the zero level.
If you carry a suitcase horizontally at the same height, you do no lifting work.
When an object falls, potential energy is turned into kinetic energy.

abschnitte.text: An object high up can achieve something when it falls, for example crack a nut or turn a water wheel. This stored ability is called **gravitational potential energy** or potential energy. To lift an object, you have to work against gravity; this work is called **lifting work**. It is stored in the object as potential energy.

The formula is: potential energy equals mass times **gravitational acceleration** times height. In Switzerland the gravitational acceleration g is about 9.81 metres per second squared. If you lift a 50 kilogram box by 10 metres, it gains 4905 **joules**. To pump 1 cubic metre of water, or 1000 kilograms, up 20 metres needs at least 196.2 kilojoules.

For potential energy only the **difference in height** matters, not the route. If a car weighing 1000 kilograms drives 2 kilometres up a winding pass road and climbs 100 metres, its potential energy increases by 981 kilojoules. If you carry a suitcase 20 metres at the same height, the lifting work is zero. You may choose freely where to set the height to zero, but this **zero level** determines the value.

An apple of 100 grams that falls one metre loses about 1 joule of potential energy. A mountaineer of 80 kilograms who climbs from 1000 to 3000 metres above sea level gains about 1.57 megajoules. When something falls, the potential energy is turned into **kinetic energy**. On a roller coaster a lift first pulls the car up, and after that it runs only on this stored energy.

Swiss **storage power stations** use the potential energy of water in high reservoirs. The water flows down through pressure pipes and drives turbines. **Pumped storage plants** such as Limmern in the canton of Glarus pump water back up and so store energy for later. Old pendulum clocks with weights and cuckoo clocks also run on potential energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: Unit of energy, named after James Prescott Joule.
Work done against gravity when lifting something.
The value g, which shows how strongly the Earth pulls, about 9.81 m/s².
Height that is set as zero for calculations.

gewusst: To lift a 100 gram bar of chocolate by one metre you need about 1 joule.
But as food, the same bar of chocolate contains more than two million joules, so you would have to lift it very high to use up that energy.
Energy is never lost; it is only turned from one form into another.

teile.einleitung: Reverberation time tells you how long a sound keeps ringing in a room after the source of the sound has stopped. In an empty church, a clap echoes for a long time; in a room with carpet and curtains, hardly at all. The right reverberation time is very important for concert halls, classrooms and theatres.
wichtigste: Reverberation time is the time it takes for the sound level to fall by 60 decibels after the sound stops.
Wallace Clement Sabine founded scientific room acoustics around 1900.
According to Sabine's formula, T = 0.161 · V / A.
If you double the absorption area, the reverberation time is halved.
Large concert halls for symphonies have a reverberation time of about 2 seconds.
In classrooms, too long a reverberation time makes speech harder to understand.
Soft materials such as curtains, carpets and upholstery absorb sound.

abschnitte.text: Sound spreads out in a room and is **reflected** again and again by the walls, ceiling and floor. That is why you still hear a sound for a while even when the source is already silent. With each reflection, part of the sound is absorbed, until the sound disappears. The **reverberation time** measures how long it takes for the level to fall by 60 decibels, that is to a millionth of the sound intensity.

The American physicist **Wallace Clement Sabine** lived from 1868 to 1919 and taught at Harvard University. He was asked to improve a lecture hall in which the speakers could hardly be understood. Using seat cushions, a stopwatch and his own hearing, he studied how materials change the reverberation. From this, around 1900, he developed his formula and then advised on the building of Symphony Hall in Boston.

The formula is T = 0.161 · V / A, where V is the volume of the room in cubic metres and A is the **equivalent absorption area** in square metres. A room of 1000 m³ with 200 m² of absorption area has a reverberation time of about 0.8 seconds. The absorption area of a wall is its area times its absorption coefficient, so for 50 m² and 0.3 it is 15 m². If a room of 600 m³ is to have a reverberation time of 1.2 seconds, it needs about 80 m² of absorption area.

For symphonic music in large concert halls, people want about **2 seconds** of reverberation so that the music sounds full and warm. Large churches often echo much longer, which is lovely for organ music but difficult for speech. The concert hall in the KKL in Lucerne is famous worldwide for its very good acoustics. There, the acoustics can even be adapted to the music with movable flaps and chambers.

In classrooms, a short reverberation time of well under a second is important. If it is too long, the words blur together and **speech intelligibility** falls. Children then have to make more effort, and the room becomes louder overall. That is why acoustic ceilings, wall panels made of porous material or pinboards are fitted.

Hard, smooth surfaces such as concrete, glass and tiles reflect sound almost completely. Soft and porous materials such as carpets, curtains, upholstered furniture or acoustic foam **absorb** it. People absorb sound too, which is why a full hall sounds different from an empty one. You can try this at home by clapping your hands in an empty room and in a furnished room.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time in which a sound in a room becomes 60 decibels quieter.
The soaking up of sound by a material.
The unit for loudness, or sound level.
The study of how rooms sound.
The bouncing back of sound from a surface.

gewusst: A room with no reverberation, a so-called anechoic chamber, feels eerily silent to many people.
Because people absorb sound, concert seats are often upholstered so that the hall sounds similar whether it is empty or full.
The unit “sabin” for absorption area is named after Wallace Clement Sabine.

teile.einleitung: Humidity tells you how much invisible water vapour there is in the air. It helps to decide whether a day feels muggy or dry, whether fog forms and whether it rains. It is measured with a hygrometer.
wichtigste: Air always contains some water in the form of invisible water vapour.
Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air.
Absolute humidity is given in grams of water vapour per cubic metre of air.
Relative humidity says in per cent how full the air is compared with its maximum.
Humidity is measured with a hygrometer.
In 1783 the Geneva naturalist Horace-Bénédict de Saussure invented the hair hygrometer.
Indoors most people find about 40 to 60 per cent comfortable.

abschnitte.text: Water is constantly evaporating from lakes, plants, the ground and even our breath. As **water vapour** it mixes invisibly into the air. How much vapour the air can hold at most depends on the temperature: warm air can take much more than cold air. When the air is full, we speak of 100 per cent humidity; then droplets, fog or dew form.

**Absolute humidity** tells you how many grams of water vapour there are in one cubic metre of air. **Relative humidity** compares this amount with the maximum at that temperature. An example: air at 20 degrees can hold at most about 17.3 grams of water vapour per cubic metre. If it contains 8.65 grams, half of that, the relative humidity is 50 per cent. In the weather forecast it is usually relative humidity that is meant.

A device for measuring humidity is called a **hygrometer**. The Geneva naturalist **Horace-Bénédict de Saussure**, who also climbed Mont Blanc in 1787, invented the hair hygrometer in 1783. It uses the fact that a human hair gets a little longer in damp air and a little shorter in dry air. This small change in length moves a pointer on a scale. Today electronic sensors are usually used, found in many weather stations and thermometers.

On hot summer days with high humidity the weather feels **muggy**. The reason is that our sweat evaporates poorly in damp air and so cools us less. In winter, on the other hand, heated flats often become very dry. The cold outside air contains only a little water, and when it is heated its relative humidity falls sharply. Dry air can irritate the lining of the nose and throat.

When moist air rises up the Alps and cools down, clouds form and it rains or snows. On the other side of the mountains the air often arrives warm and dry as the **foehn**. In autumn and winter there is often fog over the Central Plateau, because the moist air near the ground cools down. In flats a relative humidity of about 40 to 60 per cent is comfortable. If it is too damp for a long time, **mould** can form on cold walls, which is why airing the rooms regularly helps.

begriffe.erklaerung: Measuring device for humidity.
What percentage of the possible water vapour the air contains at the moment.
Amount of water vapour in grams per cubic metre of air.
Feeling of warm, damp air in which it is hard to cool down.
Temperature at which the air is so full that droplets form.

gewusst: A hair is such a good humidity sensor that it was used in measuring devices for a long time.
In the desert the relative humidity can fall below 10 per cent during the day.
At the same temperature, damp air feels hotter in summer than dry air.

teile.einleitung: The ear is our sense organ for hearing and for balance. It turns tiny changes in air pressure, which we call sound, into electrical signals that the brain understands as notes, voices and music.
wichtigste: The ear consists of the outer ear, middle ear and inner ear.
The visible part of the ear is called the auricle or pinna.
The eardrum is a thin membrane that vibrates when sound arrives.
The middle ear contains the three ossicles: hammer, anvil and stirrup.
The stirrup is the smallest bone in the human body.
The cochlea in the inner ear looks like a snail shell and turns sound into nerve signals.
The inner ear also helps with balance.
With two ears, you can hear which direction a sound is coming from.

abschnitte.text: The outer ear includes the **auricle** and the **ear canal**. The auricle works like a small funnel that catches sound waves and directs them into the ear canal. In adults, the ear canal is about 2.5 centimetres long. At its end lies the eardrum, the boundary with the middle ear.

The **eardrum** is thinner than a sheet of paper and vibrates when sound hits it. It passes these vibrations on to the three **ossicles**: the hammer, anvil and stirrup. The ossicles act like a lever and amplify the movement. The stirrup is only about three millimetres long. The middle ear is connected to the throat by the **Eustachian tube**, which is why your ears pop when you swallow in an aeroplane or a cable car.

In the inner ear lies the **cochlea**, a coiled tube filled with fluid. The stirrup presses on a small window and sets the fluid moving. Fine **hair cells** sense this movement and send signals through the auditory nerve to the brain. High notes are detected at the start of the cochlea, low notes further in. A young person can hear sounds from about 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second.

Next to the cochlea lies the **organ of balance**. It consists of three semicircular canals filled with fluid that sense when the head turns. If you spin round quickly and then stop, the fluid keeps flowing for a moment. That is why you feel dizzy. Without this organ, we could hardly walk upright or ride a bike.

Because we have two ears, a sound from the side reaches one ear a tiny bit earlier and louder than the other. The brain analyses these tiny differences. This is how we can tell where a sound is coming from, for example a car that is approaching. This is called **directional hearing**. Many animals, such as owls, use this trick very precisely too.

**Earwax** protects the ear canal from dust, dirt and germs and moves outwards by itself. That is why you should not push cotton buds deep into your ear, because they push the wax inwards and can injure the eardrum. Very loud music, fireworks or machines can permanently damage the hair cells. These cells do not grow back. That is why **ear protection** and breaks from noise are important.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin membrane at the end of the ear canal that is set vibrating by sound.
Hammer, anvil and stirrup, three tiny bones in the middle ear that pass on vibrations.
The coiled part of the inner ear in which sound is turned into nerve signals.
Three fluid-filled tubes in the inner ear that sense when the head turns.
A yellowish substance that cleans and protects the ear canal.

gewusst: The stirrup is about the size of a grain of rice.
Your ears keep hearing while you sleep, but the brain filters out most sounds.
Elephants hear very low notes that people cannot hear.

teile.einleitung: The Fukushima nuclear disaster was a serious accident at a Japanese nuclear power station in March 2011. A powerful earthquake and a huge tsunami knocked out the cooling of the reactors, and the fuel melted in three reactors. It was the worst nuclear accident since Chernobyl in 1986 and also had major consequences for energy policy in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The disaster began on 11 March 2011 at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power station in Japan.
It was triggered by a powerful earthquake followed by a tsunami.
The flood knocked out the power supply and the emergency diesel generators, so the cooling failed.
There was a meltdown in three reactor units.
Hydrogen explosions destroyed parts of the reactor buildings.
The power station was run by the company TEPCO.
Like Chernobyl, the accident was rated at the highest level, 7, on the international scale.

abschnitte.text: On 11 March 2011, a massive **earthquake** of magnitude 9 shook north-eastern Japan. Shortly afterwards, a **tsunami** rolled onto the coast: a huge flood wave that was over 13 metres high at the power station. The wave swept over the protective wall of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power station, which lies right on the Pacific. The earthquake and tsunami killed around 18,000 people in Japan altogether, most of them in the flood itself.

Even a reactor that has been shut down still produces a lot of heat for a long time and must be cooled constantly. Because of the earthquake, power from the grid failed first. Then the tsunami flooded the **emergency diesel generators** and the electrical equipment in the basement. Without electricity the pumps stopped working, and the cooling water gradually boiled away.

In reactor units 1, 2 and 3, the fuel rods became so hot that they melted; this is called a **meltdown**. This produced **hydrogen**, which got into the reactor buildings and exploded there. The explosions destroyed roofs and walls, and radioactive substances escaped into the air, soil and sea. The operator **TEPCO** and the authorities struggled for weeks to cool the reactors with water.

abschnitte.titel: Consequences for people and the environment
abschnitte.text: An exclusion zone was set up around the power station, and well over 100,000 people had to leave their homes. Some areas are still not habitable today; people have returned to others. The cooling water is treated, but radioactive **tritium** cannot be filtered out. Since 2023, the diluted, treated water has gradually been released into the Pacific, which is controversial in neighbouring countries. Dismantling the destroyed reactors will take decades more.

The disaster sparked debates worldwide about the safety of nuclear energy. In Switzerland, the Federal Council and Parliament decided in 2011 not to build any more new nuclear power stations. In 2017, voters approved the **Energy Strategy 2050**, which plans for more renewable energy and saving energy. The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was shut down in 2019. In recent years, whether the ban on building new nuclear power stations should be relaxed again has become a political topic once more.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge flood wave, usually caused by an earthquake under the sea.
An accident in which a reactor's fuel becomes so hot that it melts.
Invisible radiation given off by decaying atomic nuclei.
Diesel engines that supply electricity for important equipment during a power cut.
A radioactive form of hydrogen that cannot be filtered out of water.

gewusst: The name Daiichi means “number one” in Japanese; a few kilometres further south lies the Fukushima Daini plant, “number two”.
A reactor must be cooled for months even after it has been shut down, because the fuel keeps giving off heat.
Robots were later used in the exclusion zone to look inside the highly contaminated reactor buildings.

teile.einleitung: Leptons are a family of elementary particles, building blocks of matter that cannot be split any further. The best-known lepton is the electron, which is found in the shell of every atom. Altogether six leptons are known: three charged ones and three tiny, almost massless neutrinos.
wichtigste: Leptons are elementary particles, which include the electron, the muon, the tau and three neutrinos.
Leptons are not affected by the strong interaction.
The word “lepton” comes from Greek and means light or thin.
The muon is about 200 times heavier than the electron and was discovered in cosmic radiation in 1936.
The tau was discovered in the mid-1970s as the last charged lepton.
In all particle reactions observed so far, the lepton number is conserved.
Many muons reach the ground because of time dilation.

abschnitte.text: In the **Standard Model** of particle physics there are two groups of matter particles: quarks and **leptons**. Quarks make up protons and neutrons in the atomic nucleus, whereas leptons do not feel the strong nuclear force.
