They respond to the weak interaction and to gravity, and the charged leptons also to electromagnetic forces. The name comes from the Greek “leptos”, meaning light or thin, because the first known leptons were much lighter than protons.

There are three charged leptons: the **electron**, the muon and the tau. Each has its own **neutrino**: the electron neutrino, the muon neutrino and the tau neutrino. The muon is about 200 times heavier than the electron, and the tau as much as about 3500 times. The heavy leptons are unstable: a muon decays on average after about two millionths of a second. Every lepton also has an antiparticle, for example the positron as the counterpart of the electron.

Joseph John Thomson discovered the electron in England in 1897. Carl Anderson and Seth Neddermeyer found the muon in **cosmic radiation** in 1936. The physicist Wolfgang Pauli predicted the neutrino in 1930, when he was a professor at ETH Zurich; it was only detected in 1956. Martin Perl discovered the tau in the USA in the mid-1970s, for which he received the Nobel Prize in 1995.

When cosmic radiation hits particles of air high up, muons are produced, which race towards the Earth at almost the speed of light. Really they live too short a time for the long journey. But because time passes more slowly for them due to **time dilation**, many still reach the ground. At the Earth's surface about one muon passes through every square centimetre each minute, so they are constantly passing through your body too, completely harmlessly.

At **CERN** near Geneva the LEP accelerator ran from 1989 to 2000, in which electrons and positrons collided. The measurements there showed that there are exactly three kinds of light neutrino, and so exactly three lepton families. An important rule also applies: the **lepton number** is conserved in all reactions observed so far. That is why, when a neutron decays, an antineutrino is always produced alongside an electron.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle that cannot be split into smaller parts.
A tiny, almost massless lepton with no charge that passes through almost everything.
A heavy, short-lived relative of the electron.
A counting quantity that stays the same in particle reactions.
The theory that describes all known elementary particles and their forces.

gewusst: Every second, billions of neutrinos from the Sun pass through every square centimetre of your skin without your noticing anything.
Wolfgang Pauli was so unsure of his neutrino idea that at first he only presented it in a joking letter to colleagues.

teile.einleitung: The Chernobyl nuclear disaster was one of the worst accidents ever at a nuclear power station. On 26 April 1986, unit 4 of the power station exploded in what was then the Soviet Union, in the area of today's Ukraine. Radioactive substances spread over large parts of Europe, as far as Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Chernobyl nuclear power station lies in the north of today's Ukraine.
The disaster happened during a safety test in unit 4.
The reactor that exploded was an RBMK reactor.
A positive void coefficient played a decisive part in the surge in power.
The accident was given the highest level, 7, on the international INES scale.
The nearby town of Pripyat was completely evacuated and is still abandoned today.
An exclusion zone with a radius of around 30 kilometres was set up around the power station.
In Switzerland, Ticino was the most heavily contaminated with radioactive caesium.

abschnitte.text: The **Chernobyl** nuclear power station lies close to the border with Belarus. In 1986 the area belonged to the Soviet Union; today it belongs to Ukraine. In the night of 25 to 26 April 1986, there was an explosion in **unit 4**. A few kilometres away lay the town of Pripyat, where many of the power station workers lived.

During the night, a **safety test** was carried out with several protective systems switched off. The **RBMK reactor** had a dangerous property: if steam bubbles formed in the cooling water, the power rose further. This positive void coefficient led to an extremely rapid surge in power. Steam and an explosion destroyed the reactor, and the graphite in the core burned for days.

Large amounts of **radioactive** substances escaped into the air. Firefighters and workers, later called liquidators, fought the fire and cleaned up. Several dozen of them died of radiation sickness in the first months. How many people later fell ill as a result is still disputed today.

The day after the accident, **Pripyat**, with around 50,000 inhabitants, was evacuated. People thought they would return after a few days, but the town is still abandoned today. An **exclusion zone** with a radius of around 30 kilometres was set up around the power station. A concrete shell, the sarcophagus, was first built over the destroyed reactor, and in 2016 a huge new protective shelter made of steel.

In the days that followed, winds carried the radioactive cloud across Europe. In Switzerland, there was heavy rain at the beginning of May 1986, especially in **Ticino**, so that is where the most **caesium-137** reached the ground. The authorities issued advice on foods such as vegetables and milk. Because caesium-137 has a half-life of around 30 years, it can still be detected today in soil, mushrooms and wild boar.

Chernobyl was the first accident to be given the highest level, 7, on the **INES** scale; Fukushima in Japan followed in 2011. The disaster led to better safety rules for nuclear power stations worldwide. In many countries, including Switzerland, there was intense debate about nuclear power afterwards. Today, many wild animals such as wolves, elk and wild horses live in the exclusion zone again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A power station that produces electricity by splitting atomic nuclei.
The property of some substances of giving off invisible, dangerous radiation.
The time after which half of a radioactive substance has decayed.
When people are quickly taken out of an area because of danger.
An area that you may not enter, or only with permission, because of danger.

gewusst: In Pripyat there is a Ferris wheel that was never properly used, because the funfair was only due to open after the accident.
The new shelter over the reactor is so big that a football stadium would fit underneath it, and it was slid over the reactor on rails.

teile.einleitung: A magnet is an object that attracts things made of iron without touching them. If you hold a magnet near an iron paper clip, it jumps towards it. Magnets come in many shapes, as a bar, a horseshoe or a small disc.
wichtigste: A magnet attracts objects made of iron, for example paper clips.
Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole.
Like poles repel each other, unlike poles attract each other.
Wood, plastic, glass and paper are not attracted.
Magnetic force also works through paper or fabric.
There are permanent magnets and electromagnets.
Magnets are found in compasses, loudspeakers and motors.

abschnitte.text: A **magnet** exerts an invisible force on certain metals. Above all it attracts **iron**, but also nickel and cobalt. An iron paper clip therefore jumps towards the magnet. Copper, aluminium, wood and plastic, on the other hand, are not attracted.

Every magnet has two ends, the **north pole** and the **south pole**. The force is strongest there. If you hold two north poles together, they repel each other. A north pole and a south pole, however, attract each other.

There are **bar magnets**, **horseshoe magnets**, disc magnets and ring magnets. Fridge magnets are often small, flat discs. Neodymium magnets are especially strong and can be only a few millimetres in size. They hold much more weight than you would think.

A **permanent magnet** always stays magnetic. An **electromagnet**, by contrast, is a coil of wire that only becomes magnetic when current flows. Large electromagnets lift whole cars at scrapyards. If you switch off the current, the load falls down again.

Magnets hold notes on the fridge and keep cupboard doors shut. In every **compass** there is a small magnetic needle. Loudspeakers, headphones and electric motors also work with magnets. Even some fastenings on bags and pencil cases are magnetic.

begriffe.erklaerung: One end of a magnet, where the force is strongest.
A magnet that always stays magnetic.
A coil of wire that is magnetic only with current.
A natural rock that can be magnetic by itself.

gewusst: If you break a bar magnet, you get two smaller magnets, each with a north and a south pole.
The name magnet probably comes from the region of Magnesia in Greece, where magnetic stones were found.
The Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet.

teile.einleitung: Lagrange points are five special places in space where the gravitational pull of two large bodies and the centrifugal force just balance each other out. A small body, such as a satellite, can travel round there together with the two bodies without changing its position. That is why they are popular parking spots for space telescopes.
wichtigste: In a system of two celestial bodies there are five Lagrange points, L1 to L5.
There, in the rotating system, the gravitational forces and the centrifugal force cancel out.
L1, L2 and L3 lie on a line through the two main bodies.
L4 and L5 each form an equilateral triangle with the two main bodies.
L4 and L5 are stable if the ratio of the masses is large enough.
The James Webb Space Telescope is at the L2 point of the Sun-Earth system.
The L1 point is particularly suited to observing the Sun continuously.

abschnitte.text: When two celestial bodies orbit each other, like the Sun and the Earth, their two **gravitational forces** act on a small third body. At five points these forces and the **centrifugal force** in the rotating system balance exactly. A satellite there circles the Sun in step with the Earth. The points are named after the mathematician **Joseph-Louis Lagrange**.

In the Sun-Earth system **L1** lies about 1.5 million kilometres from the Earth in the direction of the Sun. **L2** lies roughly the same distance away on the side of the Earth facing away from the Sun. L3 is behind the Sun on the opposite side of the Earth's orbit. L4 and L5 run ahead of and behind the Earth on its orbit and each form an **equilateral triangle** with the Sun and the Earth.

The points L1, L2 and L3 are **unstable**, rather like a ball on top of a hill. A satellite there has to correct its orbit regularly with small thrusters. L4 and L5, on the other hand, are **stable** if the larger body is much heavier than the smaller one. That is why asteroids and dust collect there naturally.

The **James Webb Space Telescope** was launched in December 2021 and has been orbiting the L2 point ever since. There it always has the Sun, Earth and Moon on the same side and can shield itself from their heat with a large sunshield. At L1, the solar probe **SOHO** of ESA and NASA has been watching the Sun without interruption since the 1990s. The European Gaia telescope was also stationed at L2.

Thousands of asteroids have collected at the L4 and L5 points of the planet Jupiter. They are called **Trojans**, and many of them are named after heroes of the Trojan War, such as Achilles or Hector. NASA's **Lucy** probe has been on its way since 2021 to visit several of these asteroids. The Earth and Mars also have a few Trojans.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force of attraction between all bodies that have mass.
Apparent outward force felt in a rotating system.
Asteroids that travel round together with a planet at its L4 or L5 point.
Telescope that works in space outside the Earth's atmosphere.

gewusst: The points L1, L2 and L3 had already been described by Leonhard Euler from Basel; Lagrange later found L4 and L5.
The L2 point is about four times as far from the Earth as the Moon.
The Earth-Moon system also has five Lagrange points, and faint clouds of dust are thought to exist at L4 and L5.

teile.einleitung: Neutrinos are tiny elementary particles that have almost no mass and are electrically neutral. Every second, billions of them fly through your body without you noticing anything. Because they so rarely collide with other matter, they are sometimes called “ghost particles”.
wichtigste: Neutrinos are electrically neutral elementary particles with a tiny mass.
They interact only very weakly and so pass almost unhindered through the whole Earth.
Around 60 billion neutrinos from the Sun hit every square centimetre of the Earth each second.
They were first detected directly in 1956 at a nuclear reactor.
Neutrino oscillations prove that neutrinos have mass.
Large detectors such as IceCube at the South Pole or Super-Kamiokande in Japan track them down.
In 1987, neutrinos from an exploding star were measured for the first time, from supernova 1987A.

abschnitte.text: In 1930, physicists had a puzzle: in radioactive beta decay, energy seemed to disappear. The Austrian physicist **Wolfgang Pauli**, then a professor at ETH Zurich, therefore suggested an unknown, neutral particle that carries away the missing energy. The Italian Enrico Fermi gave it the name neutrino, which means “little neutral one”. Pauli himself feared that this particle would never be detected.

Neutrinos are **elementary particles**, which means they are not made of even smaller parts. They have no electric charge and a mass much smaller than that of an electron. They only feel the weak nuclear force and gravity. That is why they fly through walls, mountains and even the whole Earth as if nothing were there.

It was not until 1956 that the Americans Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines managed to detect neutrinos directly. They placed their detector next to a **nuclear reactor**, which produces huge numbers of neutrinos. Only very rarely did one of them collide with a particle in the detector. Reines received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this in 1995.

There are three kinds of neutrino: electron, muon and tau neutrinos. On their way, they can change from one kind into another; this is called **neutrino oscillation**. This is only possible if neutrinos have mass. Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this discovery in 2015.

Because neutrinos react so rarely, you need huge detectors. **Super-Kamiokande** in Japan lies deep in a mine and is filled with ultra-pure water, in which neutrinos sometimes cause faint flashes of light, Cherenkov light. **IceCube** at the South Pole uses a whole cubic kilometre of ice with thousands of light sensors. Such facilities lie deep underground or in the ice so that other particles do not interfere.

Neutrinos are produced in large numbers in the Sun, where hydrogen fuses into helium. In 1987, neutrinos from an exploding star were measured for the first time, from **supernova 1987A** in a neighbouring galaxy of the Milky Way. In 2011, neutrinos sent from CERN near Geneva to Gran Sasso in Italy seemed to be faster than light. But the cause was a measuring error, including a badly fitted fibre-optic connector.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle that is not made of smaller parts.
A kind of radioactive decay in which neutrinos are also produced.
The change of a neutrino into another kind of neutrino.
A measuring device that tracks down particles.
The enormous explosion of a large star.

gewusst: The human body also sends out neutrinos, because it contains tiny amounts of radioactive substances such as potassium.
Neutrinos from the Sun reach us at night too; they simply fly right through the whole Earth.
Wolfgang Pauli presented his neutrino idea in 1930 in a letter addressed to “Dear radioactive ladies and gentlemen”.

teile.einleitung: A laboratory is a room in which researchers carry out experiments, examine substances and take measurements. It is often shortened to lab, and the word comes from the Latin word for to work. New medicines, materials and scientific discoveries come out of laboratories.
wichtigste: A laboratory is a room in which researchers carry out experiments.
The word comes from the Latin “laborare”, which means to work.
There are laboratories for chemistry, biology, physics, medicine and many other fields.
Strict safety rules apply in the laboratory, for example wearing safety goggles and a lab coat.
Typical equipment includes test tubes, Bunsen burners, scales and microscopes.
Switzerland has famous research laboratories such as CERN near Geneva and the Paul Scherrer Institute in Aargau.

abschnitte.text: A **laboratory** is a workroom specially equipped for scientific investigations. It has fixed benches, water taps, gas pipes and special cupboards. Chemists, biologists or laboratory technicians, for example, work in a lab. They test hypotheses with **experiments** and measure as accurately as possible. Hospitals also have laboratories, where blood samples are examined.

Among the best-known pieces of equipment are the **test tube**, the conical flask and the pipette for measuring liquids accurately. With the **Bunsen burner**, which Robert Bunsen improved around 1855, substances are heated with a gas flame. Microscopes are used to look at tiny things such as cells. Very precise scales can measure fractions of a gram. Today many laboratories also have computers and robots that examine samples automatically.

Strict **safety rules** apply in the laboratory. You wear safety goggles, a lab coat and often gloves. Eating and drinking are forbidden so that no dangerous substances get into your mouth. Dangerous fumes are sucked away under a **fume cupboard**, a kind of hood with ventilation. Emergency showers, eye showers and fire extinguishers are ready in case of accidents.

Switzerland has world-famous research laboratories. At **CERN** near Geneva, founded in 1954, researchers from many countries study the smallest particles of matter. The Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen in the canton of Aargau is the largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering in Switzerland. ETH Zurich, EPFL in Lausanne and the pharmaceutical companies in Basel also run large laboratories. At the Swiss Science Center Technorama in Winterthur children can do experiments themselves.

As early as the Middle Ages **alchemists** had workshops in which they mixed and heated substances. They hoped, for example, to make gold from base metals. From the 17th and 18th centuries this developed into modern chemistry with precise measurements. In the 19th century universities set up the first teaching laboratories for students. Today there are even laboratories on the International Space Station in space.

begriffe.erklaerung: Specialist who prepares and carries out experiments in the laboratory.
Small glass tube for experiments with liquids.
Workplace with extraction that removes poisonous fumes.
Gas burner used to heat substances in the laboratory.

gewusst: The World Wide Web was invented at CERN by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989.
In Switzerland you can train as a laboratory technician through an apprenticeship leading to a federal certificate of proficiency.

teile.einleitung: A pinhole camera is the simplest camera in the world: a dark box with a tiny hole on one side. Light falls through the hole and draws a picture of the surroundings on the opposite side, though upside down. You can easily build one yourself from a shoebox.
wichtigste: A pinhole camera is a dark box with a small hole.
It works because light travels in straight lines.
The image is upside down and reversed left to right.
A larger hole makes the image brighter but less sharp.
A longer camera gives a larger image.
The Latin name “camera obscura” means dark room.
With a pinhole camera you can watch a solar eclipse without looking directly at the Sun.

abschnitte.text: A **pinhole camera** consists of a light-proof box with a small hole at the front. At the back there is a screen, for example of tracing paper, or photographic paper. The Latin name **camera obscura** means dark room. In the past whole rooms were even built like this, in which the image of the landscape outside appeared on the wall.

Light travels in **straight lines**. From every point of an object a narrow beam of light passes through the hole and hits a particular point on the screen. Light from the top of a tree lands at the bottom of the screen, and light from its foot at the top. That is why the image is upside down and also reversed left to right. If the camera has two holes side by side, you see two images.

The size of the image can be worked out with a ratio: image size is to object size as the depth of the camera is to the distance. A tree 10 m tall at a distance of 20 m produces an image 5 cm high in a camera 10 cm deep. If you make the camera longer, the image gets bigger. If you make the **hole** larger, the image gets brighter but less sharp, because the spots of light overlap. A lens instead of the hole makes the image bright and sharp; that is how a camera works.

The Greek philosopher Aristotle already noticed that sunlight passing through small openings produces round images of the Sun. Around the year 1000 the Arab scholar **Ibn al-Haytham** studied the camera obscura closely. Leonardo da Vinci described it around 1500, and painters later used it as a drawing aid. **Photography** developed out of the camera obscura in the 19th century.

During a **solar eclipse** you must never look at the Sun without protection, as this can seriously damage your eyes. With a pinhole camera you do not look directly at the Sun but at the image on the screen. That way you can safely watch the Moon move in front of the Sun. Even the gaps between the leaves of trees act like pinhole cameras and then throw many small crescent images onto the ground.

Take a shoebox and line the inside with black or make it thoroughly light-proof. Use a needle to prick a small hole in the front. Cut a window out of the back and stick **tracing paper** over it. In a dark room, look at the tracing paper and point the hole at a bright window; then you will see the image upside down.

begriffe.erklaerung: Latin for dark room, the old name for the pinhole camera.
Light always travels along straight lines as long as nothing is in the way.
Left and right are swapped in the image.
See-through paper on which you can see an image from behind.

gewusst: With a pinhole camera and photographic paper you can expose for over half a year and so record the paths of the Sun across the sky as glowing arcs; this is called solargraphy.
Our eye also produces an upside-down image on the retina; only the brain turns it the right way up again for us.

teile.einleitung: Length contraction is an astonishing consequence of Albert Einstein's special theory of relativity. An object moving very fast past us appears shorter in the direction of motion than when it is at rest. This can only be noticed at speeds close to the speed of light.
wichtigste: Moving objects are shortened in the direction of motion.
The shortening only happens in the direction of motion; height and width stay the same.
The length of an object in its own rest frame is called its proper length.
A spaceship 100 m long measures only 80 m at 0.6 times the speed of light.
At about 0.87 c a rod is shortened to half its proper length.
FitzGerald and Lorentz proposed the shortening to explain the Michelson-Morley experiment.
In everyday life you notice nothing of it, because everyday speeds are much lower than the speed of light.

abschnitte.text: Every object has a **proper length**, its length as measured by someone at rest with it. If the object flies past an observer, the observer measures a shorter length. The shortening affects only the direction of motion, so a cube flying past would become flatter but not narrower. The important thing is that this is not an illusion but a real property of space and time.

You get the measured length by multiplying the proper length by a factor that depends on the speed. This factor is the square root of 1 minus the square of v divided by c, where c is the **speed of light**, about 300,000 kilometres per second. At 0.6 c the factor is 0.8, so a spaceship 100 m long measures 80 m. At about 0.87 c the factor is 0.5. The closer an object gets to the speed of light, the more it is shortened.

At the end of the 19th century Albert Michelson and Edward Morley looked for an “ether” through which light was supposed to travel, but found none. To explain this surprising result, George FitzGerald (1889) and Hendrik Antoon Lorentz (1892) independently suggested that moving objects are shortened. That is why it is also called the **Lorentz contraction**. Albert Einstein, who was working at the patent office in Bern at the time, derived it anew and more simply in 1905 from his special theory of relativity.

High in the atmosphere, cosmic radiation produces tiny particles called **muons**. They decay very quickly, really too quickly to reach the ground. Even so, many of them are detected at the Earth's surface. From the muon's point of view the atmosphere is strongly shortened by length contraction, so it manages the journey. From the Earth's point of view the same thing is explained by time dilation, the slowing down of time.

abschnitte.titel: Why do we not notice anything?
abschnitte.text: Even an aeroplane flies at only a tiny fraction of the speed of light. A car on the motorway would be shortened by much less than a billionth of a millimetre. Only in particle accelerators such as CERN near Geneva, where particles fly almost as fast as light, does the effect play a big part. There physicists have to include the theory of relativity in their calculations.

begriffe.erklaerung: The length of an object measured by someone moving along with it.
The highest possible speed, about 300,000 km per second, abbreviated c.
Einstein's theory about space, time and motion.
When moving very fast, time passes more slowly.

gewusst: The Earth travels round the Sun at about 30 kilometres per second, yet it is shortened by only a few centimetres as a result.
In theory an object moving at the speed of light would have zero length, which is why nothing with mass can go that fast.
If you photograph a very fast object, because of the travel time of light it does not simply look shorter but looks rotated.

teile.einleitung: A manometer is a measuring device for the pressure of gases or liquids. You find it on bike pumps, gas bottles, heating systems and at the doctor's on the blood pressure monitor. Some manometers have a pointer; others show the pressure with a column of liquid.
wichtigste: A manometer measures the pressure of gases or liquids.
Many dial manometers have a curved tube as the measuring element, the Bourdon tube.
In a U-tube manometer the difference in height of the liquid shows the pressure difference.
Tyre gauges show the pressure above the surrounding air.
Blood pressure is traditionally given in mmHg.
For higher pressures liquid manometers are filled with mercury, because it is very dense.
For very small pressures the measuring tube is tilted so that it can be read more precisely.

abschnitte.text: The simplest manometer is a **U-tube** that is partly filled with liquid. If there is more pressure on one side, the liquid is pushed down there and rises on the other side. The pressure difference is calculated with Δp = ρ · g · h. For water and a height difference of 15 cm this gives around 1.47 kPa.

**Mercury** is about 13.6 times as dense as water. That is why the column stays much shorter for the same pressure, and greater pressures can be measured too. A pressure of 1 kPa corresponds to about 7.5 mm of mercury. For very small pressures the tube is tilted; this makes the reading distance longer and more precise.

Most manometers in everyday life have a dial with a pointer. Inside there is a curved, flat metal tube, the **Bourdon tube**, named after the Frenchman Eugène Bourdon. If the pressure in the tube rises, it straightens out a little. This small movement is passed on to the pointer through a gear wheel.

A tyre gauge measures the **gauge pressure**, that is how much more pressure there is in the tyre than outside. If it shows 2.2 bar, the absolute pressure at sea level is around 3.2 bar, because about 1 bar of air pressure is added. A completely flat tyre therefore shows 0 bar, even though there is still air in it. Devices for the air pressure of the atmosphere are called barometers.

At the doctor's, **blood pressure** is measured with a cuff on the upper arm and a manometer. The values are traditionally given in millimetres of mercury, mmHg for short. A value such as 120 over 80 means that the pressure during the heartbeat could support a mercury column of 120 mm. Today most devices are electronic, but the unit has stayed.

Manometers are fitted to heating systems, fire extinguishers, gas bottles, pressure cookers and diving cylinders. They show whether the pressure is right or whether there is danger. On track pumps for bikes a manometer helps you get the right **tyre pressure**. In industry they monitor pipes and boilers so that nothing bursts.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on a particular area, measured in pascals or bar.
A curved metal tube that straightens under pressure and so moves a pointer.
The pressure above the air pressure of the surroundings.
Millimetres of mercury, an old unit of pressure, used above all for blood pressure.

gewusst: In 1643 the Italian Evangelista Torricelli measured air pressure with a mercury column around 76 cm high.
With water instead of mercury you would need a column over 10 metres high for air pressure.
Some manometers have a red area on the scale that warns of dangerously high pressure.

teile.einleitung: A magnetic board is a board to which magnets stick. You find them in classrooms, offices and kitchens, often also as white writing boards. The secret lies in a thin layer of steel under the surface.
wichtigste: For magnets to hold, the board needs a layer of steel.
People often use magnets to put up pictures, notes and plans.
The force of attraction holds the magnet firmly on the vertical board.
On white magnetic boards you write with felt-tip pens.
Magnets can be moved around on the board.
A magnet that is too weak cannot hold a heavy picture.
Fridge magnets also stick to a magnetic board.

abschnitte.text: A magnetic board is a wall or free-standing board with a surface that magnets stick to. Under a layer of paint, enamel or plastic there is a thin **steel sheet**. Steel contains iron and is therefore attracted by magnets. A board made of pure wood, glass or aluminium, on the other hand, would not hold a magnet.

The magnet is attracted by the steel and pressed against the board. This creates **friction** between the magnet and the surface. This static friction stops the magnet from sliding down the vertical board. If you hang a picture that is too heavy on a small magnet, the weight is greater than the friction and the picture slides down.

Many magnetic boards are also **whiteboards**, that is white boards. You write on them with special felt-tip pens that can be wiped off again dry. In Swiss classrooms there are often such white boards alongside the classic green chalkboards. Many chalkboards also contain steel, so that magnets stick to them.

Teachers put up posters, pictures or timetables with magnets without making holes. With **magnetic letters** children can lay out words and rearrange them. Numbers, shapes or picture cards can also be moved easily this way. In sport, coaches show on tactics boards with small magnets where the players should stand.

A fridge door is actually also a magnetic board, because it is made of sheet steel. That is why **fridge magnets** also stick to any other magnetic board. Many magnets for boards contain ferrite, a cheap ceramic material. For heavy things people use stronger neodymium magnets.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hard material that consists mainly of iron and is attracted by magnets.
The force that stops an object from sliding away on a surface.
A white board on which you write with wipeable felt-tip pens.
A ceramic material that many cheap permanent magnets are made of.

gewusst: A sheet of paper between the magnet and the board weakens the holding force, several sheets even more.
Some wall paints contain iron powder so that a whole wall of a room can be turned into a magnetic wall.
Not every steel is magnetic; some types of stainless steel hardly attract magnets.

teile.einleitung: In physics, mass is a basic property of every body. It determines how much inertia it has and how strongly it is attracted by gravity. The difference between mass and weight is important: mass stays the same everywhere, weight depends on gravity.
wichtigste: Mass is a base quantity of physics with the unit kilogram.
Mass stays the same everywhere; weight depends on gravity.
Mass gives bodies inertia; they resist changes to their motion.
A full shopping trolley is harder to push because it has more mass.
Masses attract each other; this is called gravitation.
Weight is calculated as mass times the acceleration due to gravity.
Albert Einstein showed that mass and energy are connected.

abschnitte.text: In everyday life people say a sack of potatoes weighs 5 kilograms. In physics this is its **mass**. The **weight**, more precisely the gravitational force, is the force with which the Earth pulls on the sack. On Earth it is about 49 newtons, on the Moon only about a sixth of that, but the mass stays 5 kilograms.

Mass makes bodies **inert**. A full shopping trolley is harder to start pushing than an empty one, because it has more mass. This is true even in weightless space. Newton's second law says: force is mass times **acceleration**.

All bodies with mass attract each other; this is **gravitation**. Because the Earth has a huge mass, it pulls on us strongly. Weight is calculated as mass times the acceleration due to gravity, on Earth about 9.81 metres per second squared. Amazingly, inertial and gravitational mass are always exactly the same.

With a **beam balance** you compare a mass with known weights; this works anywhere. A spring balance or bathroom scale, on the other hand, actually measures weight. In Switzerland the Federal Institute of Metrology, **METAS** for short, in Bern-Wabern makes sure that scales measure correctly. Since 2019 the kilogram has been defined through a constant of nature.

In 1905 Albert Einstein discovered that mass and energy are connected. His famous formula is **E = mc²**. Even a tiny mass corresponds to a huge amount of energy. In the Sun, mass is constantly being turned into energy; that is where its light comes from.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which a body is attracted by a celestial body.
The force of attraction between all bodies with mass.
A body's resistance to changes in its motion.
How quickly a falling body gets faster, on Earth about 9.81 m/s².

gewusst: Einstein wrote his paper on E = mc² in 1905, when he was working at the patent office in Bern.
A person of 60 kilograms would have more than twice the weight on Jupiter as on Earth.
Through nuclear fusion the Sun loses about four million tonnes of mass every second.

teile.einleitung: Surface tension is a property of liquids that makes their surface behave like a thin, stretched skin. That is why drops of water are round and small insects can walk across a pond. You can easily watch it for yourself with a coin and a pipette.
wichtigste: Surface tension holds the surface of a liquid together like a skin.
It arises because particles at the surface are only pulled inwards.
It is given in the unit newtons per metre.
At 20 degrees, water has a surface tension of around 73 millinewtons per metre.
Washing-up liquid lowers the surface tension of water.
As the temperature rises, the surface tension decreases.
Mercury has a much higher surface tension than water.

abschnitte.text: Every liquid is made of tiny particles, the **molecules**, which attract each other. Inside the liquid, a molecule is pulled equally strongly from all sides. But at the surface there are no neighbours above, so these molecules are only pulled **inwards**. This makes the liquid try to keep its surface as small as possible, and a kind of stretched skin forms.

For a simple experiment, you clean and dry a coin and lay it down flat. Then, with a pipette, you slowly and carefully drip water onto it so that the water skin does not break. A surprisingly high, curved **hill of water** forms. Only when there are too many drops does the water overflow, and you write down how many drops fitted.

For the same volume, a **sphere** has the smallest surface. That is why small drops of water form perfect spheres in weightlessness, for example on the space station. Soap bubbles are round too, and inside them there is a slight excess pressure. For a soap bubble with a radius of 2 centimetres, it is only about 5 pascals.

Washing-up liquid and soap contain **surfactants**, which gather at the surface of the water and greatly lower the surface tension. That is why water with washing-up liquid can get into fibres and cracks better and loosen dirt. Heat also lowers the surface tension, which is why hot water cleans better. Mercury, on the other hand, has a much higher surface tension than water and forms shiny little balls.

The **pond skater** is an insect that can glide over ponds without sinking, thanks to surface tension. A metal paper clip laid down carefully can also stay lying on water. Plants use surface tension, together with other forces, to carry water upwards in fine tubes. Morning dew forms small round drops on leaves.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny particle that a substance is made of.
A substance in soap that lowers surface tension.
An insect that can walk on the surface of water.
The unit in which surface tension is measured.

gewusst: If you put a drop of washing-up liquid next to a floating paper clip, it suddenly sinks, because the water skin gives way.
Without surface tension, you could not make soap bubbles.
Water has one of the highest surface tensions of all ordinary liquids.

teile.einleitung: A marble run is a track on which small balls, the marbles, roll down through channels, bends and tunnels. You can buy one or simply build one yourself out of cardboard. While doing so, you learn a lot in a playful way about gravity, speed and friction.
wichtigste: On a marble run, marbles roll along: small balls made of glass, wood or clay.
For a marble to roll by itself, the track must slope downwards.
You can easily build your own marble run from cardboard tubes.
On bends, the track needs high edges, or fast marbles fly out.
If a marble has to roll uphill, it slows down.
On a flat carpet, the marble slows down and comes to a stop.
Lots of zigzag bends make the ride long.

abschnitte.text: A **marble run**, also called a ball track, is made of channels, tubes or building blocks with grooves. You put a **marble** in at the top, and it comes out again at the bottom. On the way, it rolls through bends, tunnels, funnels and sometimes over switches. In Switzerland, marbles are also called Chlicker.

**Gravity** always pulls the marble downwards. If the track slopes, the ball rolls downhill and gets faster. The steeper the slope, the faster it gets. If it has to go uphill for a bit, it slows down and only makes it if it has enough momentum.

A fast marble wants to keep going straight on at a bend. High edges or banked bends keep it on the track, like on a bobsleigh run. On a flat carpet, **friction** slows the ball down until it stops. On smooth wood or plastic, it rolls much further.

You can build your own track out of **cardboard tubes** from kitchen roll, sticky tape and a wall. You cut the tubes open lengthways and stick them below each other at a slant and in a zigzag. The more bends, the longer the marble is on its way. With a stopwatch, you can measure which design gives the longest ride.

The Swiss company **Cuboro** makes well-known marble runs out of wooden cubes. Grooves and tunnels are milled into the cubes, which can be put together in new ways again and again. There are also plastic systems and huge marble runs in museums and playgrounds. While building, you practise planning, trying things out and working carefully.

Around 400 years ago, the scientist **Galileo Galilei** rolled balls down sloping channels. In this way he studied how objects get faster and faster as they fall. On a marble run, you can see how height is turned into movement. If, for example, 3 red and 4 blue marbles roll, that makes 7 altogether, and you can hold races between them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small ball made of glass, clay, wood or stone for playing with.
The force with which the Earth pulls everything downwards.
A force that slows down movement when two things rub against each other.
How steeply a track is tilted downwards.

gewusst: Marbles are among the oldest toys in the world; children in ancient Egypt and ancient Rome already played with them.
On a track, a marble never quite rolls back up to the same height it started from, because friction always takes away some energy.

teile.einleitung: Matter waves are one of the most astonishing ideas in physics. Not only light but also particles such as electrons sometimes behave like waves. This idea comes from Louis de Broglie and is a cornerstone of quantum physics.
wichtigste: Every particle has a wavelength, the de Broglie wavelength λ equals h divided by p.
Here h is the Planck constant and p the momentum, that is mass times velocity.
For slow particles, twice the velocity means half the wavelength.
At the same velocity a proton has a much smaller wavelength than an electron.
In 1927 the Davisson and Germer experiment confirmed the wave nature of electrons through diffraction by a nickel crystal.
Louis de Broglie received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1929.
For everyday objects such as a tennis ball the wavelength is unimaginably small.

abschnitte.text: For a long time people thought that light was a wave and electrons were small balls. In his doctoral thesis in 1924 the Frenchman **Louis de Broglie** suggested that particles also have wave properties. These waves are called **matter waves**. The heavier and faster a particle is, the shorter its wavelength.

The **de Broglie wavelength** is calculated with λ equals h divided by p. The **Planck constant** h is a tiny constant of nature of about 6.6 times 10 to the power of minus 34. An electron at a million metres per second has a wavelength of around 0.73 nanometres. A tennis ball of 57 grams at 50 metres per second, by contrast, only reaches about 2 times 10 to the power of minus 34 metres.

In 1927 Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer in the USA fired electrons at a **nickel crystal**. The electrons were diffracted in particular directions, as only waves do. Almost at the same time George Paget Thomson in Scotland showed the same with thin metal foils. Davisson and Thomson received the Nobel Prize for this in 1937.

Matter waves explain why electrons in an atom have only very particular orbits. In the Bohr model of the atom, a whole number of wavelengths fits onto an allowed orbit as a **standing wave**. Other orbits are not possible, because the wave would cancel itself out. Modern quantum mechanics developed from this.

The **electron microscope** uses the very small wavelength of electrons. With it you can see much finer things than with light, even individual rows of atoms. Slow, so-called thermal **neutrons** also have a wavelength in the range of the distances between atoms. At the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen in the canton of Aargau, researchers use neutrons to study the structure of crystals and materials.

begriffe.erklaerung: Distance from one wave crest to the next.
Mass times velocity, a measure of how much a body is moving.
When a wave spreads out in new directions behind an obstacle or grating.
Part of physics that describes the world of the smallest particles.

gewusst: In 1999 researchers in Vienna showed that even football-shaped molecules made of 60 carbon atoms have wave properties.
Louis de Broglie came from a French noble family and first studied history before switching to physics.

teile.einleitung: Max Planck was a German physicist and is regarded as the founder of quantum physics. He discovered that energy is given off only in tiny portions. For this discovery he received the Nobel Prize, and many research institutes still bear his name today.
wichtigste: Max Planck was born in Kiel in 1858 and died in Göttingen in 1947.
In his doctoral thesis he dealt with thermodynamics, the study of heat.
In 1900 he presented his idea that energy occurs in small portions, the quanta.
He received the Nobel Prize in Physics for the year 1918.
The Planck constant h is one of the most important constants of nature.
The Max Planck Society, a large research organisation, is named after him.
The first Max Planck Medal went to Planck himself and to Albert Einstein.

abschnitte.text: **Max Planck** was born on 23 April 1858 in Kiel and grew up in Munich. He was also very gifted at music and played the piano brilliantly. His professor Philipp von Jolly is said to have advised him not to study physics, because almost everything there had already been discovered. Planck did it anyway and wrote his doctoral thesis on **thermodynamics**.

Around 1900 Planck studied what light hot bodies give off, for example glowing iron. The known formulas did not fit the measurements. Planck found a solution by assuming that energy is given off only in small packets, the **quanta**. He presented this in Berlin on 14 December 1900; this day is regarded as the birthday of quantum physics.

The size of an energy packet depends on the **Planck constant** h, which is about 6.626 times 10 to the power of minus 34 joule seconds. From h and other constants of nature Planck formed natural units. The **Planck length** is around 1.6 times 10 to the power of minus 35 metres, the Planck time around 5 times 10 to the power of minus 44 seconds. Since 2019 even the kilogram has been defined through the Planck constant.

For his discovery Planck received the Nobel Prize in Physics for the year 1918. The German Physical Society created the **Max Planck Medal**, which in 1929 went first to Planck himself and to Albert Einstein. Planck supported the young Einstein, who was then working at the patent office in Bern. He taught as a professor in Berlin for many years.

After the Second World War the Kaiser Wilhelm Society, which Planck had led, was renamed the **Max Planck Society**. Today it runs numerous research institutes in Germany. In 2009 the European Space Agency named a satellite Planck. It measured the faint heat radiation left over from the Big Bang.

begriffe.erklaerung: Smallest packet of energy that can be given off or taken in.
Constant of nature h that determines the size of the energy packets.
Part of physics that deals with heat and energy.
A number in physics that is the same everywhere in the universe.

gewusst: Planck's radiation law also says that the Sun, at around 5800 degrees, shines most strongly at about 500 nanometres, that is greenish blue light.
At first Planck thought his quanta were just a mathematical trick and did not himself believe that they really exist.
An asteroid and a crater on the Moon also bear the name Planck.

teile.einleitung: The Large Hadron Collider, LHC for short, is the largest particle accelerator in the world. It lies in a circular tunnel deep underground near Geneva, on the border between Switzerland and France. Here researchers make tiny particles collide at almost the speed of light to study the building blocks of the universe.
wichtigste: The LHC belongs to the CERN research centre near Geneva.
Its ring-shaped tunnel has a circumference of about 27 kilometres.
On average the tunnel lies about 100 metres underground.
In the LHC mainly protons, but also lead nuclei, collide.
In 2008 a particle beam circulated in the LHC for the first time.
In 2012 the Higgs boson was discovered at the LHC.
The protons fly at more than 99.9999 per cent of the speed of light.

abschnitte.titel: Where and what is the LHC?
abschnitte.text: The **LHC** is at the **CERN** research centre, which was founded in 1954 and has its headquarters in Meyrin near Geneva. Its tunnel is about 27 kilometres long and runs beneath fields and villages in the canton of Geneva and in France. Before the LHC, the same tunnel housed the **LEP** accelerator, the Large Electron-Positron Collider. The name means roughly “large hadron collider”, hadrons being particles such as protons.

In the LHC two particle beams circulate in opposite directions in pipes containing almost empty space, a **vacuum**. Electric fields accelerate the protons until they reach more than 99.9999 per cent of the speed of light. More than 1200 huge **superconducting magnets** keep them on their circular path, and for this they are cooled to about minus 271 °C. At four points the beams are made to collide, and huge detectors such as ATLAS and CMS record what is produced.

Mostly **protons** are made to collide, and for a few weeks a year lead nuclei too. When it was built, a collision energy of 14 teraelectronvolts (TeV) was planned as the design value for proton-proton collisions. In the collisions kinetic energy turns into new particles, which often exist for only tiny fractions of a second. From the tracks of these particles researchers learn how matter is built up.

The most famous discovery at the LHC is the **Higgs boson**, announced in July 2012. Physicists, including Peter Higgs, had predicted this particle as early as 1964. It belongs to a field that explains why other elementary particles have mass. Peter Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2013 for the prediction.

In September 2008 a particle beam circulated in the LHC for the first time. Only a few days later a faulty electrical connection between two magnets caused a serious breakdown, and the repair took more than a year. Since 2010 the LHC has been delivering data, interrupted by longer breaks for upgrades. With the upgrade to the **High-Luminosity LHC**, there should be many more collisions per unit of time in a few years.

Thousands of researchers from all over the world work together at CERN, and Switzerland is one of its founding members. The **World Wide Web** was also invented here in 1989, to exchange research data. A worldwide computer network has been built to analyse the huge amounts of data from the LHC. Visitors can see exhibitions at CERN and learn a lot about particle physics.

begriffe.erklaerung: Facility that brings tiny particles to very high speeds.
Positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
State of some materials at very low temperature in which current flows without resistance.
Huge measuring device that records the tracks of the particles produced.

gewusst: The protons in the LHC go round the 27 kilometre ring more than 11,000 times a second.
The ATLAS detector is about half a football pitch long and as tall as a building several storeys high.
The pressure in the beam pipes is about ten times lower than on the surface of the Moon.

teile.einleitung: In circular motion an object moves along a circular path around a centre. Examples are a merry-go-round, the hands of a clock or the Moon going round the Earth. Even if the speed stays the same, every circular motion needs a force pulling towards the centre.
wichtigste: In circular motion an object moves along a circular path.
Even at constant speed, circular motion is accelerated, because the direction keeps changing.
The force that keeps an object on its circular path is called the centripetal force.
The centripetal force points towards the centre and does no work.
If the string holding a stone breaks, it flies straight on along the tangent.
The frequency of circular motion is given in hertz.
Relative to the road, a point on the rim of a rolling bike wheel traces out a cycloid.

abschnitte.text: In **circular motion** the distance to the centre always stays the same; this distance is the **radius**. If the speed stays constant, it is called uniform circular motion. The time for one complete turn is called the **period**. The number of turns per second is the frequency, measured in hertz.

In physics acceleration means any change in velocity, including a change of direction. In circular motion the velocity always points along the **tangent**, at right angles to the radius. Because this direction keeps changing, every circular motion is accelerated. That is why, if the string of a whirled stone breaks, it flies straight on along the tangent.

For an object to stay on its circular path, a force must act towards the centre, the **centripetal force**. It is calculated as mass times speed squared, divided by the radius. A car of 1000 kilograms travelling at 20 metres per second round a bend with a radius of 50 metres needs a force of 8000 newtons. Because the force is always at right angles to the motion, it does no **work** and the speed stays the same.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the force come from?
abschnitte.text: For a stone on a string, the string provides the centripetal force. For a car going round a bend on a flat road, it is the **static friction** between the tyres and the road. If the road is icy, this force is missing and the car slides straight on. The Moon is kept in its orbit by the Earth's **gravitational force**.

On a merry-go-round you feel a force outwards, the **centrifugal force**. It is an apparent force that you only feel in the rotating system. The spin cycle of a washing machine uses circular motion to drive water out of the washing. A point on the rim of a rolling bike wheel turns around the axle, but relative to the road it traces out an arched path called a **cycloid**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Distance from the centre to the edge of the circle.
Force that pulls an object towards the centre of the circle.
Straight line that touches a circle at only one point.
Unit of frequency; one hertz is one turn per second.

gewusst: The Earth moves along its almost circular orbit round the Sun at about 30 kilometres per second.
You are also in circular motion, because the Earth turns once on its axis every day.
In a loop on a roller coaster the track pushes you inwards, which is why you do not fall out at the top.

teile.einleitung: A mobile is a hanging, moving work of art made of rods, threads and figures that float in balance. Even a light draught makes it turn and sway. The American artist Alexander Calder made this art form famous.
wichtigste: A mobile is a hanging, moving work of art.
The name comes from “mobile”, which means able to move.
Alexander Calder made the mobile famous in the 1930s.
A draught sets a mobile moving without a motor.
For a mobile to hang level, the weights must balance according to the law of the lever.
If a rod hangs at a slant, you move the hanging thread closer to the heavier figure.
A mobile often hangs above a baby's cot.

abschnitte.text: A mobile is made of several horizontal rods with figures or more rods hanging from their ends. Everything hangs on threads from the ceiling. The parts turn freely and do not touch each other. Because the picture keeps changing, the mobile is also called **kinetic art**, which means art of movement.

The American artist **Alexander Calder** lived from 1898 to 1976. He had first studied mechanical engineering and so understood balance and technology. In the early 1930s, he built his first hanging works of art from wire and painted sheet metal in Paris. The artist Marcel Duchamp gave them the name “mobile”.

Each rod of a mobile is a **lever** that hangs from its thread as if from a pivot. It hangs level when weight times distance is the same on both sides. So two fish of equal weight at the same distance from the middle keep the rod level. If one figure is heavier, it has to hang closer to the hanging point, which is why you move the thread towards the heavy side.

A mobile does not need a motor. A light **draught** from an open window or warm rising air is enough. Because the parts are so finely balanced, a tiny force is enough to make them turn. The movements are slow and calm, which is why mobiles often have a soothing effect.

Many parents hang a mobile above a baby's cot. Babies enjoy following the shapes and colours with their eyes. Mobiles also hang as decorations in classrooms, shops and museums. Large mobiles by Calder hang, for example, in museums and entrance halls in the USA and in Europe.

You can make a simple mobile from **twigs**, threads and paper figures. It is best to start at the bottom with the smallest rod and balance it. Then you hang this part from a larger rod and balance it again. This way, a floating work of art grows level by level.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rod that moves around a pivot and can balance forces.
A state in which all forces cancel each other out and nothing tips over.
Works of art that move.
The point a lever turns around; in a mobile, the hanging thread.

gewusst: As a young man, Calder also built a small circus out of wire, with which he gave performances.
Calder's counterparts to mobiles, which stand firmly on the ground, are called stabiles.
Some of Calder's mobiles are several metres in size and weigh hundreds of kilograms.

teile.einleitung: The speed of light is the speed at which light travels, almost 300,000 kilometres per second in a vacuum. Nothing in the universe is faster. It is so important that even the metre is defined by it.
wichtigste: The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second.
In physics it is written with the letter c.
In water and glass light is slower, about 200,000 km per second in glass.
According to Einstein's theory of relativity, no object with mass can reach the speed of light.
In 1676 Ole Rømer was the first to show that light has a finite speed.
Since 1983 the metre has been defined by the speed of light.
In one year light travels about 9.46 trillion kilometres; this distance is called a light year.

abschnitte.text: In a **vacuum** light travels 299,792,458 metres in one second, almost 300,000 kilometres. In one second it could go about 7.5 times round the Earth's equator. A radio signal takes about 1.3 seconds to travel from the Earth to the Moon, about 384,000 km. Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach us. So when we see the Sun, we see it as it was 8 minutes ago.

In physics the speed of light is written with the letter **c**. It probably comes from the Latin word “celeritas”, which means swiftness. Since 1983 the value has been fixed exactly. Since then the **metre** has been defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. So the speed of light is no longer measured but serves as a yardstick.

When light passes from air into water or glass, it slows down. In glass its speed is about 200,000 km per second. As a result light is bent as it crosses over; this is called **refraction**. That is why a spoon in a glass of water looks bent. Lenses in glasses, cameras and microscopes work on this principle.

For a long time people believed light was infinitely fast. In 1676 the Danish astronomer **Ole Rømer** observed the eclipses of one of Jupiter's moons and noticed delays. He realised that light needs time to travel from Jupiter to the Earth. In the 19th century precise measurements were made on Earth with toothed wheels and rotating mirrors. The **Michelson-Morley experiment** of 1887 showed that the speed of light is the same in all directions.

In 1905 **Albert Einstein** published his special **theory of relativity** in Bern. According to it, the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, however fast they are moving. No object with mass, and so no spaceship, can reach it. The closer you came to it, the more energy you would need, in the end an infinite amount. The theory also predicts that time passes more slowly for clocks moving very fast.

Because space is so vast, large distances are measured in **light years**. A light year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion kilometres. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light years away. Radio signals also travel at the speed of light. If a signal takes 10 minutes to reach a space probe, the probe is about 180 million km away.

begriffe.erklaerung: Speed of light, almost 300,000 km per second in a vacuum.
Space containing almost no particles and no air.
Distance light travels in one year.
Bending of light as it passes into another material.
Albert Einstein's theory about space, time and motion.

gewusst: When Albert Einstein developed the special theory of relativity, he was working at the patent office in Bern.
When we look at the night sky, we see some stars as they looked thousands of years ago.
A ray of light needs only about a thousandth of a second to travel from Geneva to Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Muscle power is the force that people and animals produce with their muscles. We use it to walk, jump, lift and breathe. Long before there were engines, the muscle power of people and animals was the most important driving force in the world.
wichtigste: We move our bodies with our muscles.
Humans have more than 600 muscles.
Most muscles are attached to the bones by tendons.
Muscles can only pull, not push, which is why they work in pairs.
The heart is a muscle that works without a break for a whole lifetime.
The largest human muscle is the gluteus maximus, the big buttock muscle.
A bicycle without a motor is driven by muscle power alone.

abschnitte.text: A muscle is made up of many long **muscle fibres** that can contract. As they do, the muscle becomes shorter and thicker and pulls on a bone. The commands for this come from the brain through the nerves. The muscle gets the energy for this from food and from the oxygen that the blood brings.

Most muscles are attached to the bones by **tendons**. Because muscles can only pull, there is always an opposing muscle. The **biceps** on the upper arm bends the arm, and the triceps on the back straightens it again. Bones and joints act like levers, very much as in physics.

We move skeletal muscles on purpose, for example when walking or throwing. Smooth muscles work by themselves, for example in the stomach and intestines. A special kind is the **heart muscle**, which pumps around the clock without getting tired. In children at rest, it beats about 80 to 100 times a minute.

Humans have more than 600 muscles; in adults they make up about a third to almost half of body weight. The largest is the **gluteus maximus**, the big buttock muscle, which helps us stand up and climb stairs. The smallest muscle is in the ear and is only a few millimetres long. For their size, the chewing muscles are among the strongest muscles.

A bicycle, a rowing boat or a scooter without a motor runs on muscle power alone. In the past, horses and oxen pulled ploughs and carts, and people carried heavy loads on their backs. In Switzerland, muleteers carried goods with mules over Alpine passes such as the Gotthard. Muscle power is clean and quiet and produces no exhaust fumes.

If you do sport regularly, you make your muscles stronger and give them more stamina. After an unusual amount of exercise, you often feel **sore muscles** the next day. This is caused by tiny injuries in the muscle fibres, which the body repairs within a few days. Enough sleep, protein in your food and warming up before sport help the muscles.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long, thin cell that can contract.
A tough band that connects a muscle to a bone.
A muscle that reverses the movement of another muscle.
Pain in the muscles after unusual effort.

gewusst: Breathing also happens with muscle power, because the diaphragm contracts and lets air flow into the lungs.
Dozens of muscles are also at work at the same time when you speak.
The tongue is made almost entirely of muscles.

teile.einleitung: Refraction means that a ray of light changes direction when it passes at an angle from one material into another, for example from air into water. That is why a straw in a glass of water looks bent. Without refraction there would be no glasses, no magnifying glasses and no rainbows.
wichtigste: Refraction is the change in direction of light as it passes between two materials.
It happens because light is slower in water or glass than in air.
A straw in a glass of water looks bent because of refraction.
A converging lens brings parallel rays of light together at a focal point.
Diverging lenses help short-sighted people.
A prism splits white light into the colours of the rainbow.

abschnitte.text: When light passes at an angle from air into water, it changes direction. This bend is called **refraction**. It happens because light is slower in water and glass than in air. That is why a straw in a glass looks bent, and a stream looks less deep than it really is.

You can imagine light as a row of children marching. If one end of the row reaches deep sand at an angle, it slows down and the whole row turns. If light hits the surface straight on, on the other hand, it is not bent. How strongly a material bends light is given by its **refractive index**.

Lenses are curved pieces of glass that bend light in a controlled way. A **converging lens** is thicker in the middle and brings parallel rays together at a **focal point**. Magnifying glasses, cameras and our eye contain converging lenses. A diverging lens is thinner in the middle and spreads the rays apart.

With **short-sightedness** you see well close up, but things in the distance are blurred. **Diverging lenses** help here. With long-sightedness, on the other hand, you need converging lenses. Contact lenses also work on the same principle.

A **prism** is a triangular piece of glass. It bends the different colours of light by different amounts, violet light the most and red light the least. In this way white light is split into the colours of the rainbow. In a **rainbow**, millions of raindrops do the job of the prism.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows how strongly a material bends light.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and brings light together.
A lens that is thinner in the middle and spreads light apart.
The point where a converging lens brings the rays of light together.

gewusst: A fish in the water is really in a different place from where it appears to be when seen from above.
The English scientist Isaac Newton showed with a prism that white light is made up of colours.
Hot air above a road also bends light, which is how a mirage forms.

teile.einleitung: The mixing temperature is the temperature reached when you bring a warm and a cold substance together. If you mix hot and cold water, the result lies somewhere in between. With a simple rule, you can work out exactly where.
wichtigste: The basis is that the heat given off equals the heat taken in.
Equal masses of water at 20 and 60 degrees together give 40 degrees.
The rule for calculating it is named after the physicist Georg Wilhelm Richmann.
The mixing temperature depends on mass, temperature and specific heat capacity.
Water has a very large heat capacity and therefore strongly affects the mixture.
If ice melts in the mixture, extra heat of fusion is needed.
Calculations usually ignore heat lost to the surroundings.

abschnitte.text: When two objects at different temperatures come together, **heat** flows from the warm one to the cold one. This continues until both are equally warm. This shared final temperature is called the **mixing temperature**. It always lies between the two starting temperatures.

The physicist **Georg Wilhelm Richmann** lived in Saint Petersburg in the 18th century. He realised that the heat given off by the warm substance is exactly as large as the heat taken in by the cold one. This leads to **Richmann's mixing rule**. For each substance you multiply mass, heat capacity and temperature, and divide the sum by the sum of mass times heat capacity.

With equal amounts of water, the mixture is exactly in the middle: 20 and 60 degrees give 40 degrees. If you mix 2 kilograms at 10 degrees with 1 kilogram at 70 degrees, you get 30 degrees. 30 litres at 50 degrees and 10 litres at 10 degrees give 40 degrees. The more there is of one kind, the closer the mixture is to its temperature.

Not every substance stores the same amount of heat. This is described by the **specific heat capacity**: for water around 4180 joules per kilogram and degree, for iron only around 450. If you drop 0.1 kilograms of iron at 200 degrees into 0.3 kilograms of water at 20 degrees, the water only rises to about 26 degrees. Even with 1 kilogram of hot water and 1 kilogram of cold copper, the mixture is close to the water temperature.

If you put ice into warm water, the ice first has to melt. This needs the **heat of fusion**, 334 kilojoules per kilogram for ice, without the temperature rising. That is why ice cubes cool a drink so well. 0.1 kilograms of ice in 0.5 kilograms of water at 40 degrees end up at only about 20 degrees.

If you want a bath at 37 degrees and have 50 litres of water at 15 degrees, you need around 48 litres of water at 60 degrees. The rule also helps with tea and cold milk or when cooling a baby's bottle. In reality, some heat is always lost to the air and the container. In the laboratory, it is therefore measured in a well-insulated container, the **calorimeter**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that flows from a warmer object to a colder one.
How much energy is needed to warm 1 kilogram of a substance by 1 degree.
Energy needed to melt a solid substance.
A well-insulated container in which amounts of heat are measured.

gewusst: Because water can store so much heat, large lakes such as Lake Geneva bring milder winters to their shores.
Georg Wilhelm Richmann was killed in 1753 during an experiment with lightning.

teile.einleitung: Newton's law of gravitation describes how strongly two masses attract each other. It explains why an apple falls from a tree and why the Moon circles the Earth. Isaac Newton published it in 1687, linking heaven and Earth in a single rule.
wichtigste: The larger the masses, the more strongly they attract each other.
If you double both masses, the force becomes four times as large.
If you triple the distance, the force falls to a ninth.
The apple pulls on the Earth exactly as strongly as the Earth pulls on the apple.
Spherically symmetrical celestial bodies can be treated like point masses at their centre.
The force between the Earth and the Moon is about 2 times 10 to the power of 20 newtons.
The law could not fully explain the precession of Mercury's perihelion.

abschnitte.text: Two objects attract each other with a force that is proportional to both **masses**. At the same time, the force decreases with the square of the distance. The formula is F equals G times m1 times m2 divided by r squared. G is the **gravitational constant**, a very small number of about 6.67 times 10 to the power of minus 11.

If you double both masses, the force becomes two times two, so four times as large. If you triple one mass and halve the distance, the force rises to twelve times as much. The distance is always measured between the centres. This holds exactly for planets if they are **spherically symmetrical**.

**Isaac Newton** wondered whether the same force moves the apple and the Moon. The Moon is around 60 Earth radii from the centre of the Earth. According to the law, its acceleration should therefore be only 1/3600 of the acceleration due to gravity on Earth. That matched its orbit exactly, and Newton published the law in 1687 in his work **Principia**.

According to Newton's third law, the apple pulls on the Earth just as strongly as the other way round. But because the Earth is enormous, you do not notice it move. Since the force is proportional to mass, all objects fall equally fast without air. In 1971, the astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, and both landed at the same time.

In 1798, the Englishman Henry **Cavendish** used a delicate torsion balance to measure the attraction between lead balls. This made it possible to determine G and even to calculate the mass of the Earth. Using the law, astronomers predicted the planet Neptune in 1846 before anyone had seen it. Only the small **precession of the perihelion** of Mercury remained a mystery; it was not explained until Einstein's general theory of relativity of 1915.

The pull of the Moon and the Sun on the oceans causes the **tides**. Satellites and the International Space Station stay in their orbits thanks to gravity. The paths of space probes are also calculated with Newton's law. The attraction between two people, on the other hand, is so tiny that you cannot feel it.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of attraction between all objects that have mass.
A fixed number G that tells you how strong gravity is.
How much matter an object has, measured in kilograms.
The slow shifting of the point of a planet's orbit closest to the Sun.

gewusst: Newton is said to have got the idea from a falling apple in his family's garden, but whether the story is exactly true is uncertain.
If the Earth were only half as big but had the same mass, you would be four times as heavy on its surface.

teile.einleitung: The Michelson and Morley experiment was a famous experiment from 1887 with which two American researchers wanted to detect the so-called ether. They did not find it. It was precisely this surprising result that later helped to establish the theory of relativity.
wichtigste: The experiment was meant to detect the motion of the Earth through the ether.
Albert A. Michelson and Edward W. Morley carried it out in Cleveland in the USA in 1887.
They used an interferometer.
The Earth moves round the Sun at around 30 km/s, which should have produced a measurable effect.
An ether wind would have shown up as a shift of the interference fringes when the apparatus was turned.
The apparatus lay on a stone slab that floated in mercury.
The expected shift did not appear; this is called the null result.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century people knew that light is a wave. Water waves need water, sound waves need air, so people thought that light also needed a substance. This invisible substance was called the **ether**. If the Earth moves through the ether, an ether wind should arise that makes light faster or slower depending on the direction.

Albert A. **Michelson** was a physicist and a master of precise light measurements; he had already made a first attempt in Germany in 1881. Edward W. **Morley** was above all a chemist and known for very careful measurements. Together they carried out the experiment in 1887 in **Cleveland** in the US state of Ohio. In 1907 Michelson became the first American to receive the Nobel Prize in Physics.

In the **interferometer** a beam of light is split by a half-silvered mirror into two beams that travel at right angles to each other. Mirrors send them back, and the beams meet again. In doing so they overlap to form bright and dark stripes, the **interference fringes**. To increase the sensitivity, the researchers made the light travel back and forth several times between mirrors.

The Earth races round the Sun at around 30 km/s, so the ether wind should have blown strongly. If you turn the interferometer, the fringes should shift, because the light paths change differently. So that the apparatus could be turned with little vibration, it lay on a heavy **stone slab** that floated in a basin of mercury. But the fringes hardly shifted, far less than expected.

The **null result** was a big surprise. Hendrik Antoon Lorentz and others tried to explain it with a shortening of moving bodies. In 1905 in Bern, with his special theory of relativity, Albert Einstein showed that no ether is needed at all and that light travels at the same speed for all observers. Interferometers based on Michelson's principle are now even used to detect gravitational waves from space.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imagined, invisible substance in which light was supposed to travel.
A measuring device that splits light beams and overlaps them again.
The overlapping of waves, in which they strengthen or cancel each other.
An experimental result in which the expected effect does not occur.

gewusst: The Michelson and Morley experiment is regarded as the most famous failed experiment in the history of physics.
The LIGO gravitational wave detectors have arms 4 kilometres long and work on the same basic principle.
The floating stone slab could be turned slowly with a small push without wobbling.

teile.einleitung: Moonlight is the light that reaches us from the Moon at night. But the Moon does not shine by itself; it only reflects sunlight like a big grey mirror. At full moon it is so bright that you can even cast a faint shadow outdoors.
wichtigste: The Moon does not shine by itself; it reflects sunlight.
Moonlight is brightest at full moon.
At new moon, you cannot see the Moon in the sky at all.
Moonlight is much weaker than sunlight.
Light from the Moon takes about one second to reach the Earth.
You cannot get sunburnt in moonlight, because it is too weak.
From the Earth we always see the same side of the Moon.

abschnitte.text: The Moon is a lump of rock with no light of its own. What we see as **moonlight** is sunlight reflected from its surface. The rock is rather dark grey and reflects only a small part of the light, roughly as much as old asphalt. Even so, the Moon looks brilliantly bright against the dark night sky. The light takes only about **one second** to cover the roughly 384,000 kilometres to the Earth.

Moonlight is brightest at **full moon**, when the whole side facing us is lit. At **new moon** we see the unlit side and the Moon is practically invisible. But even the full moon is several hundred thousand times fainter than the Sun. On a clear full-moon night, the light is still enough to cast a faint shadow and to make out your surroundings on a path.

In weak moonlight, our eyes mainly use the **rods**, which tell light from dark but hardly see colours. That is why a moonlit landscape looks almost black and white or slightly bluish. You cannot get sunburnt in moonlight, because it contains far too little ultraviolet radiation. If you go walking at night, it is best to let your eyes get used to the dark without a torch.

The Moon turns once on its own axis in exactly the same time that it takes to orbit the Earth. That is why it always shows us the same side, which is called **tidal locking**. People first saw the far side of the Moon in 1959, in photos from a Soviet space probe. On the near side you can see dark patches with the naked eye, the so-called **maria**, which were once thought to be seas.

Many animals are guided by moonlight, for example nocturnal birds and insects that use it to find their way. In the past, the full moon was important for people because they could travel or work on bright nights. On some clear nights, a **moonbow** even appears, which looks almost white to our eyes. Because of all the artificial lighting in towns, people notice moonlight less today than in the countryside or in the mountains.

begriffe.erklaerung: The phase of the Moon in which the whole visible side of the Moon is lit.
The phase of the Moon in which you cannot see the Moon.
The Moon turns in such a way that it always shows the Earth the same side.
Dark, flat plains on the Moon made of solidified lava.

gewusst: The Moon is actually quite dark; its rock reflects only about an eighth of the sunlight.
