When we look at the Moon, we see it as it was just over a second ago.
When there is a thin crescent moon, you can sometimes see the dark part glowing faintly, because light from the Earth falls on it.

teile.einleitung: Short-sightedness is a sight problem in which you see near things clearly but distant things blurred. The technical term for it is myopia. It can be corrected well with glasses or contact lenses, and today it is becoming more and more common among children and teenagers around the world.
wichtigste: Short-sighted people see clearly close up and blurred in the distance.
The sharp image of a distant object forms in front of the retina instead of on it.
The most common cause is an eyeball that is too long.
In children and teenagers short-sightedness can get worse, because the eyeball is still growing.
Glasses with diverging lenses or contact lenses correct short-sightedness.
Spending a lot of time outdoors in daylight helps to prevent short-sightedness.
In adults the cornea can be corrected permanently with a laser.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who is short-sighted can read a book well but sees the board in the classroom or road signs blurred. Experts call this **myopia**. The opposite is long-sightedness, in which things close up are mainly blurred. Short-sightedness is one of the most common eye conditions of all and has nothing to do with intelligence or hard work.

The eye works rather like a camera: the cornea and lens focus the light so that a sharp image forms on the **retina** at the back of the eye. In a short-sighted eye the eyeball is usually a little too long. The light from distant objects is therefore focused **in front of the retina** and arrives there only as a blurred spot. If you screw up your eyes, the image gets a little sharper through the small slit, much as with a pinhole camera.

In children and teenagers the **eyeball** is still growing, which is why short-sightedness can get worse during these years. The tendency towards it is partly inherited. Experts also suspect that a lot of close-up work such as reading or screen time and little daylight play a part. Eye doctors therefore advise children to spend a lot of time outdoors every day, because bright daylight seems to slow down the excessive growth of the eye.

Glasses for short-sighted people have **diverging lenses**, which are thinner in the middle than at the edge. They spread the light out a little so that the image forms exactly on the retina again. Their strength is given in dioptres, with a minus sign for short-sightedness. Instead of glasses you can also wear **contact lenses** directly on the eye. For children there are now also special spectacle lenses and eye drops meant to slow down its progress.

In adults whose eyes are no longer growing, short-sightedness can also be corrected by surgery. A **laser** makes the cornea a little flatter so that it bends light less strongly. Well-known methods include LASIK. Whether such treatment makes sense is decided by an eye doctor after thorough examinations.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technical term for short-sightedness.
Light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye on which the image forms.
Lens that is thinner in the middle and spreads rays of light apart.
Unit for the strength of a spectacle lens.
Transparent, curved layer at the front of the eye.

gewusst: In some big cities in East Asia most young adults are short-sighted.
An eyeball that is only about one millimetre too long can already cause noticeable short-sightedness.
Short-sighted people can often still read without reading glasses in old age if they take off their distance glasses.

teile.einleitung: A longitudinal wave is a wave in which the particles vibrate back and forth in the same direction as the wave travels. The best-known example is sound. In it, denser and thinner regions form in the air one after another and travel through space.
wichtigste: In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel.
Along the wave, compressions and rarefactions take turns.
Longitudinal waves travel through solids, liquids and gases.
Sound is a longitudinal wave, and it is much faster in steel than in air.
In a thin rod the speed depends on the modulus of elasticity and the density.
On a long coil spring you make a longitudinal wave by moving one end back and forth lengthways.
Elephants also communicate over long distances with infrasound.

abschnitte.text: A wave carries energy without the material travelling with it. In a **longitudinal wave**, the particles vibrate forwards and backwards, parallel to the direction in which the wave is moving. This creates **compressions**, where the particles are close together, and **rarefactions**, where they are further apart. The opposite is the transverse wave, in which the particles vibrate across the direction of travel, as in a wave on a rope.

A longitudinal wave can be seen well on a long, soft **coil spring**, such as a Slinky. You lay it on the floor and briefly move one end back and forth lengthways. Then a zone of tightly squeezed coils travels along the spring, followed by a zone of stretched-out coils. Each individual coil moves only a little way forwards and backwards.

**Sound** is a longitudinal wave. A loudspeaker squeezes the air in front of it and then pulls it apart again, creating changes in pressure that make our eardrum vibrate. In air at 20 °C sound travels at about 343 metres per second, in water at about 1500 and in steel at about 5000 metres per second. In solids the speed depends on the **modulus of elasticity**, in other words the stiffness, and on the density. In empty space there is no sound, because there are no particles there to vibrate.

If you breathe in helium, your voice sounds high and squeaky. This is not because your vocal cords vibrate faster. Sound is almost three times as fast in helium as in air, so the **resonances** in the throat and mouth shift to higher notes. You should still not breathe in helium, because then your body gets too little oxygen.

Elephants communicate with very low sounds below the limit of our hearing, called **infrasound**. These sounds carry many kilometres. Earthquakes also send out longitudinal waves, the **P waves**, which stands for primary waves. They are the fastest earthquake waves and therefore arrive first at the measuring stations, including those of the Swiss Seismological Service.

begriffe.erklaerung: Wave in which the particles vibrate in the direction of travel.
Wave in which the particles vibrate across the direction of travel.
A region in which the particles are squeezed closer together.
Sound so low that humans cannot hear it.
The fastest earthquake wave, a longitudinal wave.

gewusst: If someone knocks at the other end of a long metal railing, you hear the knock sooner with your ear against the metal than through the air, because sound is much faster in metal.
Whales can communicate with sound under water over hundreds of kilometres.

teile.einleitung: Lenz's law describes the direction in which an induced current flows. In short, a current produced by induction always works against its cause. That is why a copper pipe slows down a magnet falling through it, and why eddy current brakes work in trains and roller coasters.
wichtigste: An induced current always flows in such a direction that it works against its cause.
The law is named after the physicist Emil Lenz, who formulated it in 1834.
It follows from the conservation of energy.
In the law of induction, the minus sign expresses Lenz's law.
If you bring a north pole close to a closed metal ring, a north pole also forms on that side of the ring.
A strong magnet falls through an upright copper pipe much more slowly than in free fall.
A ring with a slit in it hardly moves, because no current can flow round it.

abschnitte.text: If you move a magnet near a loop of wire, the magnetic field inside the loop changes and a current is produced. This is called **electromagnetic induction**. **Lenz's law** says which way this current flows: so that its own magnetic field slows down the change. If you bring a north pole close to a closed metal ring, a north pole also forms on that side of the ring, and ring and magnet repel each other. If you pull the magnet away, the ring attracts it.

**Heinrich Friedrich Emil Lenz** was a Baltic German physicist who did research in Saint Petersburg. He formulated the law in 1834, only a few years after Michael Faraday had discovered induction. Lenz also studied how wires heat up when current flows. In today's law of induction a **minus sign** stands for his law.

Lenz's law follows from the **conservation of energy**. If the induced current attracted the magnet instead of slowing it down, the magnet would get faster and faster and produce energy out of nothing. That would be a perpetual motion machine, which cannot exist. Because the current brakes it, you have to do work to move the magnet, and exactly this work ends up in the electrical energy.

If you drop a strong neodymium magnet through an upright **copper pipe**, it floats through almost slowly. Eddy currents form in the pipe, and their magnetic field slows it down, even though copper itself is not magnetic. In **Elihu Thomson's jumping ring experiment**, an aluminium ring sits on a coil with an iron core, and when the current is switched on the ring jumps up. If the ring has a slit, almost nothing happens, because no current can flow round it.

**Eddy current brakes** use the law to slow down trains, roller coasters and drop towers without friction or wear. Modern high-speed trains such as the ICE also have such brakes. In old-style electricity meters, a magnet braked a turning aluminium disc. Induced currents also play an important part in induction hobs and in transformers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Producing an electric current with a changing magnetic field.
Circular current produced in a piece of metal by induction.
Energy cannot come out of nothing and cannot disappear.
A wound-up wire that can produce a magnetic field.

gewusst: A magnet falling through a thick copper pipe can take several seconds, although outside the pipe it would reach the bottom in a fraction of a second.
Eddy current brakes can never bring an object completely to a stop, because the braking force almost disappears at low speed.

teile.einleitung: Transmission loss is the electrical energy lost while it is carried through cables and lines. Because every wire has an electrical resistance, it gets warm when current flows through it. With high voltage and thick lines these losses can be kept small.
wichtigste: Every line has a resistance and turns part of the electrical energy into heat.
The power lost is resistance times current squared.
Over long distances electricity is carried at high voltage, because then the current, and with it the loss, is smaller for the same power.
At ten times the voltage, the line losses fall by a factor of 100.
If you double the cross section of the conductor, the losses halve for the same current.
Swissgrid runs the Swiss transmission grid at 380 kV and 220 kV.
For very long distances high-voltage direct current transmission is also used.

abschnitte.text: Every wire has an **electrical resistance**, measured in ohms. When current flows through it, the electrons bump into the atoms of the metal and the wire heats up. This heat is lost for the transmission of electricity; it is called **transmission loss**. The power lost is calculated as resistance times current squared. An extension cable of 0.6 ohms with 10 amperes flowing through it therefore loses 60 watts.

The power transmitted is voltage times current. If you want to carry a certain power, you can therefore choose a high voltage and a small current. Because the current is squared in the losses, this pays off enormously: ten times the voltage means a tenth of the current and only a hundredth of the loss. A line of 0.5 ohms carrying 100 kW at 10 kV has only 10 A and loses just 50 W. With **transformers** the voltage is stepped up at the power station and stepped down again before it reaches the houses.

Switzerland's extra-high-voltage grid belongs to the national grid company **Swissgrid**. It runs at 380,000 and 220,000 volts and connects power stations, cities and the neighbouring countries. Below it come grids with lower voltages, until the electricity comes out of the socket at 230 volts. The wiring in a house also has losses: on a supply cable of 0.4 ohms, 6.4 volts are lost at 16 amperes.

A thicker wire has a smaller resistance. If you double the **cross section of the conductor**, the resistance halves, and so does the loss for the same current. That is why cables for a cooker or an electric car charging point are thicker than for a bedside lamp. Overhead lines are usually made of aluminium cables with a steel core, because aluminium is light and conducts well. Copper conducts even better but is heavier and more expensive.

With alternating current, extra **reactive currents** arise in long cables, because the cable keeps charging up like a capacitor. **High-voltage direct current transmission**, HVDC for short, avoids this. It is used above all for very long lines and for submarine cables under the sea, for example between Norway and other European countries. Superconductors, which have no resistance at all, only work at very low temperatures and so far are used only in small pilot projects.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly a material holds back the flow of current, measured in ohms.
The electrical pressure that drives the current, measured in volts.
A device that raises or lowers the voltage of alternating current.
Very high electrical voltage; on long-distance lines hundreds of thousands of volts.
Abbreviation for high-voltage direct current transmission.

gewusst: On damp days you can often hear a crackling under high-voltage lines; it comes from small electrical discharges in the air.
A coiled extension cable can heat up so much with a strong current that it melts, so you should always unwind it completely under a heavy load.

teile.einleitung: The microwave oven is a kitchen appliance that heats food up in a few minutes. It uses invisible waves, which are also called microwaves. These make above all the water in the food vibrate and so warm it up.
wichtigste: The microwave oven heats food with invisible waves, microwaves.
Above all the water in the food gets warm.
In many appliances a plate turns so that the food heats up more evenly.
The mesh in the door keeps the rays inside the appliance.
Forks and other metal do not belong in the microwave oven.
A raw egg in its shell can burst in the microwave oven.
After heating, you should stir the food.
When the food is ready, you hear a beep or a ping.

abschnitte.text: **Microwaves** are invisible electromagnetic waves, similar to light or radio waves. Their wavelength lies between about one millimetre and one metre. In the kitchen appliance they usually have a frequency of 2.45 gigahertz and a wavelength of about 12 centimetres. Wi-Fi and mobile phones also use microwaves, but with much less power.

abschnitte.titel: How does the food get warm?
abschnitte.text: In the appliance a component called a **magnetron** produces the waves. They make the water molecules in the food turn back and forth very quickly. This movement turns into **heat**. That is why foods containing water, such as soup, get hot quickly, whereas a dry plate hardly does.

Inside, the waves form spots where it heats more strongly or more weakly. The **turntable** moves the food through these spots so that it heats up more evenly. Even so there are often cold and very hot spots. That is why you should stir after heating and wait a moment.

In the door there is a fine metal mesh. Its holes are much smaller than the wavelength of the microwaves, so the waves cannot get through. Light has a much shorter wavelength and passes through, so you can look inside. This principle is called a **Faraday cage**, and the appliance switches off immediately when the door is opened.

**Metal** such as forks or aluminium foil can make sparks and damage the appliance. A raw egg in its shell builds up steam pressure inside and can burst. Water can also sometimes be heated above its boiling point and suddenly bubble up. That is why you use microwave-safe dishes and let adults help.

In the 1940s the American engineer **Percy Spencer** was working on radar equipment. He noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. He tried it with maize kernels, which popped into popcorn. The first microwave ovens were as big as a fridge; today there is one in a great many kitchens.

begriffe.erklaerung: Component that produces the waves in a microwave oven.
How often a wave vibrates per second.
Metal casing or mesh that screens off electromagnetic waves.
Smallest particle of a substance, for example of water.

gewusst: Ice thaws only slowly in a microwave oven, because the water molecules in solid ice can hardly turn.
Microwaves penetrate only a few centimetres into the food; the inside then gets warm through heat conduction.

teile.einleitung: Michael Faraday was an English natural scientist who is among the most important discoverers in the field of electricity. He showed that you can produce electricity with a magnet and a coil of wire. It is remarkable that he never went to university but started out as a bookbinder.
wichtigste: Michael Faraday lived from 1791 to 1867 and came from England.
As a teenager he did an apprenticeship as a bookbinder.
He started as an assistant to the famous chemist Humphry Davy at the Royal Institution in London.
In 1831 he discovered electromagnetic induction, on which generators and bike dynamos are based.
He built one of the first electric motors and represented magnetic forces with field lines.
He discovered benzene and introduced the terms anode and cathode.
The unit farad for electrical capacitance is named after him.

abschnitte.text: Michael Faraday was born in London in 1791, the son of a poor blacksmith. At the age of 14 he began an apprenticeship as a **bookbinder**. In the process he read many of the books he bound, especially ones about chemistry and electricity. A customer gave him tickets for lectures by the famous chemist **Humphry Davy**. Faraday wrote the lectures out neatly, bound them into a book and sent it to Davy, who took him on as his assistant in 1813.

Faraday did research at the **Royal Institution** in London for most of his life. As Davy's assistant he also travelled through Europe and visited Geneva, among other places. Later he himself became a professor and head of the laboratory. In 1823 he was one of the first to liquefy the gas **chlorine** by pressure and cooling. In 1825 he discovered the compound **benzene** in lighting gas.

In 1821 Faraday built a device in which a wire carrying current turned round a magnet, one of the first **electric motors**. In 1831 he discovered **electromagnetic induction**: if you move a magnet in a coil of wire, current flows. All the generators in power stations and the **dynamo** on a bike are based on this discovery. To picture the force acting round a magnet, Faraday drew imaginary lines that are now called **field lines**. Iron filings round a magnet make these lines visible.

Faraday also investigated how electric current breaks substances down, which is called **electrolysis**. He set up laws for this that still apply today. In doing so he introduced technical terms such as **anode**, **cathode** and electrode. He also showed that a metal cage protects its inside from electric fields. This **Faraday cage** explains why you are safe in a car during a thunderstorm.

Faraday wanted to make science accessible to everyone. At Christmas he gave exciting **lectures for children and young people** at the Royal Institution. His lectures on the chemical history of a **candle** became especially famous and were later published as a book. These Christmas lectures still take place today and are shown on British television. Faraday died in 1867 and is regarded as one of the greatest experimental scientists of all time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The production of current in a coil when a magnetic field in it changes.
Imaginary lines that show how a magnetic or electric force acts.
Breaking down a substance with the help of electric current.
The unit of electrical capacitance, that is how much charge a component can store.
A liquid chemical compound of carbon and hydrogen.

gewusst: Faraday knew hardly any higher mathematics and described his discoveries almost without formulas.
He refused to be knighted and wanted simply to remain Mr Faraday.
The physicist Albert Einstein had a picture of Michael Faraday on the wall of his study.

teile.einleitung: A loudspeaker turns electrical signals into sounds that we can hear. It is found in mobile phones, headphones, radios and huge concert sound systems. Its secret is a cone that vibrates back and forth very quickly and so sets the air moving.
wichtigste: The cone of a loudspeaker makes the air vibrate.
In a dynamic loudspeaker the cone is connected to a voice coil.
Next to the voice coil is a permanent magnet.
The sound signal is an alternating current, so the cone moves back and forth.
Woofers mainly reproduce low notes, tweeters the high ones.
A crossover divides the sounds between tweeters and woofers.
A dynamic microphone works on the same principle, only the other way round.

abschnitte.text: A **loudspeaker** is a device that turns electrical signals into **sound**. Sound consists of tiny changes in air pressure that our ear picks up. A loudspeaker produces these changes by making a thin surface, the **cone**, move back and forth. The faster it vibrates, the higher the note, and the further it moves, the louder.

Most loudspeakers are **dynamic loudspeakers**. At the back of the cone is a coil of wire, the **voice coil**, which sits in the field of a **permanent magnet**. When current flows through the coil, it becomes a magnet itself and is attracted or repelled by the permanent magnet. Because the sound signal is an alternating current that keeps changing direction, the coil moves back and forth with the cone.

A single loudspeaker cannot reproduce all notes equally well. That is why there are large **woofers** for bass, midrange speakers and small **tweeters** for high notes. A woofer for particularly deep bass is called a subwoofer. An electrical circuit, the **crossover**, divides the sounds in a speaker box between the right loudspeakers.

The cone pushes the air not only forwards but at the same time backwards too. Without a cabinet, the sound waves from the front and back would cancel each other out, especially for low notes. That is why loudspeakers are built into a closed **cabinet** or into a large baffle. The shape and material of the box strongly affect how good the loudspeaker sounds.

A **dynamic microphone** works exactly the opposite way to a dynamic loudspeaker. There the sound makes a membrane vibrate, and the coil in the magnetic field produces a weak current from this. That is why a small loudspeaker can even be used as a simple microphone. The principle is based on electromagnetic induction.

You find loudspeakers everywhere: in mobile phones, televisions, cars and doorbells. **Headphones** contain very small loudspeakers right at the ear. The basic idea of today's dynamic loudspeaker was developed in the USA in the 1920s. With very loud music, for example at concerts, earplugs protect the ears from permanent damage.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thin, movable surface that vibrates and so produces sound.
Coil of wire on the cone that moves in the magnetic field.
Circuit that divides high and low notes between different loudspeakers.
Number of vibrations per second; it decides the pitch.

gewusst: For a very high note, the cone of a tweeter vibrates more than 10,000 times a second.
Humans hear roughly notes between 20 and 20,000 vibrations per second; with age the upper limit usually gets lower.
At concerts you often feel deep bass from a subwoofer in your stomach rather than in your ears.

teile.einleitung: A spinning top is an object that spins fast around an axis and stays astonishingly stable while doing so. Almost every child knows it as a toy, but in physics and technology it is an important tool. Spinning tops, or gyroscopes, are found in compasses, aircraft, satellites and even smartphones.
wichtigste: A spinning top turns fast around its own axis and balances on its point.
In physics a top is a rigid body that rotates about a fixed point.
A fast-spinning top does not fall over straight away, because gravity only changes the direction of its angular momentum.
If it gets too slow, it falls over.
The wobbling of the axis is called nutation, and the slow circling of the axis precession.
The gyrocompass finds north with the help of the Earth's rotation, without a magnetic field.
Figure skaters spin faster in a pirouette when they pull in their arms.

abschnitte.text: A **spinning top** is an object that turns fast around an axis. Toy tops usually have a point on which they spin and a stem at the top for starting them. Many old tops are made of wood; today they are also made of metal and plastic. A **humming top** hums as it spins, because air flows through openings. When a colourful top spins very fast, its colours seem to mix.

abschnitte.titel: Why does it not fall over?
abschnitte.text: If you stand a top at an angle on the table without spinning it, it falls over at once. But if it spins fast, it stays upright. The reason is **angular momentum**: a fast-rotating object keeps its axis of rotation as far as possible. Gravity does not simply tip the top over but only slowly changes the direction of its angular momentum. When the top slows down because of friction, it can no longer stay up and falls over.

The axis of a top standing at an angle slowly moves round in a circle; this is called **precession**. In addition, the axis can tremble or wobble slightly; this is called **nutation**. The Earth is also a giant spinning top whose axis undergoes a very slow precession. It takes about 26,000 years for one circuit. That is why in the distant future a star other than the Pole Star will stand above the North Pole.

A figure skater spins faster in a **pirouette** when she pulls her arms in close to her body. If she stretches her arms out again, she slows down. This is because of the **conservation of angular momentum**, which also applies to tops. Divers and gymnasts also use this effect when doing somersaults. When cycling, the spinning of the wheels helps a little with keeping your balance.

The **gyrocompass** uses the rotation of the Earth and a fast-spinning top to find north without a magnetic field. It was developed at the beginning of the 20th century and is important on large ships, because the steel hull can disturb a magnetic compass. Aircraft, rockets and satellites use gyroscopes to work out their position. Smartphones contain tiny electronic **gyroscopes** that detect how you turn the device. Bullets fired from rifled barrels also get a spin that stabilises their direction of flight.

In space the laws of spinning tops show especially clearly. In 1985 the Russian cosmonaut Vladimir Dzhanibekov watched a wing nut keep flipping over in weightlessness. This **Dzhanibekov effect** occurs when an object spins around the axis with the middle moment of inertia. This rotation is unstable, while rotations around the other two axes are stable. Satellites are sometimes set spinning on purpose so that they keep their orientation.

begriffe.erklaerung: A physical quantity that describes how much spin a rotating object has.
The slow circling of the axis of a spinning top.
A trembling or wobbling of the axis of a spinning top.
A spinning instrument that measures rotations and position in space.

gewusst: Spinning tops are among the oldest toys in the world and were already known in ancient times.
In 1852 the French physicist Léon Foucault gave the gyroscope its name, which means “rotation observer”.
A good toy top can keep spinning for several minutes.

teile.einleitung: Newton's theory of colour is the explanation by the English scientist Isaac Newton that white light is made up of many colours. Around 1666, he used glass prisms to split sunlight into a band of rainbow colours. His experiments are seen as the beginning of modern colour research.
wichtigste: Newton showed that white light is made up of many colours.
Around 1666, he split sunlight into a spectrum with a prism.
A single spectral colour could not be split any further by a second prism.
With a prism placed the other way round, he combined the colours back into white light.
Newton divided the spectrum into seven colours, adding indigo to do so.
In 1704, he published his findings in the book “Opticks”.
In 1810, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe criticised Newton in his work “Theory of Colours”.

abschnitte.text: Around 1666, the University of Cambridge had to close because of the plague, and the young **Isaac Newton** carried on his research at home. He let a narrow beam of sunlight fall through a small hole in the window shutter onto a triangular piece of glass, a **prism**. On the wall, there was no white spot but a long coloured band from red to violet. This band of colours is called a **spectrum**.

Newton wanted to know whether the prism makes the colours or whether they are already in the light. He sent a single colour through a second prism, and it stayed the same and was not split any further. Then he placed a second prism the other way round and combined all the colours back into white light. This proved that white light is a mixture of all the spectral colours.

abschnitte.titel: Seven colours and the colour wheel
abschnitte.text: Newton divided the spectrum into seven colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, **indigo** and violet. He chose the number seven because he compared the colours with the seven notes of the musical scale. To show how colours mix, he arranged them in a **colour wheel**. Colour wheels like this are still used in art and design today.

Newton published his findings about light and colours in 1704 in the book **“Opticks”**. In it, he described light as a stream of tiny particles. He also explained why lenses in telescopes produce coloured edges. That was why, as early as 1668, he had built a reflecting telescope that avoids this problem.

The poet **Johann Wolfgang von Goethe** did not agree with Newton. In 1810 he published his own work, “Theory of Colours”, and argued that colours arise from the interplay of light and darkness. In physics, Newton's explanation won. But Goethe's observations about how people perceive and feel colours are still interesting for art and psychology today.

Newton's theory of colour explains how a **rainbow** forms: water drops act like little prisms and split the sunlight. Splitting light led to spectroscopy, which is used today to find out what stars are made of. Screens and cameras also rely on mixing colours of light. So Newton's experiments with simple glass prisms still have an effect in modern technology.

begriffe.erklaerung: A triangular piece of glass that bends light and splits it into colours.
The band of colours produced when light is split.
A pure colour of the spectrum that cannot be split any further.
A circular arrangement of colours that shows how they are related.

gewusst: Newton included indigo mainly so that he would end up with exactly seven colours.
Newton was only in his early twenties when he did his famous prism experiments.
A rainbow always shows the colours in the same order, with red on the outside and violet on the inside.

teile.einleitung: A measuring jug is a container with lines and numbers with which you can measure out liquids and sometimes also flour or sugar. In every kitchen it is an important helper for cooking and baking. With it you learn along the way how litres, decilitres and millilitres are related.
wichtigste: In the kitchen you measure out amounts with a measuring jug.
Lines with amounts are printed on the outside of the jug.
A measuring jug is usually see-through so that you can see how full it is.
You read it at eye level.
When reading it, the jug stands on a flat table.
3 decilitres are the same as 300 millilitres.
To measure out 2 litres, you fill a half-litre jug 4 times.

abschnitte.text: A measuring jug is a jug with a **scale**, that is with lines and numbers on the side. It usually has a handle and a spout so that you can pour well. Many hold half a litre or a litre. It is made of glass, plastic or metal, and see-through jugs are the most practical.

Measuring jugs often show **millilitres** (ml), decilitres (dl) and litres (l). One litre has 10 decilitres or 1000 millilitres, so one decilitre is 100 millilitres. Swiss recipes very often use decilitres, for example 3 dl of milk. For this you fill up to the line at 300 ml.

Put the jug on a flat table and bring your eyes down to the level of the liquid. If you look at an angle from above, you read a wrong value; this is called **parallax**. With water the surface curves slightly upwards at the edge; this curve is called the **meniscus**. You read it at the lowest point in the middle.

If you pour 200 ml and then 300 ml into the jug, there are 500 ml in it altogether. If you need 2 litres but the jug holds only half a litre, you fill it 4 times. Some measuring jugs also have scales for **flour** and sugar in grams. Because flour is lighter than water, 100 g of flour needs more space than 100 g of water.

For the household a measuring jug is quite enough. In the laboratory a slim **measuring cylinder** is used for more precise values, on which the lines are further apart. Pipettes and volumetric flasks are even more precise. When baking, many people prefer to weigh the ingredients with kitchen scales, because that is more precise still.

begriffe.erklaerung: A row of lines with numbers for reading off values.
A thousandth of a litre, abbreviated ml.
A tenth of a litre, that is 100 millilitres, abbreviated dl.
The curved surface of a liquid in a narrow container.

gewusst: One litre of water weighs almost exactly one kilogram, which is why you can also measure water out with scales.
In the USA many recipes use cups, which corresponds to about 2.4 decilitres.
The words milli and deci come from Latin and mean thousandth and tenth.

teile.einleitung: Fog is a cloud that lies right on the ground. It is made of countless tiny droplets of water that float in the air and make it hard to see. In the Swiss Plateau, fog is so common in autumn and winter that people often talk about a “sea of fog”.
wichtigste: Fog is made of tiny water droplets floating in the air.
It is called fog when visibility falls below one kilometre.
Very light fog with better visibility is called mist.
Fog often forms in the morning over lakes and rivers.
When the Sun warms it up, fog often clears.
In fog, drivers should drive more slowly and leave a bigger gap.
Ships warn each other in thick fog with a foghorn.

abschnitte.text: Air always contains invisible **water vapour**. When the air cools down, it can hold less water vapour, and this condenses into tiny droplets. If these droplets float close to the ground, fog forms. Meteorologists call it fog when visibility falls below one kilometre, otherwise **mist**.

On clear, still nights, the ground cools down a lot, and so does the air above it. This creates **radiation fog**, especially in valleys and hollows. The air over lakes and rivers is damp, which is why fog often forms there in the morning. Fog also forms when warm, damp air flows over cold ground or cold water, for example on sea coasts.

abschnitte.titel: Sea of fog over the Swiss Plateau
abschnitte.text: In autumn and winter, a blanket of fog often lies over the Swiss Plateau for days. Cold air collects between the Jura and the Alps, with warmer air lying above it like a lid; this is called an **inversion**. If the fog does not lie on the ground but a few hundred metres higher up, it is called **high fog**. Anyone who climbs the Uetliberg, Pilatus or the Napf then often sees a beautiful sea of fog in the sunshine.

Fog is dangerous because you only see obstacles and other vehicles late. Drivers should therefore drive more slowly, switch on their lights and increase the **gap** to the car in front. Cars have special fog lights that may only be used in thick fog. At airports, taking off and landing in very thick fog is sometimes difficult, but modern instruments help the pilots.

Ships warn each other in thick fog with a loud **foghorn**. In the past, there were foghorns and bells at lighthouses on dangerous coasts. Today, radar and satellite navigation also help to avoid collisions. On Swiss lakes, passenger boats travel slowly in fog and give sound signals.

On foggy mornings, spider webs suddenly become easy to see, because many tiny water drops cling to the threads. When the Sun warms up the fog, the droplets evaporate and it clears. In fog, sounds seem muffled and the landscape looks mysterious. In some dry parts of the world, people even collect drinking water from fog with nets.

begriffe.erklaerung: When water vapour cools down and turns into liquid droplets.
Light fog in which you can still see more than a kilometre.
Fog that lies like a grey blanket above the ground.
A weather situation in which cold air lies below and warmer air above it.

gewusst: Fog and clouds are made of exactly the same thing; fog is just on the ground.
In the Atacama Desert in Chile and on other dry coasts, nets catch fog droplets as water.
When you walk in fog, your clothes can get wet even though it is not raining at all.

teile.einleitung: The Moon is the Earth's only natural companion and our nearest neighbour in space. It is much smaller than the Earth, and its gravity is only about one sixth as strong. In 1969, with Apollo 11, people walked on its surface for the first time.
wichtigste: On average, the Moon is about 384,000 kilometres from the Earth.
It is about a quarter as wide as the Earth.
Its gravity is only about one sixth of the gravity on Earth.
It takes about four weeks to go once around the Earth.
It has almost no air, because its gravity is too weak.
The Moon's pull causes the tides on Earth.
In 1969, with Apollo 11, the first people landed on the Moon.

abschnitte.text: The Moon has a diameter of about 3474 kilometres, making it about **a quarter as wide** as the Earth. On average it is around **384,000 kilometres** away. Light takes only just over a second to travel this distance. The Moon orbits the Earth in about four weeks and always shows us the same side.

Because the Moon is much smaller and lighter than the Earth, its **gravity** is only about one sixth as strong. A bathroom scale that shows 30 kg on Earth would show only about 5 kg on the Moon. A stone falls more slowly there, and astronauts could make long jumps. The weak gravity can hardly hold on to any air either, which is why the Moon has almost no **atmosphere**.

The large dark areas are called **lunar seas**, even though there is no water there. They are made of solidified lava from the Moon's early days. The bright areas are highlands full of **craters**, which were formed by rocks crashing into them. During the day it gets hotter than 100 °C on the Moon, and at night far colder than 100 °C below zero. Because there is neither wind nor rain, footprints stay for a very long time.

The Moon's pull tugs at the Earth's oceans and creates the **tides**. Depending on how the Sun lights up the Moon, we see it as a full moon, half moon or new moon. These **phases of the Moon** repeat about every 29.5 days. Scientists think that the Moon formed about 4.5 billion years ago after a huge collision between another body and the young Earth.

On 20 July 1969, the **Apollo 11** mission landed in the Sea of Tranquillity. **Neil Armstrong** was the first person to step onto the Moon, followed shortly afterwards by Buzz Aldrin. By 1972, a total of twelve astronauts had been on the Moon. Together they brought several hundred kilograms of moon rock back to Earth.

As the first scientific experiment, Buzz Aldrin set up a **solar wind sail** from the University of Bern. It was a kind of aluminium foil that caught particles from the solar wind. The experiment was led by the Bern physicist **Johannes Geiss**. The Bern sail was also taken along on later Apollo flights.

begriffe.erklaerung: The changing shapes in which we see the lit part of the Moon.
A round hollow formed by an impact.
A large dark plain of solidified lava on the Moon.
The regular rising and falling of the sea level.

gewusst: The Moon moves about 3.8 centimetres further away from the Earth every year.
The far side of the Moon was not photographed until 1959, by a Soviet space probe.
On the Moon, the sky is black even during the day, because there is no air to scatter the light.

teile.einleitung: Otto von Guericke was a German natural scientist, inventor and mayor of Magdeburg in the 17th century. He invented the air pump and proved with spectacular experiments that empty space, the vacuum, really exists. His Magdeburg hemispheres, which not even horses could pull apart, are famous.
wichtigste: Otto von Guericke lived from 1602 to 1686.
He was mayor of his home town of Magdeburg.
Around 1650 he invented the air pump.
With the Magdeburg hemispheres, he showed the enormous force of air pressure.
He disproved the old teaching that there can be no empty space.
With a ball of sulphur, he built an early machine that produced electricity.
The University of Magdeburg is named after him today.

abschnitte.text: Otto Gericke was born in Magdeburg in 1602 and studied law and mathematics, among other subjects. In the **Thirty Years' War**, Magdeburg was captured in 1631 and almost completely destroyed. Guericke survived and then helped rebuild the town as an engineer. From 1646 he was **mayor** of Magdeburg for many years, and later he was made a nobleman, hence the “von” in his name. He died in Hamburg in 1686.

abschnitte.titel: The invention of the air pump
abschnitte.text: At that time, many scholars, relying on the Greek thinker Aristotle, believed that nature could not tolerate empty space. Guericke wanted to test this and built the first **air pump** around 1650. With it, he pumped air out of containers and created a **vacuum**. He showed that in airless space no candle burns, no sound is carried and animals cannot breathe.

His most famous experiment: two hollow copper hemispheres were put together and the air was pumped out. After that, the **air pressure** from outside pressed the hemispheres together so tightly that teams of horses on both sides could not separate them. When air was let back in, the halves fell apart by themselves. Guericke gave such demonstrations in front of princes, including at the Imperial Diet in Regensburg in 1654.

Guericke also built a rotating **sulphur ball** that became electrically charged when rubbed by hand. It attracted light things such as feathers and is considered one of the first machines for producing electricity. He also noticed that air pressure varies and used this to predict changes in the weather. This made him a pioneer of meteorology.

He described his experiments in a large book in **Latin**, the language of scholars. It was published in Amsterdam in 1672 under the title “Experimenta nova Magdeburgica de vacuo spatio”, roughly “New Magdeburg experiments on empty space”. Today the Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg bears his name. The vacuum technology he founded is found today in light bulbs, vacuum flasks and vacuum packaging.

begriffe.erklaerung: A space in which there is (almost) no air and no other particles.
The force with which the air of the Earth's atmosphere presses on everything.
A device for sucking air out of a container.
A great war in Europe from 1618 to 1648.

gewusst: A well-known picture shows 16 horses, eight on each side, pulling at the hemispheres in vain.
Guericke also built a water barometer more than ten metres high on his house.
In Magdeburg, the hemisphere experiment is still re-enacted at town festivals today.

teile.einleitung: Marie Curie was a Polish and French physicist and chemist who researched the radiation given off by substances. Together with her husband Pierre she discovered the elements polonium and radium, and she coined the term radioactivity. She was the first person to receive two Nobel Prizes in two different natural sciences.
wichtigste: Marie Curie was born in Warsaw in 1867 as Maria Skłodowska.
She researched radiating substances with her husband Pierre Curie.
In 1898 the two of them discovered the elements polonium and radium.
She coined the technical term radioactivity.
She received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911.
From 1906 she taught at the Sorbonne in Paris as the first woman to do so.
Her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie also received a Nobel Prize, in 1935.
In 1995 she became the first woman to be buried in the Panthéon in Paris for her own achievements.

abschnitte.text: Maria Skłodowska was born on 7 November 1867 in **Warsaw**. At that time part of Poland belonged to Russia, and women were not allowed to study at a university there. Maria was an excellent pupil and secretly carried on learning. For several years she worked as a governess to save money for her studies. In 1891 she moved to Paris, where she called herself Marie.

In Paris she studied physics and mathematics at the **Sorbonne** and finished each as one of the best. In 1895 she married the physicist **Pierre Curie**, with whom she did research from then on. The two had two daughters, Irène and Eve. Irène also became a scientist; Eve later wrote a well-known biography of her mother. The family lived modestly and put a lot of money into research.

The physicist Henri Becquerel had discovered that uranium sends out invisible rays. Marie Curie examined this phenomenon more closely and called it **radioactivity**. In a poorly equipped shed the Curies processed tonnes of rock, pitchblende. In 1898 they discovered two new elements: **polonium**, named after her home country Poland, and **radium**, which glows faintly in the dark. It took years before they could obtain a tiny amount of pure radium.

In 1903 Marie Curie received the **Nobel Prize** in Physics together with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. She was the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize. In 1906 Pierre died in an accident with a horse-drawn carriage in Paris. Marie took over his professorship and taught at the Sorbonne as the first woman. In 1911 she received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on her own.

abschnitte.titel: Work in the First World War
abschnitte.text: In the First World War Marie Curie developed mobile **X-ray vehicles** with which wounded soldiers could be examined right near the front. These vehicles were affectionately called “petites Curies”, that is little Curies. She also trained many women who could operate the equipment. Her daughter Irène helped her with this while still a teenager. In this way her work saved many people's lives.

The danger of radiation was hardly known at that time, and Marie Curie even carried radium in the pocket of her lab coat. Years of exposure to **radiation** are thought to be the likely cause of her serious illness. She died on 4 July 1934 in a sanatorium in the French Alps, not far from Geneva. The chemical element curium is named after the Curie couple. In 1995 she became the first woman to be buried in the **Panthéon** in Paris for her own achievements.

begriffe.erklaerung: The giving off of radiation from decaying atomic nuclei.
Basic substance that consists of only one kind of atom.
Radioactive element named after Poland.
Strongly radiating element that glows faintly in the dark.
Famous award, among others for physics and chemistry.

gewusst: Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive today and are kept in lead boxes.
The Curie family won five Nobel Prizes altogether, if you count Pierre, Irène and her husband Frédéric.
Marie Curie is still the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different natural sciences.

teile.einleitung: The coefficient of performance tells you how well a heat pump or a fridge works. It compares the useful heat that the machine delivers or removes with the energy that has to be supplied to it as electricity. A good heat pump delivers about three to five times more heat than the electricity it uses.
wichtigste: The coefficient of performance of a heat pump is the heat delivered divided by the work supplied.
If a heat pump delivers 4 kW of heat with 1 kW of electricity, its coefficient of performance is 4.
A coefficient of performance greater than 1 does not break the conservation of energy, because heat from the surroundings is added.
The smaller the temperature difference, the larger the coefficient of performance can be.
As a heat pump, the coefficient of performance is 1 greater than for the same machine working as a refrigerator.
The seasonal performance factor measures the ratio of heat to electricity used over a whole year.
In English the coefficient of performance is abbreviated COP.

abschnitte.text: A **heat pump** takes heat from the surroundings, for example from the air, the ground or groundwater, and brings it to a higher temperature to heat a house. For this it needs electricity for the compressor. The **coefficient of performance** is the heat delivered divided by this work supplied. If a heat pump delivers 4 kW of heating power and needs 1 kW of electricity, its coefficient of performance is 4. In English it is often called the COP.

At first sight a coefficient of performance of 4 seems like magic. But the energy does not come out of nothing: the electricity only moves the heat, most of which comes free from the surroundings. The heat delivered is the sum of the heat from the environment and the electricity. That is why the **law of conservation of energy** still holds. An electric heater, on the other hand, has a coefficient of performance of 1 at best.

The French physicist Sadi Carnot showed that there is an upper limit. The ideal coefficient of performance of a heat pump is the warm temperature divided by the temperature difference, both measured in **kelvin**. Between 5 °C outside and a flow temperature of 35 °C this gives 308 K divided by 30 K, or about 10.3. Real devices reach only about half of this. For a refrigerator that cools at 255 K and gives off heat at 300 K, the ideal coefficient of performance is 255 divided by 45, or about 5.7.

A **fridge** is a heat pump that pumps heat from the inside into the kitchen. With a fridge, what counts is the heat removed, so its coefficient of performance is 1 less than that of the same machine working as a heat pump. A fridge with a coefficient of performance of 3 that removes 600 J from the inside needs 200 J of electricity and gives off 800 J altogether to the kitchen. That is why it is always a little warm behind a fridge.

In Switzerland heat pumps are installed in most new houses, and many old oil and gas heating systems are being replaced by them. What matters in practice is the **seasonal performance factor**, the ratio of heat to electricity used over a whole year. Heat pumps with ground probes usually reach higher values than air-to-water heat pumps, because the ground is warmer than the air in winter. Underfloor heating with a low flow temperature improves the coefficient of performance further.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that pumps heat from cold to warm in order to heat.
A machine that squeezes the working gas together and so heats it.
Temperature scale that starts at absolute zero; 0 °C is 273 K.
Average coefficient of performance of a heat pump over a whole year.

gewusst: A heat pump can even get heat out of air at minus 10 °C, because cold air still contains heat energy.
Switzerland's first heat pump heating system warmed Zurich town hall from 1938 with heat from the River Limmat.

teile.einleitung: An oscilloscope is a measuring device that makes electrical voltages visible as a curve on a screen. This lets you see how a voltage changes within fractions of a second. For electronics engineers and technicians, it is one of the most important tools.
wichtigste: An oscilloscope shows time horizontally and voltage vertically.
The screen is divided into squares with which you can read off times and voltages.
The trigger makes sure that a repeating signal appears as a still picture.
Classic analogue oscilloscopes produced their image with a cathode ray tube.
Today's digital oscilloscopes sample the signal and store it.
Current is measured indirectly through the voltage across a known resistor.
In XY mode, two oscillations create Lissajous figures.

abschnitte.text: An oscilloscope draws a graph in real time. **Time** runs along the horizontal axis, and **voltage** is shown on the vertical axis. This turns an invisible electrical oscillation into a visible curve. You can see, for example, whether a signal looks like a gentle wave, a square or a zigzag.

The screen has a grid of squares. With the **timebase**, you set how much time one square stands for horizontally, for example 0.5 milliseconds. If one oscillation is 4 squares wide, it lasts 2 milliseconds and the frequency is 500 hertz. The same applies vertically: if a signal reaches 3 squares high at 2 volts per square, the peak value is 6 volts.

Without help, the curve would race across the screen and flicker. The **trigger** always starts the drawing at the same point of the oscillation, for example when the voltage rises above a certain value. This makes all the sweeps lie exactly on top of each other. The result is a still, easy-to-read picture.

In the past, oscilloscopes worked with the **cathode ray tube**, which Karl Ferdinand Braun invented in 1897. In it, the voltage deflected an electron beam that drew a dot on a glowing layer. Today most oscilloscopes are digital. They measure the signal very many times a second and show it on a flat screen, and the sampling rate must be more than twice the highest frequency in the signal.

Oscilloscopes are found in workshops, laboratories and schools, and are used when repairing cars and appliances. As the device only measures voltages, you send a current through a known resistor and measure the voltage across it. In **XY mode**, a second voltage controls the horizontal direction instead of time. This produces pretty loops and curves, the Lissajous figures.

begriffe.erklaerung: The setting for how much time one square on the screen stands for.
A starting signal that makes the curve stand still.
The number of oscillations per second, measured in hertz.
The highest value a voltage reaches in an oscillation.
Loop patterns created by combining two oscillations.

gewusst: For a long time, the cathode ray tube from the oscilloscope was also the picture tube in old televisions.
Good oscilloscopes can show events that last only billionths of a second.
The logo of the Australian broadcaster ABC is a Lissajous figure.

teile.einleitung: A light-emitting diode, LED for short, is a tiny electronic component that lights up when current flows through it. Today LEDs are found in lamps, mobile phones, televisions and huge stadium displays. They use much less electricity than light bulbs and last much longer.
wichtigste: LED stands for light-emitting diode.
An LED only lights up when the current flows in the right direction.
The longer leg of an LED goes to the positive terminal.
LEDs stay much cooler than light bulbs and last much longer.
The colour depends on the band gap of the semiconductor.
White light usually comes from a blue LED with a yellow phosphor.
The Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded in 2014 for efficient blue LEDs.

abschnitte.text: A **light-emitting diode** is an electronic component made of a **semiconductor**. A single LED is usually very small, often only a few millimetres across. As a **diode**, it only lets current through in one direction: if you connect it the wrong way round to a battery, it does not light up. On a simple LED the longer leg goes to the positive terminal.

In the semiconductor there are electrons and so-called **holes**, places where an electron is missing. When current flows, electrons meet holes and combine; this is called recombination. Energy is released as light. The colour depends on the **band gap** of the semiconductor: at 2.0 eV, red light with a wavelength of about 620 nm is produced.

The first LED with visible red light was built by the American Nick Holonyak in 1962. Later green and yellow LEDs were added, but a bright blue LED was missing for a long time. In the 1990s the Japanese researchers Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura succeeded. They received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 2014, because only with blue LEDs did white LED light become possible.

Most white LEDs consist of a blue LED coated with a yellow **phosphor**. The blue and yellow light together look white to our eyes. Other lamps mix red, green and blue light. This even makes it possible to change the colour of the light from warm to cold.

A small LED shows on many devices that they are switched on. The pixels of large display boards in stadiums consist of many thousands of light-emitting diodes. For the same brightness LED lamps need only a fraction of the electricity of a light bulb and often last 15,000 hours or more. Since the 2010s light bulbs have gradually been taken off sale in Switzerland and the EU.

An LED usually needs a **series resistor** that limits the current, otherwise it breaks. A red LED with 2.0 V and 20 mA needs a resistor of 150 ohms at 5 V. You calculate the remaining voltage of 3 V divided by 0.02 A. That is why in electronics kits and when programming with small computers, LEDs are often the first component people try out.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material such as silicon that conducts current or not, depending on conditions.
A component that only lets current through in one direction.
The amount of energy released in the semiconductor when it lights up, which decides the colour.
A resistor that protects the LED from too much current.

gewusst: A light bulb turns most of the electricity into heat and only a few per cent into light.
The television remote control also has an LED, but it sends out invisible infrared light.
With a mobile phone camera you can often see the invisible flashing of a remote control.

teile.einleitung: Magnetic poles are the two ends of a magnet where its force is strongest. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole. How two magnets behave depends on which poles meet.
wichtigste: A bar magnet has two poles, a north pole and a south pole.
On school magnets the north pole is often marked red and the south pole green.
The north pole is often labelled with the letter N.
Like poles repel each other, unlike poles attract each other.
A magnet with only one pole never exists.
A bar magnet is strongest at its two ends.
The north pole is called that because it points north when the magnet hangs freely.

abschnitte.text: Every magnet has exactly two kinds of poles: a **north pole** and a **south pole**. On a bar magnet they lie at the two ends; that is where it holds the most paper clips. In the middle it has almost no effect. At school the north pole is usually red and labelled N, the south pole green or sometimes blue.

If you bring two magnets together, a simple rule applies. **Like poles** repel each other, that is north and north or south and south. Unlike poles attract each other. You can feel these forces clearly when you push two magnets towards each other.

If you break a bar magnet in the middle, you do not get a north pole and a south pole on their own. Instead two smaller magnets form, each with two poles. This goes on and on, down to tiny regions in the material, the **elementary magnets**. A magnet with only one pole, a so-called monopole, has never been found.

If you hang a bar magnet freely on a thread, it turns until one end points north. This end is the north pole, and that is how it got its name. The **compass** works on this principle; it was already used in China around 1000 years ago to find the way. Hikers in the Swiss mountains still use it today together with a map.

The Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet. The English doctor William Gilbert described this in 1600. Because unlike poles attract, there is actually a **magnetic south pole** near the geographic North Pole. The Earth's magnetic poles also move slowly, and in the course of the Earth's history they have often swapped.

begriffe.erklaerung: The end of a magnet that points north.
The end of a magnet that points south.
A device with a magnetic needle that shows the direction of north.
A tiny region in iron that acts like a small magnet.

gewusst: The Earth's magnetic north pole does not lie exactly at the geographic North Pole and moves many kilometres every year.
Horseshoe magnets also have only two poles; they are simply bent into a U.
Migratory birds and sea turtles can probably find their way using the Earth's magnetic field.

teile.einleitung: Mass tells you how much matter there is in a body and how hard it is to set it moving. Its base unit is the kilogram. One litre of water has a mass of roughly one kilogram.
wichtigste: Mass tells you how much matter there is in a body.
The base unit of mass is the kilogram.
One kilogram is 1000 grams, so 2.5 kilograms are 2500 grams.
One litre of water has a mass of about 1 kilogram.
Mass is the same everywhere, on the Earth as on the Moon.
With a beam balance you determine mass regardless of the place.
The greater the mass, the greater a body's inertia.

abschnitte.text: **Mass** is a property of every body. It tells you how much matter it contains and how hard it is to move. A stone has more mass than a sponge of the same size. In everyday life people often say weight, but they actually mean mass.

The base unit of mass in the international **system of units** is the **kilogram**, kg for short. Smaller masses are measured in grams; one kilogram is 1000 grams. For very large masses the tonne is used, which is 1000 kilograms. So 2.5 kilograms are exactly 2500 grams.

Originally the kilogram was defined so that one litre of water has a mass of exactly one kilogram. This is still roughly true today. So a one-litre carton of milk has a mass of about one kilogram. Since 2019 the kilogram has been defined through a constant of nature, the **Planck constant**.

If an astronaut flies to the Moon, his mass stays the same, because he still consists of just as much matter. Only his **weight** is about six times smaller there, because the Moon pulls less strongly. That is why astronauts could hop about there with heavy equipment. A **beam balance** would nevertheless show the same mass on the Moon as on Earth.

Bodies with mass have **inertia**. That means they want to keep their state of motion. A full shopping trolley is harder to push and harder to stop than an empty one. The greater the mass, the greater this **inertia**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The base unit of mass, kg for short.
A balance that compares a mass with known weights.
The property of a body of keeping its state of motion.
The force with which a body is attracted by the Earth.

gewusst: From 1889 to 2019 the kilogram was defined by a metal cylinder in a safe near Paris, the international prototype kilogram.
An adult blue whale can have a mass of well over 100 tonnes.
Air has mass too; one cubic metre of air has about 1.2 kilograms.

teile.einleitung: Lise Meitner was an Austrian physicist who was the first to explain nuclear fission in terms of physics. She worked with the chemist Otto Hahn in Berlin for about thirty years. As a woman and because of her Jewish background, she had to overcome many obstacles.
wichtigste: Lise Meitner was born in Vienna in 1878 and died in Cambridge in 1968.
She studied in Vienna and attended lectures by the famous physicist Ludwig Boltzmann.
In Berlin she worked with the chemist Otto Hahn for about thirty years.
In 1926 she became the first woman in Germany to be a professor of physics.
In 1938 she had to flee from Germany to Sweden because of her Jewish background.
In 1939, with her nephew Otto Robert Frisch, she explained nuclear fission.
The chemical element meitnerium is named after her.

abschnitte.text: Lise Meitner was born in **Vienna** in November 1878. At that time girls in Austria were not yet allowed to attend a grammar school, so she prepared privately for the Matura, the school-leaving exam. From 1901 she studied physics, mathematics and philosophy at the University of Vienna. She was especially inspired by the lectures of **Ludwig Boltzmann**. In 1906 she became one of the first women at the University of Vienna to gain a doctorate in physics.

In 1907 she moved to **Berlin** and began research with the chemist **Otto Hahn**. Because women were not allowed into the Chemical Institute, at first she had to work in a former woodwork shop in the basement. She became assistant to **Max Planck**, one of the first women in Prussia in this position. With Hahn she discovered the element protactinium in 1918. In 1926 she became the first woman in Germany to be a professor of physics.

When the Nazis annexed Austria to Germany in 1938, Lise Meitner was in great danger because of her **Jewish background**. In July 1938, with the help of friends, she fled via the Netherlands to **Sweden**. In Stockholm she found refuge and work at a research institute. She lost almost all her possessions and had to start again. But she stayed in touch with Otto Hahn by letter.

At the end of 1938 Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin bombarded uranium with neutrons and afterwards found the much lighter element **barium**. They could not explain the result and wrote to Meitner about it. Over Christmas 1938 Lise Meitner thought about it with her nephew **Otto Robert Frisch**. Using the **liquid drop model** of the atomic nucleus, they explained that a uranium nucleus can break into two parts like a wobbling drop of water. They also calculated that a great deal of energy is released, and published their explanation in 1939.

The 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery of nuclear fission went only to Otto Hahn, not to Lise Meitner. Today this is regarded as a great injustice. Lise Meitner refused to work on the development of the atomic bomb. In 1966, together with Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann, she received the **Enrico Fermi Award**. In her honour, the element with atomic number 109 is called **meitnerium**.

begriffe.erklaerung: When a heavy atomic nucleus breaks into two lighter nuclei and energy is released.
An electrically neutral particle in the atomic nucleus.
An idea according to which an atomic nucleus behaves like a drop of liquid.
A heavy, radioactive metal whose nuclei can be split.
The school-leaving qualification that allows you to study at a university.

gewusst: Albert Einstein once called Lise Meitner “our Marie Curie”.
Lise Meitner was nominated for the Nobel Prize many times but never received it.
Meitnerium is one of the few chemical elements named after a woman.

teile.einleitung: A body is in mechanical equilibrium when all the forces and turning effects acting on it cancel each other out. Then it stays at rest or carries on moving steadily. Whether a seesaw, a mobile or a construction crane, this principle is at work everywhere.
wichtigste: In equilibrium the sum of all forces is zero.
In addition, the sum of all torques must be zero.
A freely movable rigid body in space must satisfy 6 independent conditions.
A distinction is made between stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium.
A ball at the bottom of a bowl lies in stable equilibrium.
For a suspended body in stable equilibrium, the centre of gravity lies vertically below the point of suspension.
A construction crane carries a counterweight so that the torque of the load is balanced.

abschnitte.text: A body is in **equilibrium** when it neither starts moving nor begins to turn. For this two conditions must be met: the sum of all forces is zero, and the sum of all **torques** is zero. A book on the table is an example, because its weight is exactly balanced by the table top. In space this gives six conditions, three for the forces and three for the turning.

Torque is force times distance from the pivot, that is the **lever arm**. On a seesaw a child of 30 kg sits 2 m from the pivot. A child of 40 kg must then sit 1.5 m from the pivot, because 30 · 2 = 40 · 1.5. The Greek Archimedes already described this law of the lever more than 2000 years ago.

On a mobile, figures hang from rods that are exactly balanced. If a figure of 0.2 kg hangs on the left 0.3 m from the point of suspension, a figure of 0.3 kg must hang on the right 0.2 m from the point of suspension. Then the torques are equal and the rod stays horizontal. The American artist Alexander Calder made such **mobiles** famous.

If a ball lies at the bottom of a bowl, it rolls back after a push; this is **stable equilibrium**. If it lies on top of an upturned bowl, it rolls down at the slightest push; this is called **unstable equilibrium**. On a flat table it stays wherever it is; this is neutral equilibrium. A hanging picture is stable if its centre of gravity lies vertically below the nail.

For bridges and beams, engineers calculate which forces the supports carry. If a beam 4 m long weighing 200 N rests on both ends and a load of 600 N hangs 1 m from the left end, the left **support** carries 550 N. A construction crane has a heavy counterweight of concrete blocks on its short jib. This balances the torque of the load, and the crane does not tip over.

Tightrope walkers often hold a long pole with which they can correct their balance more easily. A roly-poly toy always stands up again, because its centre of gravity is low down. When cycling or skiing in the Alps we also keep our balance all the time without thinking about it. Stacked stone cairns on hiking trails show how delicate a balance can be.

begriffe.erklaerung: The turning effect of a force, force times distance from the pivot.
The point where you can imagine the whole weight of a body to be concentrated.
The distance between the pivot and the place where the force acts.
The place where a beam or a bridge is held up.

gewusst: A roly-poly toy is always in stable equilibrium, however you push it.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa only stands because its centre of gravity still lies above its base.
A skydiver falling at a constant speed is also in equilibrium of forces, even though he is moving.

teile.einleitung: The Magnus effect explains why a spinning ball curves in the air. Because of the spin, the air flows differently on the two sides of the ball, and a sideways force arises. Footballers, tennis players and golfers use it every day.
wichtigste: In the Magnus effect a spinning body is deflected sideways in a flow.
It is named after the German physicist Heinrich Gustav Magnus.
The force arises from different air flow on the two sides of the ball.
In football a ball that curves because of spin is called a banana cross.
Topspin makes a tennis ball drop down faster.
Backspin gives a golf ball lift, so that it flies further.
Flettner rotors use the effect to drive ships with spinning cylinders.

abschnitte.text: If a ball flies and spins at the same time, it moves away from the straight path. This **Magnus effect** was described by the Berlin physicist **Heinrich Gustav Magnus** in 1852. At that time he was investigating why cannonballs sometimes veered off to the side. The effect occurs in air and also in water.

A spinning ball drags the air at its surface along a little. On the side that turns with the oncoming air, the air flows past faster. On the other side it is slowed down. As a result the air behind the ball is deflected to one side, and the ball is pushed to the other side according to the principle of **action and reaction**.

If a footballer strikes the ball on its side, it flies a **banana cross**. This way you can curl the ball round a wall into the goal. A famous example is the free kick by the Brazilian Roberto Carlos against France in 1997. The ball first flew far past the goal and then suddenly bent into the net.

With **topspin** the tennis ball spins forwards, and the force pushes it down. This way you can hit hard and the ball still lands in the court. With a **slice** with backspin the ball flies flat and slowly. Golf balls get backspin when teed off, which lifts them and makes them fly further.

In the 1920s the German engineer Anton Flettner built ships with large spinning cylinders instead of sails. These **Flettner rotors** use the wind and the Magnus effect for propulsion. For a long time they were forgotten. Today some cargo ships are being given such rotors again to save fuel.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rotation of a ball about itself during flight.
Forward spin, in which the top of the ball turns forwards.
Shot with backspin in tennis.
Large spinning cylinder that drives ships using wind power.
Force that pushes a body upwards.

gewusst: The small dimples on a golf ball help the Magnus effect to work more strongly, so that the ball flies further.
In table tennis the small, light ball spins so fast that it sometimes flies extreme curves.
A basketball dropped from a high dam with backspin flies off in a big arc.

teile.einleitung: Ohm's law describes how voltage, current and resistance are related in an electric circuit. It was formulated in 1826 and 1827 by the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm. With the formula U = R · I, you can answer many questions about electrical appliances.
wichtigste: Ohm's law is U = R · I.
The current is proportional to the voltage and inversely proportional to the resistance.
Georg Simon Ohm formulated the relationship in 1826/1827.
The unit of resistance is the ohm, written Ω.
For an ohmic resistor, the characteristic curve is a straight line through the origin.
For a light bulb, the law does not hold exactly, because the resistance rises with temperature.
Electrical power can be calculated with P = U · I.

abschnitte.text: **Ohm's law** links three quantities: voltage U in volts, current I in amperes and **resistance** R in ohms. It says U = R · I. If you double the voltage, the current doubles too. If the resistance is twice as large, only half as much current flows.

If there is a voltage of 12 V across a resistance of 4 Ω, a current of 3 A flows. A **kettle** that draws a current of 10 A at 230 V has a heating element of 23 Ω. If 2 A flow through a resistance of 50 Ω, **heating power** of 200 W is produced. For this you use P = U · I or P = R · I².

If you plot voltage and current on a graph, you get a **characteristic curve**. For an ohmic resistor, it is a straight line through the origin. For a **light bulb**, it is curved. The filament gets very hot, and as it does, its resistance rises sharply.

**Georg Simon Ohm** lived from 1789 to 1854 and came from Erlangen in Bavaria. He was a teacher and did his experiments with equipment he built himself. In 1826 and 1827 he published the relationship between voltage, current and resistance. At first his work was hardly noticed; later the unit of resistance was named after him.

Electricians and engineers use the law every day. With it, they work out how thick cables must be and which **fuses** are needed. Light-emitting diodes also need a suitable series resistor so that they do not break. With a **multimeter**, you can measure voltage, current and resistance yourself.

begriffe.erklaerung: What drives the current, measured in volts.
How much electricity flows per second, measured in amperes.
How strongly a component slows down the current, measured in ohms.
A graph that shows how current and voltage are related.

gewusst: The symbol for the ohm is the Greek letter omega, Ω.
The human body also has an electrical resistance; it is greater when the skin is dry than when it is wet.
A memory aid for the law is the word URI: U equals R times I.

teile.einleitung: Some materials let electric current through easily, while others block it almost completely. The first are called conductors, the others non-conductors or insulators. Both are equally important: conductors carry the current, and insulators protect us from it.
wichtigste: Conductors are materials through which electric current can flow easily.
Metals such as copper, silver, aluminium and iron conduct electricity particularly well.
Non-conductors, also called insulators, let hardly any current through.
Wood, glass, plastic, rubber and dry air are non-conductors.
The human body also conducts electricity, which is why electricity is dangerous.
Power lines hang from insulators made of glass or porcelain so that no current flows into the pylon.
Semiconductors such as silicon lie in between and are the basis of computer chips.

abschnitte.text: A **conductor** is a material in which electric charges can move easily. Metals contain many **free electrons**, which move between the atoms like a swarm. If you apply a voltage, they drift in one direction and current flows. That is why a metal spoon and a paper clip conduct electricity, and copper and silver especially well.

A **non-conductor** or **insulator** has hardly any freely moving charges. That is why almost no current can flow through it. A dry wooden spoon, a rubber, glass, plastic, rubber and porcelain are non-conductors. Dry air also normally does not conduct electricity; only at extremely high voltage, as in lightning, does it briefly become conductive.

With a battery, a small bulb and a few wires you can build a **circuit** and leave a gap open. If you hold different objects in the gap, you can see straight away whether they conduct electricity. If the bulb lights up, the object is a conductor; if it stays dark, it is a non-conductor. Experiments like this must only be done with small batteries, never with the mains socket.

The **human body** also conducts electricity, because it contains a lot of water with dissolved salts. That is why electricity from the socket or from high-voltage lines can kill. Pure water hardly conducts, but tap water, sea water and rainwater contain dissolved substances and therefore conduct electricity. So electrical devices never belong near the bath.

Non-conductors are very important for our safety. The wires in cables are covered with plastic, plugs have plastic casings, and electricians' tools have insulated handles. Power lines hang from pylons on parts made of glass or porcelain, the **insulators**, so that no current flows into the pylon. On the railways, too, insulators like these carry the overhead line.

Between conductors and insulators there are **semiconductors**, for example silicon. Their conductivity can be changed on purpose, which is why they are the basis of computer chips, solar cells and light-emitting diodes. At the very other end are superconductors, which conduct electricity with no resistance at all at very low temperatures. They are used, for example, in magnets for medical equipment and particle accelerators.

begriffe.erklaerung: Material through which current can flow well, for example metal.
Non-conductor that blocks current, for example plastic or glass.
Tiny, negatively charged particles that carry the current in metals.
Material whose conductivity lies between that of a conductor and an insulator, such as silicon.
