gewusst: Birds can sit safely on a power line because they touch only one wire and no current flows through them.
Silver is the best metallic conductor, but because of its price it is rarely used for cables.
Graphite, the material in pencil leads, conducts electricity even though it is not a metal.

teile.einleitung: The harmonic series is the ordered sequence of all the partials that sound along with a fundamental. Their frequencies are whole-number multiples of the fundamental. The most important intervals in music, such as the octave, fifth and third, can be derived from it.
wichtigste: The partials of an ideal harmonic series are whole-number multiples of the fundamental frequency.
With a fundamental of 110 hertz, the 3rd partial is 330 hertz.
The 2nd and 3rd partials form a fifth.
The 3rd and 4th partials form a fourth.
The 4th and 5th partials form a major third.
There are two octaves between the 1st and the 4th partial.
The strength of the individual overtones decides the tone colour of an instrument.
Fourier analysis can break a sound down into its sine waves.

abschnitte.text: A note from an instrument is made up of many **partials**. The lowest is the fundamental, and above it lie the overtones. If you arrange them by pitch, you get the **harmonic series**, also called the natural series. With a fundamental of 110 hertz, the partials are 110, 220, 330, 440, 550 hertz and so on.

The gaps between the partials give the familiar **intervals**. From the 1st to the 2nd partial is an octave, in the ratio 2 to 1. The 2nd and 3rd partials form a fifth in the ratio 3 to 2, the 3rd and 4th a fourth. The 4th and 5th partials form a major third, the 5th and 6th a minor third.

If the series starts on low C, it is followed by c, g, c', e' and g'. So the first six partials make a **major chord**. Further up, the gaps get smaller and smaller. Some notes, such as the 7th and 11th partials, do not fit exactly into our modern scale.

The Greek scholar **Pythagoras** is said to have studied the number ratios of intervals with a stretched string, the monochord. If you halve the string, it sounds an octave higher. In the 19th century, Hermann von Helmholtz investigated how overtones shape sound. Before that, the mathematician Joseph Fourier had shown how to break vibrations down into simple parts: **Fourier analysis**.

Brass instruments without valves, such as the alphorn, hunting horn or fanfare trumpet, can only play notes of the harmonic series. Only valves, or a slide as on the trombone, make all notes possible. The **clarinet**, with its almost cylindrical tube, mainly emphasises the odd-numbered partials in its low register, which gives it its typical, slightly hollow sound. A tuner or a music app uses Fourier analysis to show which partials are present and how strong they are.

The harmonic series explains why some notes sound especially harmonious together. With the octave and the fifth, many overtones of the two notes match exactly. Instrument makers use this knowledge to shape the sound of bells, organ pipes and strings. In electronic music, too, sounds are built up from individual **sine tones**.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the individual tones a sound is made of; the fundamental is the first.
The distance between two notes, for example an octave or a fifth.
An interval in which the upper note has double the frequency.
A calculation method that breaks a sound down into simple sine waves.
A completely pure tone without overtones.

gewusst: Our ears can pick out a fundamental from the overtones even when it is not sounding at all; that is how we hear deep voices even from small mobile phone speakers.
The notes of an alphorn all come from the harmonic series, which is why old alphorn melodies sometimes sound unusual.

teile.einleitung: Leonhard Euler was a mathematician and physicist from Basel and is regarded as one of the most important mathematicians of all time. He wrote more than almost any other researcher, even when he was nearly blind. Many symbols and formulas that are learnt at school today go back to him.
wichtigste: Leonhard Euler was born in Basel in 1707.
He worked mainly at the academies in St Petersburg and Berlin.
Frederick II of Prussia brought him to Berlin in 1741.
Euler's number e, with a value of about 2.718, is named after him.
He made the notation f(x) for functions well known.
In the last years of his life he was almost completely blind.
He appeared on the former Swiss 10-franc note.

abschnitte.text: Leonhard Euler was born on 15 April 1707 in **Basel** and grew up in Riehen. He studied at the University of Basel and learnt mathematics from the famous Johann Bernoulli. At the age of 20, in 1727, he went to the academy in **St Petersburg** in Russia. In 1741 King Frederick II of Prussia brought him to Berlin; in 1766 he returned to St Petersburg, where he died in 1783.

**Euler's number** e, with a value of about 2.718, is named after him; it plays a big part in growth and interest. Euler also made the notation f(x) for functions, the summation sign Σ and the letter π for the circle number well known. The formula e to the power iπ plus 1 equals 0 is famous, as it links five important numbers. He also found that the sum 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 and so on gives exactly π²/6, the solution of the “Basel problem”.

In 1736 Euler solved the **Königsberg bridge problem**: can you walk through the town and cross each of the seven bridges exactly once? He proved that it is impossible and in doing so founded graph theory. According to his **polyhedron formula**, for solids like the cube: vertices minus edges plus faces equals 2. So a solid with 8 vertices and 12 edges has 6 faces.

Euler disproved a conjecture by Pierre de Fermat by showing that 2³² + 1 is divisible by 641 and therefore not a prime number. Euler's **totient function** counts how many numbers up to n have no common factor with n; φ(10), for example, is 4. This function is used today in encryption on the internet. But Euler also worked on music theory, stars and shipbuilding.

Euler's equations of fluid mechanics describe how frictionless liquids move. With Euler's **buckling formula** engineers calculate the load at which a slender rod buckles sideways, which is important for columns and bridges. Euler also studied the motion of planets and the optics of lenses. Many of his ideas are still used in engineering and building today.

As early as around 1738 Euler largely lost the sight of one eye, and in the last years of his life he was almost completely blind. Even so he kept working; he did calculations in his head and dictated his texts. Altogether he wrote more than 800 works, and his collected works fill more than 70 thick volumes. Switzerland honoured him on the 10-franc note of the sixth series of banknotes, which was in circulation until the 1990s.

begriffe.erklaerung: The special number e, with a value of about 2.718.
A rule that assigns to each number x exactly one other number f(x).
A solid with only flat faces, for example a cube.
Branch of mathematics that studies points and the connections between them.

gewusst: Euler published so much that the academy in St Petersburg was still bringing out new works by him decades after his death.
An asteroid and a crater on the Moon are named after Leonhard Euler.
Euler also wrote a well-known work on physics and philosophy in the form of letters to a German princess.

teile.einleitung: The mains voltage is the electrical voltage available at our sockets. In Switzerland it is 230 volts alternating voltage, in the USA around 120 volts. It is strong enough to run cookers and kettles, and that is why it is dangerous for people.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, the socket supplies 230 volts of alternating current.
For large appliances such as cookers, the three-phase connection with 400 volts is used.
In the USA, the mains voltage in homes is around 120 volts.
Alternating voltages from about 50 volts upwards are considered dangerous.
From power and voltage you can work out the current: current equals power divided by voltage.
Chargers convert the mains voltage into a small direct voltage.
The label “230 V” on the rating plate tells you which voltage an appliance is built for.

abschnitte.text: **Voltage** is a kind of pressure that drives the electric charges through a cable. It is measured in **volts**, named after the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta. In a Swiss home, the socket carries 230 volts of alternating voltage at 50 hertz. For comparison: a normal battery has only 1.5 volts.

The power grid brings three wires, the so-called phases, into the house. Between one phase and the neutral wire there are 230 volts, which lamps, televisions and vacuum cleaners use. Between two phases there are 400 volts; this is **three-phase current**. Large appliances such as cookers, ovens or heat pumps use this connection.

The power of an appliance is voltage times current. A kettle with 2300 watts at 230 volts therefore needs a current of **10 amperes**. A hairdryer with 1150 watts needs 5 amperes. Fuses switch off the current if too many appliances are on one circuit at the same time and the current becomes too large.

In Europe 230 volts is usual, whereas in the USA, Canada and parts of Japan it is around 120 volts. The plugs are different too; Switzerland has its own three-pin plug, type J. That is why you often need a travel adaptor when travelling. An appliance built only for 120 volts can break at 230 volts.

Mobile phones, laptops and games consoles only need small **direct voltages** of a few volts. A charger or power supply converts the 230 volts from the socket accordingly. The **rating plate** shows which input voltage an appliance is built for. Many chargers today can handle anything between 100 and 240 volts and so work all over the world.

Alternating voltages from about **50 volts** are considered dangerous, and 230 volts can cause a life-threatening electric shock. That is why you must never put objects into sockets or use damaged cables. A **residual current device**, or RCD, switches off the current in a flash if current flows through a person. Electrical appliances do not belong near a bath or washbasin.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of electrical voltage.
Voltage whose direction regularly reverses.
Current from three phases, which makes 400 volts available.
A device that converts mains voltage into a smaller voltage.
A safety switch that cuts off the power immediately in an electrical accident.

gewusst: With 230 volts alternating voltage, the voltage actually changes all the time and reaches peaks of around 325 volts.
Switzerland used to have a mains voltage of 220 volts; it was standardised across Europe to 230 volts.
A flat two-pin Europlug also fits into Swiss sockets.

teile.einleitung: Loudness describes how loud or quiet we feel a sound to be. A whisper is quiet, while a pneumatic drill or a rock concert is very loud. The strength of sound is usually measured in decibels.
wichtigste: Sound consists of tiny vibrations in the air that our ear picks up.
The more strongly the air vibrates, the louder we hear a sound.
The strength of sound is measured in decibels, abbreviated dB.
The further you move away from a source of sound, the quieter it becomes.
Unpleasant, disturbing sound is called noise.
Very loud music can permanently damage your hearing.
If you hit a drum harder, it vibrates more strongly and sounds louder.

abschnitte.text: When a drum, a guitar string or our vocal cords vibrate, they make the air vibrate. These **sound waves** travel through the air to our ear. The stronger the vibrations, the louder we hear the sound. If you hit a drum harder, the skin vibrates more strongly and the sound gets louder. How high or low a note is, on the other hand, depends on how fast something vibrates.

The strength of sound is given in **decibels** (dB). 0 dB is roughly the threshold of hearing, the quietest sound a healthy ear can just hear. A whisper is about 30 dB, a normal conversation about 60 dB and a pneumatic drill about 100 dB. From about 120 to 130 dB sound hurts your ears. Important: we feel 10 dB more as roughly twice as loud.

The further you move away from a **source of sound**, the quieter it becomes, because the sound spreads out in all directions. That is why you hear a distant thunderstorm only as a faint rumble. Walls, curtains and trees also absorb sound. That is why **noise barriers** are built along motorways, so that residents are less disturbed.

Very loud sounds can damage the fine **sensory hairs** in the inner ear. This can lead to hearing loss or a ringing in the ears that does not go away. What matters is not only how loud it is but also how long you are exposed to the noise. That is why you should wear ear protection at concerts and not turn headphones up too loud. In Switzerland there are limits for loud events, and above a certain loudness free ear protection must be handed out.

Unpleasant, disturbing sound is called **noise**. In Switzerland road traffic is the biggest source of noise. In many places there are quiet hours, for example the night-time quiet period, often from 10 pm, which is set out in the rules of the municipality or the house rules. In a library you should be especially quiet so that others can read and learn in peace. Being considerate about noise is part of living well together.

begriffe.erklaerung: Vibrations in the air that we hear with our ears.
Unit used to give the strength of sound, abbreviated dB.
The quietest sound a person can just hear.
Sound that we find disturbing or unpleasant.
Earplugs or ear defenders that muffle sound that is too loud.

gewusst: In space there is complete silence, because there is no air to carry sound.
A difference of 10 decibels sounds to us roughly twice as loud.
Some animals, such as dogs and bats, hear sounds that are far too high for humans.

teile.einleitung: An objective lens is the lens system of a camera, telescope or microscope that faces the object being looked at. It gathers the light and forms a sharp image from it. Depending on its design, a lens can show wide landscapes, distant animals or tiny insects.
wichtigste: The objective is the lens or group of lenses that points towards the object being looked at.
The most important property of a lens is its focal length.
A wide-angle lens has a shorter focal length than a standard lens.
With a zoom lens, the focal length can be changed.
A macro lens is used for close-ups of small things such as insects.
A fast lens has a large aperture and lets in a lot of light.
A fisheye lens has an angle of view of about 180 degrees.

abschnitte.text: The word **objective** comes from the Latin “obiectum”, the thing you look at. So the objective is the lens that points towards the **object**. In a telescope or microscope, it forms an intermediate image that you look at through the eyepiece. In a camera, it projects the image directly onto the sensor, or in the past onto the film. A lens usually does not consist of a single lens element, but of several glass lenses one behind the other.

A **converging lens** bends the light rays so that they meet at one point behind the lens. The distance from the lens to this point is called the **focal length** and is given in millimetres. But a single lens produces coloured fringes and blurred edges. That is why several lenses made of different kinds of glass are combined, cancelling out each other's faults. Good lenses therefore often have more than ten elements.

A **wide-angle lens** has a short focal length and shows a large area, such as a whole mountain range. A **telephoto lens** has a long focal length and brings distant things close, for example an ibex on a rock face. A fisheye lens covers an angle of view of about 180 degrees and strongly curves straight lines. With a **zoom lens**, the focal length can be changed, so you can switch from wide to close. With a macro lens, you photograph small things such as insects or flowers from very close up.

A lens has an adjustable opening, the **aperture**. If it is wide open, a lot of light gets in; if it is almost closed, only a little. A lens with a very large opening is called **fast**, and it is good for pictures at dusk. With a wide-open aperture, only a narrow zone is sharp and the background becomes blurred. Photographers like to use this for portraits.

Every smartphone has lenses too, often several with different focal lengths. They are tiny and usually made of plastic lenses. Large objective lenses are found in the **telescopes** of observatories, where they are meant to gather as much light as possible from distant stars. Microscopes usually have several objectives on a turret, so that you can switch between different magnifications. Security cameras, projectors and binoculars also have lenses.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between the lens and the point where the light rays meet.
An adjustable opening in the lens that decides how much light gets in.
A lens whose focal length can be changed.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and brings light rays together at one point.

gewusst: Fisheye lenses are called that because fish under water are said to have a similarly wide view upwards.
Some telephoto lenses for sport and wildlife photos are longer than a forearm and weigh several kilograms.
A microscope always needs two lens systems: the objective near the specimen and the eyepiece near the eye.

teile.einleitung: Minergie is a Swiss building standard for buildings that use very little energy and are still comfortable to live and work in. It has existed since 1998. A house with a Minergie certificate is well insulated, has automatic ventilation and uses renewable energy wherever possible.
wichtigste: Minergie is a Swiss label for energy-efficient buildings.
The standard has existed since 1998.
The Minergie association is supported by the federal government, the cantons and businesses.
Very good thermal insulation and comfort ventilation are important.
As well as low energy use, high living comfort is a stated goal.
Minergie-P has especially strict requirements, similar to a passive house.
The ECO addition also pays attention to health and building ecology.

abschnitte.text: Minergie is a voluntary **label**, a quality mark for buildings. A house only gets it if it follows certain rules on energy use and comfort. This applies to new houses and also to renovated old buildings. Schools, offices and hospitals can also be Minergie-certified.

The most important thing is a well-insulated **building envelope**: the walls, roof, floor and windows. Thick layers of insulation and triple-glazed windows keep the warmth inside in winter and the heat outside in summer. This means much less energy is needed for heating. You can think of it as a thick winter coat for the house.

**Comfort ventilation** is typical of Minergie buildings. It constantly brings fresh air into the house and takes stale air out, without anyone having to open the windows. A heat exchanger takes the warmth from the outgoing air and passes it to the cold fresh air. You can still open the windows at any time.

The basic standard is simply called Minergie. **Minergie-P** requires an even better building envelope and is comparable to a passive house. With Minergie-A, the building produces much of its own energy over the year, usually with solar panels on the roof. The **ECO** addition can be combined with any of the standards and requires healthy, environmentally friendly building materials and plenty of daylight.

In the 1990s, experts in Switzerland developed the idea of a simple standard for economical houses. The Minergie association was founded in 1998. Today it is supported jointly by the federal government, the cantons and businesses. There are now tens of thousands of Minergie buildings in Switzerland.

In Switzerland, buildings use a large share of all energy, mainly for heating and hot water. Using less energy protects the climate and saves on heating costs. Many Minergie houses are heated with heat pumps instead of oil or gas. Some cantons support Minergie buildings with grants.

begriffe.erklaerung: Materials that stop heat escaping through walls and the roof.
A system that automatically brings fresh air into the house and takes stale air out.
A device that passes heat from warm outgoing air to cold fresh air.
A house that is so well insulated that it hardly needs any heating.
A quality mark that confirms certain properties.

gewusst: In a Minergie house, the people, lamps and appliances noticeably help to heat it too.
The filters of a comfort ventilation system also keep out many pollen grains, which helps people with hay fever.
Even old houses can get a Minergie certificate after a good renovation.

teile.einleitung: Magnetic flux describes how much magnetic field passes through a particular surface. You can picture it as the number of field lines that go through a loop of wire. If this flux changes, an electric voltage arises, and this is exactly how power stations produce electricity.
wichtigste: Magnetic flux has the symbol Φ (phi).
Its unit is the weber, abbreviated Wb.
The unit is named after the physicist Wilhelm Eduard Weber.
1 weber corresponds to 1 volt second (V · s).
For a flat surface Φ = B · A · cos α.
If a surface lies parallel to the field lines, the flux is zero.
Through a closed surface the total magnetic flux is always zero.

abschnitte.text: Imagine a loop of wire in a magnetic field. The **magnetic flux** tells you how much field passes through this loop. It depends on the strength of the field, the size of the surface and its tilt. The more field lines pierce the surface, the greater the flux.

For a uniform field Φ = B · A · cos α, where B is the **flux density**, A the area and α the angle between the field and the normal to the surface. If the surface is at right angles to the field, cos α = 1. An area of 0.05 m² in a field of 0.4 T thus gives 0.02 Wb. With B = 0.2 T, A = 0.1 m² and 60 degrees you get 0.01 Wb, because cos 60° = 0.5.

A coil consists of many turns, all of which the flux passes through. This is called the **flux linkage**, which is the flux of one turn times the number of turns. With 200 turns and 0.003 Wb each, this gives 0.6 Wb. That is why coils with many turns have an especially large effect.

The Englishman Michael Faraday discovered **electromagnetic induction** in 1831. It says: if the magnetic flux through a coil changes, a voltage arises in it. The faster the flux changes, the greater the voltage. That is why the unit weber fits the volt second so well.

In the generators of Swiss hydroelectric power stations, magnets turn past coils and so constantly change the flux. **Transformers**, induction hobs and wireless chargers for mobile phones also use changing fluxes. A bike dynamo works on the same principle. Without magnetic flux there would hardly be any electricity from the socket.

Wilhelm Eduard **Weber** (1804 to 1891) was a German physicist who did research in Göttingen. Together with the mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss he built one of the first electromagnetic telegraphs in 1833. He developed precise methods of measuring current and magnetism. In his honour the unit of magnetic flux is called the weber.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of magnetic flux, 1 Wb = 1 V · s.
An imaginary line standing at right angles to a surface.
The production of a voltage by a changing magnetic flux.
A single loop of wire in a coil.

gewusst: Because magnetic field lines are always closed, exactly as many field lines come out of any closed surface as go into it.
If you turn a loop of wire in a magnetic field, the flux changes constantly and alternating current arises.
In 1833 the telegraph of Gauss and Weber in Göttingen linked two buildings over around one kilometre of wire.

teile.einleitung: A fire blanket is a fireproof blanket used to smother small fires. It usually hangs in a container on the wall, for example in the kitchen or the laboratory. With it you can put out a pan fire in seconds, without water and without a big mess.
wichtigste: A fire blanket can be used to smother small fires.
Today it is usually made of fireproof glass fibre fabric.
The blanket takes the oxygen away from the fire.
It is particularly good for burning pans with oil or fat.
You pull it quickly out of its case by two tapes.
After putting out the fire, the blanket stays in place until everything has cooled down.

abschnitte.text: A **fire blanket** is a cloth made of material that does not burn. In the past blankets of wool or even asbestos were used; today they are usually made of **glass fibres**. The blanket is folded up in a case with two tapes hanging out of it. If you pull hard on the tapes, the blanket falls out and is ready straight away. Fire blankets are small, cheap and easy to use.

A fire needs fuel, heat and **oxygen** from the air. This is called the **fire triangle**: if one of these three sides is missing, the fire goes out. The fire blanket covers the fire so that no more fresh air can get to it. Without oxygen the flame dies after a short time. This is the same principle as putting a lid on a pan.

First you pull the blanket out of the case by the two tapes. Then you wrap the top edges round your hands so that they are protected from the heat. You hold the blanket in front of your body like a shield and carefully lay it over the fire, away from yourself. If possible, you then switch off the cooker. The blanket stays in place for at least a quarter of an hour, otherwise the hot fat can flare up again.

The fire blanket is best for a **fat fire** in a pan, which you must never put out with water. A burning waste-paper basket or a small fire in the laboratory can also be smothered with it. If a person's clothes are on fire, you can wrap them in the blanket and so put out the flames. But a fire blanket is too small for large fires. Then you must get to safety and call the fire brigade on 118.

A fire blanket belongs in every kitchen, clearly visible and easy to reach. It should not hang right above the cooker, but where you can reach it safely even when there is a fire, for example next to the kitchen door. It is worth talking with your family once about where the blanket hangs. A fire blanket that has been used should be replaced. Good fire blankets meet the European standard EN 1869.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fireproof blanket for smothering small fires.
The three things a fire needs: fuel, heat and oxygen.
Very thin threads of glass that do not burn.
Put out a fire by taking away its air.

gewusst: A fire blanket can be used even without practice, which is why it is especially recommended for households.
Unlike a fire extinguisher, a fire blanket leaves no powder behind in the kitchen.

teile.einleitung: Air pressure is the weight of the air pressing on us and on everything around us. We hardly feel it, but it holds suction cups in place and makes our ears pop when we travel up a mountain. On the weather map it shows whether good or bad weather is on the way.
wichtigste: Air pressure comes from the weight of the layer of air above us.
At sea level it is about 1013 hectopascals on average.
The higher you go, the lower the air pressure.
Our body pushes back from inside just as hard, which is why we are not squashed flat.
An area of low air pressure is called a low, one of high air pressure a high.
Rising air pressure often means good weather.
Air pressure is measured with a barometer.

abschnitte.text: The Earth is surrounded by a thick layer of air, the **atmosphere**. Air also has weight, and this presses on everything below it. On every square centimetre it presses about as much as one kilogram. We do not notice this, because there is an equally strong **counter pressure** inside the body.

abschnitte.titel: Less at the top than at the bottom
abschnitte.text: On the shore of a lake in the valley the air pressure is greater than on a mountain, because there is more air above. For roughly every 5.5 kilometres of height, the air pressure about halves. If you take a sealed **crisp packet** up a high mountain, it puffs up. If you travel up quickly in a cable car, you feel a **popping or pressure** in your ears until the pressure has evened out.

Fill a glass **right to the top** with water and lay a postcard on it. Then carefully turn it upside down over a sink and let go of the card. The card stays in place, because the **air pressure from below** pushes against it. If you tilt the glass and air gets in, the water runs out. A **suction cup** on a smooth tile holds on by the same principle.

On the weather map, areas of high air pressure are marked as **highs** and areas of low air pressure as **lows**. In a high, the air sinks, clouds dissolve, and the weather is often good. In a low, the air rises, and clouds and rain form. Wind arises because the air flows from the high to the low.

Air pressure is measured with a **barometer** in the unit hectopascal. In 1643 the Italian **Evangelista Torricelli** built the first mercury barometer. Later the mayor of Magdeburg, Otto von Guericke, showed with two hemispheres from which he had pumped the air how strong air pressure is. Even two teams of horses could not pull the hemispheres apart.

begriffe.erklaerung: The shell of air around the Earth.
Measuring device for air pressure.
Unit for air pressure, abbreviated hPa.
Area of low air pressure, often with clouds and rain.

gewusst: At the top of Mount Everest the air pressure is only about a third of the value at sea level.
On high mountains water boils below 100 °C, because the air pressure there is lower.
Aircraft cabins are pressurised; otherwise we could not breathe at great height.

teile.einleitung: The neutron is a tiny particle that, together with the protons, makes up the nucleus of an atom. It has no electric charge, hence its name, which means something like “the neutral one”. It was discovered in 1932 by the English physicist James Chadwick.
wichtigste: Neutrons sit in the atomic nucleus together with protons.
A neutron has no electric charge.
Its mass is almost the same as that of a proton.
The total number of protons and neutrons is called the mass number.
A free neutron decays on average after just under a quarter of an hour.
A neutron star is an extremely dense remnant of a star made almost entirely of neutrons.
The Paul Scherrer Institute in Aargau uses neutrons to study the inside of materials.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of atoms, and in the middle of every atom there is a tiny **atomic nucleus**. It consists of positively charged protons and uncharged **neutrons**. A neutron is almost exactly as heavy as a proton, just very slightly heavier. It is itself made of three even smaller particles, the quarks. The most common form of hydrogen is the only atom with no neutron at all in its nucleus.

The number of protons decides which element it is. If you add the protons and neutrons together, you get the **mass number**. Uranium-238, for example, has 92 protons, so its nucleus has 238 minus 92, that is 146 neutrons. Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are called **isotopes**, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14.

For a long time, only protons and electrons were known. But people wondered why atomic nuclei were heavier than the protons alone could explain. In 1932, the English physicist **James Chadwick** detected the uncharged particle and received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1935. A few years later, researchers discovered that neutrons can split heavy atomic nuclei such as uranium; this is the basis of **nuclear fission** in nuclear power stations.

Inside the atomic nucleus, a neutron is usually stable. Outside a nucleus, however, a free neutron **decays** on average after just under a quarter of an hour into a proton, an electron and another tiny particle. In space there are **neutron stars**, the remains of very large stars that have exploded. They consist almost entirely of neutrons, are only about as big as a city and yet are heavier than our Sun.

Because neutrons have no charge, they go deep into materials and are not deflected by electric forces. That makes them good for looking at the **inside of materials**. The Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen in the canton of Aargau runs the neutron source **SINQ** for this. Researchers there study, for example, batteries, engine parts, magnets or old works of art without destroying them.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny, heavy centre of an atom made of protons and neutrons.
The number of all protons and neutrons in an atomic nucleus.
An atom of an element with a different number of neutrons.
An extremely dense remnant of a star made almost entirely of neutrons.
An even smaller particle that protons and neutrons are made of.

gewusst: A teaspoon of material from a neutron star would weigh billions of tonnes on Earth.
The name neutron comes from the word neutral, because the particle is uncharged.
With neutron beams you can look inside an engine or an old statue without cutting it open.

teile.einleitung: A nutcracker is a tool for breaking open hard nutshells. It works according to the law of the lever: a small force on the handles produces a large force on the nut. The colourful wooden nutcracker figures and the Christmas ballet “The Nutcracker” are also famous.
wichtigste: A nutcracker is a lever that multiplies the force of your hand.
You put a hard nut close to the hinge, where the force is greatest.
The macadamia nut has a particularly hard shell.
Well-known wooden nutcrackers often look like a soldier or a king.
Pyotr Tchaikovsky composed the ballet “The Nutcracker”.
In Switzerland, the walnut is usually called Baumnuss.
In mountain forests, the nutcracker bird cracks Swiss stone pine seeds and hides them as a winter store.

abschnitte.text: A classic nutcracker consists of two handles joined at one end by a **hinge**. The hinge is the pivot of a **lever**. If you press at the long end of the handles, a much larger force is produced close to the hinge. That is why it is much easier to crack a nut with a nutcracker than with your bare hand.

For a lever: effort times effort arm equals load times load arm. If, for example, the distance from your hand to the hinge is five times as large as the distance from the nut to the hinge, five times as much force acts on the nut. That is why you put a hard nut as close to the hinge as possible. Pliers, scissors and wheelbarrows use the same principle.

Hazelnuts and **walnuts**, which in Switzerland are called Baumnüsse, can easily be opened with a simple nutcracker. The **macadamia nut** from Australia has a particularly hard shell and needs special crackers. As well as lever nutcrackers, there are also ones with a screw that presses harder and harder, slowly. Some people also crack walnuts by pressing two nuts against each other in their hand.

The colourful wooden nutcrackers that look like a soldier, king or forester are well known. You put the nut in the figure's mouth and press a lever on its back downwards. The figures from the **Ore Mountains** in Germany, where they have been turned on lathes since the 19th century, are especially famous. Today they are mainly a popular Christmas decoration.

The Russian composer **Pyotr Tchaikovsky** wrote the music for the ballet “The Nutcracker”, which was first performed in Saint Petersburg in 1892. The story is based on a fairy tale by the German writer E. T. A. Hoffmann. A girl is given a nutcracker for Christmas, which comes to life at night and fights the Mouse King. That is why the ballet is mostly performed at Christmas time, including in Swiss theatres.

Animals crack nuts too. The **spotted nutcracker**, a bird of the crow family in Swiss mountain forests, opens the cones of the Swiss stone pine with its strong beak. It hides thousands of stone pine seeds in the ground as a winter store and finds most of them again. New stone pines grow from the forgotten seeds, so the bird helps the mountain forest.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rod that turns around a pivot and can increase forces.
The point a lever moves around; in a nutcracker, the hinge.
The Swiss word for the walnut.
A conifer of the Alps, also called Arve or Zirbe, with edible seeds.

gewusst: In German the bird is called Tannenhäher, but in English it is simply called the nutcracker.
A spotted nutcracker can carry many stone pine seeds at once in a pouch in its throat.
A special instrument plays in the ballet “The Nutcracker”: the celesta, whose notes sound like little bells.

teile.einleitung: In physics, power tells you how quickly work is done or energy is converted. Power is work per unit of time. A strong motor does the same work faster than a weak one.
wichtigste: Power is work per unit of time.
The unit of power is the watt, abbreviated W.
One watt means one joule of work per second.
The faster a piece of work is done, the greater the power.
On electrical appliances the power is often shown on the rating plate.
In the past the power of engines was measured in horsepower.

abschnitte.text: When you carry a rucksack up to the third floor, you do **work**. If you run up the stairs, you need less time than when you stroll. The work is the same, but your **power** is greater. So power is work divided by time.

The formula is P = W : t. Here P stands for power, W for work and t for time. The unit is the **watt**, named after the Scottish inventor James Watt. One watt means that one **joule** of work is done per second. If a motor does 6000 joules of work in 30 seconds, it has a power of 200 watts.

Electrical appliances often show their power in watts. An LED lamp needs about 5 to 10 watts. A **kettle** often has about 2000 watts, or 2 **kilowatts**. The greater the power, the more electrical energy an appliance uses in the same time.

In the past the power of engines was given in **horsepower**, in German PS. One PS (metric horsepower) is about 735 watts. Today kilowatts are used officially, but you still often hear horsepower for cars. A small car, for example, has about 70 kilowatts, or around 95 PS.

Humans also produce power. A well-trained cyclist can pedal at about 200 to 300 watts for a long time. For short sprints top athletes manage more than 1000 watts. With a **power meter** on the bike, professional cyclists can measure their power precisely.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of power, one joule per second.
When a force moves an object over a distance.
1000 watts, abbreviated kW.
An old unit for engine power, about 735 watts in its metric form.

gewusst: James Watt compared the power of his steam engines with horses so that people could understand them better.
A large hydroelectric power station in the Alps can deliver hundreds of millions of watts of power.
The human brain works with a power of only about 20 watts.

teile.einleitung: The phases of the Moon are the different shapes in which we see the Moon in the sky: from a thin crescent to a half moon to a full moon. The Moon does not really change its shape. Depending on the positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon, we simply see a different part of its lit side.
wichtigste: The Moon is always half lit by the Sun.
Depending on the position, we see a larger or smaller part of this lit half.
It takes about 29.5 days from one new moon to the next.
The main phases are called new moon, first quarter, full moon and last quarter.
If the crescent is lit on the right and looks like a bracket “)”, the Moon is waxing.
There are 12 or 13 full moons in a year.
You can often see the Moon during the day too.

abschnitte.titel: How do the phases of the Moon happen?
abschnitte.text: The Sun always lights up exactly one half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits the Earth, we look at it from changing directions. Sometimes we see a lot of the bright side, sometimes a little, sometimes none. This creates the **phases of the Moon**. People often think that the Earth's shadow covers the Moon, but that is not true; that only happens during a lunar eclipse.

About **29.5 days** pass from one new moon to the next. At new moon, the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun and is invisible. After that, a thin **crescent** appears in the evening, growing day by day until, after about a week, you can see the waxing **half moon**. Around two weeks after new moon it is **full moon**; after that the Moon wanes again to the waning half moon and the next new moon.

In the northern hemisphere, which includes Switzerland, the rule is: if the right side is bright and the crescent looks like a bracket “)”, the Moon is waxing. If the left side is bright, like “(”, it is waning. An old German memory aid says that if you can add one stroke to make a handwritten **a**, the Moon is waning (abnehmen means to wane). In the southern hemisphere, for example in Australia, it is exactly the other way round.

You can often see the Moon during the **day** too, for example the waxing half moon in the afternoon or the waning one in the morning. It looks pale then, because the bright sky outshines it. Only around new moon can you not see it at all, because it is almost in the same direction as the Sun. The full moon, on the other hand, rises at about sunset and sets at about sunrise.

Because the Moon returns so regularly, many peoples based their **calendars** on it. Our word “month” comes from the word moon. The Islamic calendar is still a pure lunar calendar today, and the date of Easter depends on the first full moon in spring. As a lunar month is shorter than most calendar months, there are sometimes two full moons in one month; the second is often called a **blue moon**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The shape in which we see the lit part of the Moon.
The thin, curved shape of the Moon shortly after or before new moon.
The phase in which exactly half of the visible disc of the Moon is bright.
The lit part of the Moon gets bigger from day to day.
A common name for the second full moon in a calendar month.

gewusst: A blue moon is not blue; the name just means that it is a rare event.
A lunar eclipse can only happen at full moon, a solar eclipse only at new moon.
Astronauts on the Moon also see the Earth in phases, just the exact opposite of our phases of the Moon.

teile.einleitung: Nikola Tesla was an inventor and engineer who is famous above all for his work with alternating current. He was born in what is now Croatia and lived in the USA from 1884. Many of his ideas are still found in motors, power stations and electricity grids today.
wichtigste: Nikola Tesla was born in 1856 in Smiljan in what is now Croatia and died in 1943 in New York.
From 1884 he lived and worked in the USA, at first briefly for Thomas Alva Edison.
He developed the induction motor, an electric motor that runs on alternating current.
He sold his patents for the alternating current system to the businessman George Westinghouse.
With his alternating current, a large power station was built at Niagara Falls in 1895.
The Tesla coil produces very high voltages and artificial lightning.
The unit tesla for magnetic flux density is named after him.

abschnitte.text: Nikola Tesla was born on 10 July 1856 in **Smiljan**, a village in what is now Croatia, which then belonged to the Austrian Empire. His parents were Serbs, and his father was a priest. Even as a child he had an excellent memory and could picture machines precisely in his head. He studied engineering in **Graz** and then worked in Budapest and Paris. In Budapest he came up with the idea for a motor with a rotating magnetic field.

In 1884, Tesla emigrated to **New York**. At first he worked for the famous inventor **Thomas Alva Edison**, who backed direct current. But the two quarrelled, and after a short time Tesla went his own way. He developed the **induction motor**, an electric motor that runs on alternating current and is found in many machines today. He sold his patents for the alternating current system to the businessman **George Westinghouse**.

At the end of the 19th century, Edison on one side and Westinghouse and Tesla on the other argued about which kind of current should win. This dispute is called the **war of the currents**. **Alternating current** has the advantage that transformers can easily raise it to high voltages so that it can be carried over long distances. In 1893, Westinghouse lit up the World's Fair in Chicago with alternating current. In 1895, a large hydroelectric power station with Tesla's system started working at **Niagara Falls**, and alternating current won the day.

Tesla invented the **Tesla transformer**, also called the Tesla coil, which produces very high voltages and artificial lightning. In 1898 in New York he demonstrated a **remote-controlled boat**, which seemed like magic at the time. He dreamed of sending electricity through the air without cables. For this he had the Wardenclyffe Tower built on Long Island, but it was never finished because the money ran out. Altogether he received several hundred patents worldwide.

Despite his many inventions, Tesla was poor at the end of his life. He lived a withdrawn life in hotel rooms in New York and liked to feed pigeons. He died on 7 January 1943 at the age of 86. Today he is considered one of the most important pioneers of electrical engineering. Since 1960, the unit of **magnetic flux density** has been called the tesla, and a well-known maker of electric cars also bears his name.

begriffe.erklaerung: Current that constantly changes direction, like the current from a socket.
Current that always flows in the same direction, like the current from a battery.
A device that raises or lowers electrical voltage.
A right that protects an inventor's invention for a certain time.
An electric motor driven by a rotating magnetic field.

gewusst: Tesla spoke several languages and is said to have known whole books by heart.
In Belgrade there is a Nikola Tesla Museum, where his urn is also kept.
At 1.5 to 3 tesla, the magnet in a hospital MRI scanner is tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth's magnetic field.

teile.einleitung: A logarithmic scale is a scale on which each equal step increases not by a fixed amount but by a fixed factor, for example always times 10. This lets tiny and huge values fit onto a single diagram. In physics and everyday life you meet it with loudness, earthquakes, pH and the brightness of stars.
wichtigste: On a logarithmic scale every step means multiplying by the same factor.
The base-10 logarithm of 1000 is 3, because 10 to the power 3 equals 1000.
The decibel is a tenth of the unit bel, which is named after Alexander Graham Bell.
If the magnitude of an earthquake is 1 higher, the measured ground movement is ten times greater.
A solution with pH 3 contains 100 times more hydronium ions than one with pH 5.
According to the Weber-Fechner law, our sensation grows roughly logarithmically with the strength of the stimulus.
For stars, a difference of five magnitudes equals a brightness factor of 100.

abschnitte.text: On a normal ruler the gap between 1 and 2 is the same as between 9 and 10. On a **logarithmic scale**, however, there is as much space between 1 and 10 as between 10 and 100 or between 100 and 1000. Such a step of ten is called a **decade**. The human hearing range from 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz, for example, covers exactly three decades.

The basis is the **logarithm**: it asks to which power you must raise a base to get a number. The base-10 logarithm of 1000 is 3, because 10 times 10 times 10 equals 1000. The Scottish mathematician John Napier published the first tables of logarithms in 1614. Engineers calculated with the **slide rule**, which has logarithmic scales engraved on it, until the 1970s.

Our ears hear a huge range of sound strengths, from the quietest whisper to a jet engine. That is why sound level is measured in **decibels**, a tenth of the unit bel, named after the telephone pioneer Alexander Graham Bell. Ten times more sound intensity means 10 dB more. An intensity that is only a hundredth of the reference intensity has a level of minus 20 dB.

The strength of earthquakes is given as a **magnitude**, a scale that Charles Richter introduced in 1935. If the magnitude is 1 higher, the measured ground movement is ten times greater, and around 30 times more energy is released. **pH** is also logarithmic: a solution with pH 3 contains 100 times more hydronium ions than one with pH 5. The Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich reports earthquakes in Switzerland using this magnitude.

The Greek astronomer Hipparchus already divided stars into classes according to their brightness. Today a difference of 5 **magnitudes** means a brightness factor of exactly 100. Our senses also work roughly logarithmically; this is described by the **Weber-Fechner law**. That is why ten candles in a room instead of one do not look ten times brighter, just noticeably brighter.

Logarithmic scales help to compare values that differ by many powers of ten. In diagrams of the growth of bacteria or the spread of diseases, steady growth appears as a straight line. This lets you see at a glance whether something is growing faster or more slowly. But when reading them it is important always to look at the labelling of the axes, otherwise it is easy to underestimate large differences.

begriffe.erklaerung: The power to which you must raise a base to get a number.
A range in which a value becomes ten times larger, for example from 10 to 100.
Logarithmic measure, above all for loudness.
Logarithmic measure of the strength of an earthquake.
Number that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is.

gewusst: There is no zero on a logarithmic scale, because however often you divide by 10, you never quite reach zero.
The musical scale on the piano is built logarithmically: each octave higher doubles the frequency.

teile.einleitung: Magnetic flux density tells you how strong a magnetic field is at a particular place and in which direction it points. Its symbol is B and it is measured in tesla. With it you can compare whether a magnetic field is as weak as the Earth's or as strong as in a hospital machine.
wichtigste: Magnetic flux density has the symbol B.
Its unit is the tesla, abbreviated T.
It is a vector quantity, so it has magnitude and direction.
In Switzerland the Earth's magnetic field has a flux density of around 50 microtesla.
Around a long straight conductor B decreases with distance; at three times the distance it falls to a third.
An iron core strengthens the field of a coil by the relative permeability.
Because there are no magnetic monopoles, magnetic field lines are closed.

abschnitte.text: You can picture a magnetic field with **field lines**, as iron filings show them around a magnet. If the field lines lie close together, the field is strong and the flux density B is large. Because B also has a direction, it is a **vector quantity**. The direction points where the north pole of a compass needle would point.

The unit is the **tesla**, named after the inventor Nikola Tesla. One tesla corresponds to one volt second per square metre. Because 1 tesla is a great deal, people often calculate in millitesla (mT) or microtesla (µT). In the past the unit gauss was also used; 10 000 gauss equal 1 tesla.

Every current produces a magnetic field that runs in rings around the conductor. For a long straight conductor B = µ₀ · I / (2π · r), where **µ₀** is the magnetic constant. With a current of 10 A and a distance of 2 cm this gives 100 µT. If you triple the distance, B falls to a third.

Inside a long coil the field is almost uniform. Here B = µ₀ · N · I / l, where N is the number of turns and l the length. A coil with 1000 turns, 0.5 m long and with a current of 2 A, produces around 5 mT. With an **iron core** the field is strengthened by the relative permeability, for iron by a hundred to a thousand times.

At about 50 µT in Switzerland, the Earth's magnetic field is rather weak. A fridge magnet reaches a few millitesla, a strong neodymium magnet right at its surface about 1 tesla. Machines for **magnetic resonance imaging** in hospital often work at 1.5 or 3 tesla. B is measured with a Hall probe, which produces a small voltage in the magnetic field.

The flux density determines how strongly a magnetic field acts on moving charges and currents. This force is called the **Lorentz force** and drives every electric motor. B also plays a central role in the generators of hydroelectric power stations, in loudspeakers and in particle accelerators such as at CERN. The magnets of the large accelerator LHC reach over 8 tesla.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of magnetic flux density.
Imaginary lines that show the direction and strength of a magnetic field.
A quantity with magnitude and direction, shown as an arrow.
Tells you how strongly a substance strengthens a magnetic field.

gewusst: The Earth's magnetic field is about a hundred thousand times weaker than the field in an MRI machine.
Researchers have even made a frog float in a very strong magnetic field of around 16 tesla.
Magnetic field lines have no beginning and no end; they are always closed loops.

teile.einleitung: A folding rule is a measuring tool that folds up and can usually be opened out to 2 metres. Carpenters, bricklayers and DIY enthusiasts often carry it in their trouser pocket. In Switzerland it is called a “Meterstab”, in Germany a “Zollstock”.
wichtigste: A usual folding rule is 2 metres long when opened out.
It usually consists of 10 sections of 20 centimetres each.
Classic folding rules are made of wood.
You fold it up so that it fits in your pocket.
Carpenters often need it at work.
For large objects such as a table it is better suited than a ruler.
In Germany it is often called a “Zollstock”.

abschnitte.text: A folding rule consists of several **sections** of equal length that are connected by joints. Usually there are 10 sections of 20 centimetres each, so 200 centimetres or 2 metres altogether. Centimetres and millimetres are printed on every section. Folded up, it is only a little over 20 centimetres long and fits in any pocket.

Classic folding rules are made of **wood**, often beech, and painted yellow or white. There are also folding rules made of plastic, aluminium or fibreglass. The joints are made of metal and click into place when straight. To keep it accurate for a long time, you should not bend it sideways.

**Joiners**, carpenters, bricklayers and electricians use it to measure boards, doors and walls. It is also handy when moving house or buying furniture. Because it is stiff, you can also use it to measure freely upwards or across a gap, which is difficult with a soft tape measure. For a table it is much better suited than a short ruler.

If a room is 5 metres long, a folding rule is not enough. Then you lay it down several times one after the other and mark the end each time. Twice in full and then one more metre gives 5 metres. For even longer distances you use a **tape measure** or a laser measuring device.

The folding rule measures in **metres**, a unit that was introduced in France after the Revolution. In 1875 Switzerland also signed the international Metre Convention. For a long time a metal rod in Paris, the original metre, was the model for all metres. Since 1983 the metre has been defined through the speed of light, as the distance that light travels in a tiny fraction of a second.

In Switzerland people say **“Meterstab”** or sometimes “Doppelmeter”, double metre. In Germany it is called a “Zollstock”, inch stick, even though it does not measure in inches at all. The name dates from the time when lengths were still given in inches. Experts speak of a “Gliedermassstab”, jointed rule.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single straight piece of the folding rule.
The movable connection between two sections.
The base unit of length, 1 m = 100 cm.
An old unit of length, today about 2.54 centimetres.

gewusst: A 2-metre folding rule with 10 sections has 9 joints.
Folding rules often carry an accuracy class that states how large the deviation may be at most.
Many people like to fold a folding rule into shapes such as triangles or stars.

teile.einleitung: The metre is the most important unit of measurement for length and is abbreviated with a small “m”. With it you measure how long, wide, high or far something is, from a classroom to the highest mountain. Almost all countries in the world use it, Switzerland too.
wichtigste: The metre is the base unit of length and is abbreviated “m”.
One metre has 100 centimetres or 1000 millimetres.
One kilometre has 1000 metres, so half a kilometre is 500 metres.
A normal room door is about 2 metres high.
The metre was introduced in France at the end of the 18th century.
Today the metre is defined through the speed of light.
The Dufourspitze, Switzerland's highest mountain, is around 4600 metres high, exactly 4634 metres.

abschnitte.text: The metre is a **unit of measurement** for length, that is for distances and spaces between things. It belongs to the international system of units **SI**, which experts all over the world use. The abbreviation is a small “m”. A metre is roughly as long as a big step of an adult. A normal room door is about 2 metres high, a school bus about 12 metres long.

Because the metre belongs to the **decimal system**, it is easy to convert. One metre has 100 **centimetres** or 1000 millimetres. So 2 metres and 50 centimetres together are 250 centimetres. 1000 metres make a **kilometre**, so half a kilometre is 500 metres. That is also why 1 metre is longer than 90 centimetres: 10 centimetres are missing.

In the past almost every town had its own measures of length such as the foot, the ell or the fathom, which made trade complicated. During the French Revolution it was decided to create one measure for everyone. The metre was to be the ten-millionth part of the distance from the **North Pole** to the equator, measured through Paris. From this a measuring rod of platinum was made, the **original metre**. In 1875 several states, including Switzerland, signed the Metre Convention to secure common measures.

A metal rod can expand in heat or be damaged, so a more precise definition was sought. Since 1983 the rule has been: one metre is the distance that **light** travels in a vacuum in one 299 792 458th of a second. This way the metre can be measured in any well-equipped laboratory. In Switzerland the Federal Institute of **Metrology** in Bern-Wabern makes sure that measuring devices are right. This is important so that, for example, fabrics, cables or components are measured to the same length everywhere.

In everyday life we measure with a ruler, a **folding rule** or a tape measure. Signposts on Swiss hiking trails show the time, but maps show the height above sea level in metres. At 4634 metres, the **Dufourspitze** in Valais is Switzerland's highest mountain. In sports competitions athletes run over 100 metres or jump several metres. Heights of people are also given in metres and centimetres, for example 1 metre 45.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed quantity with which you measure and compare something.
The platinum measuring rod that used to define how long a metre is.
The science of precise measurement.
1000 metres, the usual measure for long distances.

gewusst: The word metre comes from the Greek “metron”, which simply means measure.
Light is so fast that it travels a metre in about three billionths of a second.
The folding rule that craftspeople use is usually two metres long.

teile.einleitung: A crane is a machine used to lift, lower and move heavy loads sideways. On building sites, in ports and in factory halls cranes do jobs that would be impossible with muscle power alone. They use physical principles such as the lever, the pulley and the counterweight.
wichtigste: A crane is used to lift heavy loads.
Many building sites have a tall tower crane.
The load hangs from a hook on a steel cable.
A trolley moves back and forth along the jib.
Heavy concrete blocks as a counterweight stop the crane from tipping over.
A mobile crane is a crane on a lorry.
You must never stand under a suspended load.

abschnitte.text: A crane is a **lifting device** that raises loads with a cable and takes them to another place. The load hangs from a **hook** attached to a steel cable. The cable is wound up and down by a winch with an electric motor. Cranes come in many sizes, from the small loading crane on a lorry to the giant crane in a port.

On Swiss building sites you usually see the **tower crane**. It consists of an upright tower and a horizontal **jib** that can turn in a circle. Along the jib moves the **trolley**, a small carriage with the hook. The crane operator often sits in a cab at the top of the crane or controls it by radio remote control from the ground.

A tower crane works like a giant **lever** whose pivot is the tower. On the short side of the jib there are heavy concrete blocks as a **counterweight**. They balance the turning effect of the load so that the crane does not tip over. The further out the load hangs, the lighter it must be.

A **mobile crane** sits on a lorry and can drive quickly from one building site to the next. Before lifting it supports itself on legs that slide out. In factory halls **overhead cranes** run along rails under the ceiling. In ports container cranes unload the containers from the ships.

You must never stand under a suspended load, because it could fall. In strong wind tower cranes have to stop working and are released so that they can turn like a weathervane. The ancient Greeks and Romans already built wooden cranes with **pulleys**. In the Middle Ages people drove the cranes used to build cathedrals by walking in large treadwheels.

begriffe.erklaerung: Long horizontal arm of the crane from which the load hangs.
Small carriage that moves back and forth along the jib.
Heavy load on the opposite side that keeps the crane balanced.
Arrangement of wheels and ropes that lets you lift with less force.

gewusst: The name crane comes from the bird, because the long jib is reminiscent of its neck.
Tower cranes are often put up with a second crane or a mobile crane, but some can put themselves up.
In the Middle Ages people had to walk in treadwheels like hamsters in a wheel to haul up heavy stones.

teile.einleitung: Kitchen scales are a small measuring device used to weigh ingredients for cooking and baking. They usually show the weight in grams. Weighing accurately is especially important when baking, so that cakes, bread and biscuits turn out well.
wichtigste: Kitchen scales are used to weigh ingredients.
Most kitchen scales show the weight in grams.
The tare button takes away the weight of the bowl.
Digital kitchen scales usually need a battery.
Kitchen scales usually only weigh up to about 5 kilograms; a bike is too heavy.
When baking you weigh accurately so that the cake turns out well.
In physics terms the scales measure the force of weight and convert it into a mass.

abschnitte.text: **Kitchen scales** measure how heavy ingredients such as flour, sugar or butter are. The reading is usually in **grams**, sometimes also in millilitres for water or milk. Many kitchen scales weigh up to about 5 kilograms and show the result to the nearest gram. Heavy things like a bike cannot be weighed on them.

Older **mechanical kitchen scales** have a spring that is squashed by the weight and moves a pointer. Modern **digital scales** contain a sensor, the load cell, which bends very slightly under the load. This tiny change in shape changes an electrical resistance, which a chip converts into a number. That is why digital scales need a battery.

If you put a bowl on the scales, its weight is measured too. The **tare** button sets the display back to zero. After that the scales show only the weight of the ingredient in the bowl. In this way you can weigh several ingredients one after another into the same bowl, setting it back to zero each time.

When baking, the amounts have to be right, otherwise the dough becomes too dry or too runny. If you need 200 grams of sugar and there are already 150 grams on the scales, 50 grams are still missing. If you have weighed out 300 grams of flour but need only half, that is 150 grams. If you want to double a **recipe**, you simply double all the amounts.

Strictly speaking, kitchen scales measure the **force of weight** with which the ingredient presses down. From this they work out the **mass** in grams. On the Moon, where gravity is about six times weaker, a spring scale would therefore show far too little. A balance that compares with weights, on the other hand, would measure correctly on the Moon too.

begriffe.erklaerung: Weight of the packaging or bowl, which is subtracted.
Unit of mass; 1000 grams are one kilogram.
Sensor in digital scales that measures the load.
How much matter an object contains, measured in kilograms.

gewusst: The word tare comes from Arabic and means roughly deduction.
One litre of water weighs almost exactly one kilogram, so you can weigh water instead of measuring it.
Professional bakers even weigh liquids and eggs, because it is more accurate than measuring jugs.

teile.einleitung: The Lorentz force is the force that a magnetic field exerts on moving electric charges. It steers electrons and protons onto circular paths and drives electric motors. It is named after the Dutch physicist Hendrik Antoon Lorentz.
wichtigste: The Lorentz force acts only on charges moving in a magnetic field.
Its size is F equals q times v times B when the charge moves at right angles to the field.
If a charge moves parallel to the field lines, no Lorentz force acts.
The force is always at right angles to the motion, so it changes only the direction, not the speed.
Twice the speed means twice the Lorentz force.
On a wire carrying a current the force is F equals I times L times B.
Electric motors use this force to produce movement.

abschnitte.text: When an electrically charged particle moves through a **magnetic field**, it is pushed sideways. This sideways force is called the **Lorentz force**. Hendrik Antoon Lorentz (1853 to 1928) described it precisely and received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1902. Charges at rest, on the other hand, feel nothing from the magnetic field.

If a charge q moves at speed v at right angles to a field of strength B, then F equals q times v times B. A proton travelling at 2 million metres per second in a field of 0.5 **tesla** feels about 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 13 newtons. That sounds tiny, but for such a light particle it is huge. The direction of the force is shown by the **three-finger rule**, in which the thumb, index finger and middle finger are held out at right angles to each other.

Because the Lorentz force always points across the motion, it forces particles onto a **circular path**. A proton travelling at one million metres per second in a field of 0.1 tesla circles with a radius of about 10 centimetres. In the school experiment with the **fine beam tube** you can see electrons as a glowing circle. From the radius you can work out the specific charge e/m of the electron.

When current flows through a wire in a magnetic field, the force acts on all the electrons in the wire and so on the whole **conductor**. A wire 0.5 metres long carrying 5 amperes in a field of 0.2 tesla is pushed with 0.5 newtons. In an **electric motor** this force turns a coil. Loudspeakers and headphones also move their membrane in this way.

Charged particles from the Sun are deflected by the Earth's magnetic field and guided to the poles. There they make the air glow as the **aurora**. At the CERN research centre near Geneva, strong magnets keep particles on their path in the 27 kilometre LHC accelerator ring. The loud knocking noises of an MRI scanner are also caused by Lorentz forces on the coils.

begriffe.erklaerung: Property of particles such as electrons and protons of being electrically positive or negative.
Region around a magnet in which magnetic forces act.
Unit for the strength of a magnetic field.
Glass sphere containing a little gas in which the path of electrons can be seen glowing.
Memory aid using three outstretched fingers for the direction of the Lorentz force.

gewusst: The time a particle takes to go round in a magnetic field does not depend on its speed; faster particles simply travel on larger circles.
Old tube televisions used magnetic fields to steer the electron beam across the screen, which is why a magnet nearby distorted the picture.
Without the Lorentz force there would be no aurora.

teile.einleitung: The Lorentz transformation is a rule of calculation for converting position and time measurements from one moving observer to those of another. It is the heart of Einstein's special theory of relativity. Something astonishing follows from it: time and length are not the same for everyone.
wichtigste: The Lorentz transformation is named after the Dutch physicist Hendrik Antoon Lorentz.
It replaces the Galilean transformation of classical mechanics.
At speeds far below the speed of light it gives approximately the Galilean transformation again.
The Lorentz factor is γ = 1 / √(1 minus v²/c²).
The spacetime interval between two events stays unchanged by the transformation.
Maxwell's equations of electrodynamics keep their form under the Lorentz transformation.
Time dilation and length contraction follow from it.

abschnitte.text: Hendrik Antoon **Lorentz** (1853 to 1928) was a physicist from the Netherlands and received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1902. He set out the formulas around 1904 to explain why no ether wind had been found in the Michelson-Morley experiment. The Frenchman Henri **Poincaré** gave the conversion its name. Albert Einstein derived it anew in Bern in 1905, while he was working at the Federal Patent Office.

In everyday life we simply add speeds. If you walk forwards in a train at 5 km/h and the train is travelling at 100 km/h, you are moving at 105 km/h for someone on the platform. This simple rule is called the **Galilean transformation**. But it does not work for light, because light is equally fast for all observers, about 300,000 km per second.

If a frame S' moves at speed v along the x axis, then x' = γ · (x minus v·t) and t' = γ · (t minus v·x/c²). The **Lorentz factor** γ is always at least 1 and becomes huge as v approaches the speed of light c. An example: at v = 0.6 c, γ = 1.25. An event with t = 0 and x = 4 light years then has the coordinates x' = 5 light years and t' = minus 3 years in S'.

Moving clocks run slow; this is called **time dilation**. Moving objects are shorter in the direction of motion; this is **length contraction**. Also, two events that are simultaneous for one observer are not necessarily simultaneous for another. What stays the same, on the other hand, is the spacetime interval, a kind of distance in four-dimensional spacetime.

GPS navigation satellites have to take relativistic effects into account, otherwise positions would quickly be kilometres out. Muons from cosmic radiation only reach the ground because their time runs more slowly from our point of view. At **CERN** in Geneva particles are accelerated almost to the speed of light, and their behaviour matches the Lorentz transformation exactly. Because Maxwell's equations stay the same under it, the theory of electricity and magnetism fits it perfectly too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A point of view with its own clocks and measuring rods, from which motion is described.
The speed of light in empty space, about 300,000 km per second, the same for all observers.
Moving clocks run more slowly as seen by an observer at rest.
Space and time thought of together as a four-dimensional whole.

gewusst: For a car travelling at 100 km/h the Lorentz factor is so close to 1 that you only see a difference in the 15th decimal place.
Albert Einstein developed the special theory of relativity during his time in Bern, where his flat can now be visited as the Einstein House.
According to the Lorentz transformation nothing with mass can reach the speed of light, because γ would then become infinitely large.

teile.einleitung: A magnifying glass is a simple glass for making things look bigger. With it you can see small things such as ants, stamps or the veins of a leaf much larger. It consists of a converging lens that bundles light.
wichtigste: A magnifying glass is a converging lens in a frame with a handle.
It makes small things look bigger.
The lens is thicker in the middle than at the edge.
A magnifying glass bundles the sun's rays onto one point.
This point is called the focal point and can get very hot.
Magnifying glasses usually magnify about two to ten times.

abschnitte.text: A **magnifying glass** is a round piece of glass or plastic in a frame with a handle. The glass is a **converging lens** that is thicker in the middle than at the edge. If you hold it close above a small object, you see it much bigger. There are hand magnifiers, stand magnifiers and reading magnifiers.

Light is bent as it passes through the curved glass. As a result the object looks bigger to your eye than it really is. How strongly a magnifying glass magnifies depends on its **focal length**. The more strongly the glass is curved, the greater the **magnification**.

A magnifying glass bundles the sun's rays onto a small point. This point is called the **focal point**. It gets so hot there that paper can start to burn. That is why you must never leave a magnifying glass lying in the sun and never look at the sun through it.

Researchers and children use magnifying glasses to examine insects, stones or plants. People with weak eyes read small print with a **reading magnifier**. Watchmakers wear a small magnifier right at the eye. Stamp collectors and jewellers also need them every day.

Even in ancient times people knew that curved pieces of glass or glass balls filled with water make things bigger. In the Middle Ages these led to **reading stones** and later to the first spectacles. The magnifying glass finally developed into the **microscope** and the telescope. These instruments consist of several lenses one behind the other.

begriffe.erklaerung: A lens that is thicker in the middle and bundles light.
The point where the bundled light rays meet.
The distance between the lens and the focal point.
How much bigger something looks through the magnifying glass.

gewusst: A drop of water on a leaf acts like a tiny magnifying glass.
Sherlock Holmes, the famous detective from the books, is often shown with a magnifying glass.
With a magnifying glass you can light a fire without a match when the sun is shining.

teile.einleitung: The critical point is a special state of a substance in which liquid and gas can no longer be told apart. Above this point there is no boiling any more, just a single, strange state. This property is used, for example, to decaffeinate coffee.
wichtigste: The critical point is defined by a critical temperature and a critical pressure.
Above it there is no longer any difference between liquid and gas.
A substance in this state is called a supercritical fluid.
For water the critical point is at about 374 °C and about 221 bar.
For carbon dioxide the critical temperature is only about 31 °C.
Supercritical carbon dioxide is used to decaffeinate coffee.
Thomas Andrews coined the term critical point in 1869 during experiments with carbon dioxide.

abschnitte.text: Normally a liquid boils at a certain temperature and turns into gas. If you raise the pressure, this boiling point rises. But this cannot go on for ever: at the **critical point**, liquid and vapour become equally dense and can no longer be told apart. It is defined by the **critical temperature** and the **critical pressure**.

For water the critical point is at about 374 °C and a pressure of about 221 bar, more than 200 times normal air pressure. For **carbon dioxide** the critical temperature is much lower, at about 31 °C, and the critical pressure is about 74 bar. That is why carbon dioxide can easily be brought into the supercritical state. Every substance has its own critical point.

If you heat liquid and vapour in a tightly sealed, strong glass tube, at first you see a clear boundary, the **meniscus**. The closer you get to the critical point, the more alike liquid and vapour become. Just before it, the substance turns milky and cloudy; this effect is called **critical opalescence**. At the critical point the meniscus finally disappears completely.

abschnitte.titel: Why pressure is not always enough
abschnitte.text: Above its critical temperature a gas can no longer be liquefied by pressure alone. Nitrogen has a critical temperature of about minus 147 °C. Because room temperature is much higher, nitrogen cannot be made liquid at room temperature even with enormous pressure; it first has to be cooled strongly. That is why such gases used to be called “permanent gases”, until people learnt to liquefy them with enough cold.

A **supercritical fluid** has properties of both gas and liquid at the same time: it gets into the finest pores like a gas and dissolves substances like a liquid. Supercritical carbon dioxide, for example, dissolves caffeine out of coffee beans without leaving poisonous residues. It is also used to extract hop aromas or spice oils. Some modern coal-fired power stations work with supercritical steam, because this lets them get more electricity from the same heat.

As early as 1822 the French researcher Charles Cagniard de la Tour observed that liquids in sealed tubes suddenly disappear when strongly heated. In 1869 the Irish chemist **Thomas Andrews** studied carbon dioxide closely and coined the term critical point. A little later the Dutch physicist Johannes Diderik van der Waals provided an equation that explains this behaviour. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1910.

begriffe.erklaerung: Temperature above which a gas can no longer be liquefied by pressure.
Pressure at the critical point.
State above the critical point, neither really liquid nor gas.
Visible boundary between liquid and vapour.

gewusst: In the deep sea there are hot springs whose water is so hot and under such high pressure that it comes close to the critical point or even goes beyond it.
Carbon dioxide in a fire extinguisher is liquid in cool weather, but on a very hot summer's day it can go above its critical temperature.
A pressure of 221 bar is about the water pressure at a sea depth of around 2200 metres.

teile.einleitung: A magnetic field is the invisible area around a magnet in which its force acts. You can make it visible with iron filings. The Earth and every wire through which current flows also have a magnetic field.
wichtigste: A magnetic field is the space around a magnet in which magnetic forces act.
With iron filings you can make the field lines visible.
Like magnetic poles repel each other, unlike poles attract each other.
Iron is attracted by a magnet.
The compass needle lines up with the Earth's magnetic field and points roughly north.
A magnetic field forms around a wire carrying current.
More turns and an iron core make an electromagnet stronger.

abschnitte.text: Around a magnet there is an area in which it exerts forces. This area is called the **magnetic field**. You cannot see it, but you can feel its effect. Close to the magnet the field is strong; further away it becomes weaker.

If you sprinkle **iron filings** on a sheet of paper above a magnet, they arrange themselves in lines. These lines are called **field lines**. They run from the north pole to the south pole. Where they lie close together, the field is especially strong.
