The Earth has its own magnetic field, which arises in the liquid iron deep inside the Earth. A **compass needle** is a small magnet that lines up with this field. That is why it points roughly north. The Earth's magnetic field also protects us from charged particles from the Sun, and where these enter the atmosphere, **auroras** appear.

When current flows through a wire, a ring-shaped magnetic field forms around it. The Dane **Hans Christian Ørsted** discovered this in 1820. If you wind the wire into a coil, the field becomes much stronger. This creates an **electromagnet**.

An electromagnet becomes stronger if the coil has more **turns**. An **iron core** in the coil also strengthens the field considerably. A third possibility is a stronger current. Electromagnets are found in door openers, electric motors and in MRI scanners in hospital.

begriffe.erklaerung: Imaginary lines that show how a magnetic field runs.
A device with a magnetic needle that shows the direction.
A wire that has been wound up many times.
Coloured glow in the night sky, especially near the poles.

gewusst: Migratory birds can sense the Earth's magnetic field and use it to find their way.
The Earth's magnetic poles move slowly and have often swapped places in the course of the Earth's history.
Auroras can sometimes even be seen in Switzerland, most recently especially beautifully in May 2024.

teile.einleitung: The gravitational field strength tells you how strongly a celestial body pulls on one kilogram of mass at a particular place. In Switzerland it is about 9.81 newtons per kilogram. On the Moon it is much smaller, which is why astronauts can hop about so easily there.
wichtigste: Gravitational field strength is the weight per kilogram of mass.
It is given the letter g and is stated in newtons per kilogram (N/kg).
The unit N/kg equals m/s², which is why g is also called the acceleration due to gravity.
In Switzerland, the gravitational field strength is about 9.81 N/kg.
It is slightly smaller at the equator than at the poles, and slightly smaller on high mountains than in the valley.
On the Moon it is only about 1.6 N/kg, at the surface of the Sun about 274 N/kg.
Among the planets, Jupiter has the greatest gravitational field strength, and Venus has one similar to the Earth's.

abschnitte.text: Every object is pulled by the Earth; this force is called **weight**. The gravitational field strength tells you how much weight acts on one kilogram of mass. The formula is: weight equals mass times gravitational field strength. So in Switzerland, a child with a mass of 30 kilograms is pulled downwards with about 294 newtons.

The unit newtons per kilogram is exactly the same as metres per second squared. That is why g is also called the **acceleration due to gravity**. Without air resistance, a falling stone gets about 9.81 metres per second faster every second. After one second of free fall, it is therefore travelling at around 35 kilometres per hour.

The Earth is not a perfect sphere but is a little fatter at the equator. There you are further from the centre of the Earth, and the Earth's fast rotation also pushes a little outwards. That is why the gravitational field strength is about 9.78 N/kg at the equator and about 9.83 N/kg at the poles. **Height** plays a part too: on the summit of the Matterhorn, the gravitational field strength is a tiny bit smaller than in Zurich.

abschnitte.titel: Gravitational field strength in the solar system
abschnitte.text: The bigger and heavier a celestial body is, the greater its gravitational field strength usually is. On the **Moon** it is only about 1.6 N/kg, roughly a sixth of the Earth's value. On Mars it is about 3.7 N/kg, and on Venus about 8.9 N/kg, almost as much as on Earth. Jupiter has the greatest value of all the planets at almost 25 N/kg, and at the surface of the Sun it would even be about 274 N/kg.

The gravitational field strength can be measured with a pendulum or with falling experiments. Very precise measuring devices are called **gravimeters**. Geologists use tiny differences in the gravitational field strength to track down dense rocks or hollows underground. For scales in shops and laboratories, the exact gravitational field strength is important so that they measure correctly everywhere.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much matter there is in an object, measured in kilograms. It is the same everywhere.
The force with which a celestial body pulls on an object, measured in newtons.
The unit of force, named after Isaac Newton.
How much faster a falling object gets every second.

gewusst: On the Moon, a child who jumps 30 centimetres high on Earth would get almost two metres high.
Your mass stays the same on all planets; only your weight changes.
An object weighs about half a per cent more at the poles than at the equator.

teile.einleitung: Muscle output tells you how much work a person or animal can do with their muscles per second. Like the power of machines, it is measured in watts. A healthy person can manage about 100 watts over a longer time, as much as a bright old light bulb uses.
wichtigste: Power is work divided by time and is measured in watts.
A healthy person can produce about 100 watts over a longer time.
You only reach your highest power briefly, for example in a sprint.
Muscles have an efficiency of about 25 per cent.
Most of the energy turns into heat, which is why we get warm during sport.
In cycling, riders are compared using watts per kilogram.
A cyclist weighing 70 kg who produces 280 W manages 4 W/kg.

abschnitte.text: In physics, **power** is the work done in a certain time. If you lift something faster, the power is greater, even though the work stays the same. The unit is the **watt**, named after the Scot James Watt. One watt means one joule of work per second.

When you lift a mass, the work is weight times height. An example: 30 squats in 60 seconds, each lifting 40 kg by 0.4 m. With 10 N/kg, each squat gives 160 joules, 4800 joules altogether, and divided by 60 seconds that makes **80 watts**. If you lift a 2 kg dumbbell 0.5 m twenty times in 10 seconds, that is 20 watts.

How much power you can produce depends strongly on how long you keep it up. Over hours, a healthy person manages about **100 watts**, for example when cycling at an easy pace. Well-trained professional cyclists can hold several hundred watts for an hour. In a short **sprint** of a few seconds, top athletes even reach over 1000 watts.

Muscles turn only about a quarter of the energy from food into movement. This **efficiency** of around 25 per cent means that 400 watts of energy use produce about 100 watts of mechanical power. The remaining three quarters become heat. That is why we sweat during sport: the sweat cools the skin as it evaporates.

In cycling, especially uphill, it is not only power that counts but also body weight. That is why power is divided by mass, giving **watts per kilogram**. A cyclist weighing 70 kg who produces 280 watts reaches 4 W/kg. A light rider with the same W/kg is about as fast uphill as a heavy one.

In the past, power was measured in horsepower; one horsepower is around 735 watts. So over time a person produces much less than a horse. A small car, on the other hand, has a power of many thousands of watts. Even so, a person on a bicycle is one of the most efficient means of getting around there is.

begriffe.erklaerung: Work done per unit of time.
The unit of power, one joule per second.
The share of energy that is turned into useful work.
A training machine, for example an exercise bike, that measures power in watts.

gewusst: Anyone who cycles at 100 watts for an hour could in theory keep a light bulb glowing for an hour.
In very short sprints on the cycling track, the best sprinters reach peak power of well over 2000 watts.
A person at rest turns about as much energy into heat as a lamp of around 80 to 100 watts.

teile.einleitung: The Magdeburg hemispheres are two metal shells with which Otto von Guericke demonstrated the force of air pressure in the 17th century. After he had pumped the air out, even teams of horses could hardly separate the spheres. The experiment is one of the most famous in the history of physics.
wichtigste: Otto von Guericke put two hemispheres together and pumped almost all the air out.
The outside air pressure pressed the hemispheres together with enormous force.
In the well-known picture 16 horses are pulling, 8 on each side.
In 1654 Guericke showed his vacuum experiments before the Imperial Diet in Regensburg.
When a valve was opened and air let in, the hemispheres fell apart quite easily.
Larger hemispheres need an even greater pulling force.
Magdeburg lies in today's federal state of Saxony-Anhalt in Germany.

abschnitte.text: **Otto von Guericke** lived from 1602 to 1686 and was mayor of Magdeburg for a long time. Besides politics he was interested in the natural sciences. He wanted to find out whether an empty space, a **vacuum**, can really exist. For this he invented one of the first **air pumps**.

Guericke put two hollow copper hemispheres together with a sealing ring. Then he pumped the air out. Horses were harnessed on each side, eight on each in the well-known picture. The animals pulled with all their strength, but the spheres held together.

The air around us presses from all sides with **air pressure** on every surface, about 10 newtons on every square centimetre. Normally the air inside pushes back just as strongly. If the air inside is missing, only the outside air presses and squeezes the shells firmly together. If you tie one side to a tree, nothing changes, because the tree holds against it like a second team.

In 1654 Guericke presented his vacuum experiments before the **Imperial Diet** in Regensburg, in front of the emperor and princes. The experiment with the horses took place a few years later in Magdeburg. Guericke described his results in a book of his own in 1672. The experiments showed impressively that air has weight and exerts pressure.

The pulling force needed depends on the size of the hemispheres, because a larger surface means more pressing force. On a high mountain the air pressure is lower. There the spheres could therefore be separated somewhat more easily, on the Jungfraujoch for example clearly more easily than at Lake Geneva. In many schools today the experiment is repeated with small hemispheres and a vacuum pump.

begriffe.erklaerung: A space in which there is almost no air and no other particles.
The force with which the air presses on every surface.
Device that sucks air out of a container or pumps it in.
Small closure with which you can let air in or out.

gewusst: Original hemispheres of Guericke's are kept today in the Deutsches Museum in Munich.
A suction cup on a window pane also holds because the outside air pressure presses it on.
In Magdeburg the experiment is still re-enacted with horses at festivals today.

teile.einleitung: A mechanical wave is a vibration that spreads through a substance such as air, water or a rope. Sound, water waves and earthquake waves belong to this group. Energy travels on, but the particles themselves stay almost in their place.
wichtigste: A mechanical wave always needs a medium, that is a substance.
It transports energy, but not matter over long distances.
The particles of the medium must be coupled to one another by forces.
Sound travels in water at about 1480 metres per second, much faster than in air.
Sound is faster in warm air than in cold air.
In a deep-water wave the water particles move in circles.
If you double the distance from a sound source, the intensity falls to a quarter.

abschnitte.text: If you throw a stone into water, rings spread out. But the water itself does not flow away; a leaf on the lake only rocks up and down. Only the **energy** of the movement is passed on. So a **mechanical wave** is a disturbance that travels from particle to particle.

The particles of a substance are connected to each other by forces, like balls with springs in between. If one particle is pushed, it pulls or pushes its neighbours along. That is why a mechanical wave always needs a **medium**. In empty space there is no sound, whereas light gets through even without a substance.

In a **transverse wave** the particles vibrate across the direction of travel, for example in a wave on a rope. In a **longitudinal wave** they vibrate back and forth in the direction of travel; this is how sound arises in air. The velocity at which the air particles vibrate is called the particle velocity. In water waves in the deep sea the particles move in small circles.

Every wave has a **wavelength**, a frequency and an amplitude, that is a height. Speed is wavelength times frequency. At 20 degrees sound travels at about 340 metres per second in air, about 1480 in water and much faster still in steel. On a rope with 0.01 kilograms per metre and a tension of 100 newtons, a wave travels at 100 metres per second.

**Earthquake waves** are also mechanical waves that travel through rock. The Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich measures them with many measuring stations throughout the country. Ultrasound at the doctor's, the echo in the mountains and music from loudspeakers are also based on mechanical waves. Because the energy spreads out, a sound gets quieter as the distance grows.

begriffe.erklaerung: The substance through which a wave moves, for example air or water.
The greatest displacement of a vibration, that is how high the wave is.
How many vibrations take place per second, measured in hertz.
Wave in which the particles vibrate back and forth in the direction of travel.
Wave in which the particles vibrate across the direction of travel.

gewusst: When spectators in a stadium do a Mexican wave, everyone stays in their seat, and yet the wave travels round the whole stadium.
Whales can communicate with deep sounds over hundreds of kilometres in the sea, because sound travels so well in water.
If you put your ear to a railway track, you hear a train earlier than through the air.

teile.einleitung: The shot put is an athletics event in which you push a heavy metal ball as far as possible. The shot is not thrown but pushed away from the neck with a powerful arm movement. There is a lot of physics behind the sport, because momentum, release angle and force decide the distance.
wichtigste: The women's shot weighs 4 kilograms, the men's 7.26 kilograms.
The shot is put from a circle with a diameter of just over 2 metres.
The shot is pushed away from the neck, not thrown.
The shot flies furthest when it is pushed at an upward angle.
Many athletes gain more momentum with a spin or a glide.
The shot put has been part of the programme since the first modern Olympic Games in 1896.
The Swiss Werner Günthör was world champion in the shot put three times.

abschnitte.text: In the shot put you try to send a **metal ball** as far as possible. The women's shot weighs 4 kilograms and the men's 7.26 kilograms; for young people they are lighter. You place the shot against your neck and push it away by straightening your arm, which is why it is called **putting** and not throwing. Anyone who takes the shot back behind the shoulder and throws it makes an invalid attempt.

The shot is put from a **throwing circle** with a diameter of 2.135 metres. At the front it is bordered by a curved wooden board, the stop board. The shot must land in a marked sector, and the athlete may only leave the circle once the shot has landed, and then from the back. The distance is measured from the edge of the circle to the dent the shot leaves in the ground when it lands.

The distance depends above all on the **release speed**, then on the angle and the release height. If you push flat, the shot comes down too early; if you push too steeply, it flies high but not far. The best is an upward angle, usually a little less than 45 degrees for top athletes. A heavy shot flies less far than a tennis ball, because with the same force you can give it much less speed.

To make the shot faster, athletes build up momentum in the circle. In the **glide** you slide backwards across the circle and then turn for the put. In the **spin** technique you turn once around yourself, much as in the discus. The spin often gives more distance but is harder to control. Both techniques are allowed.

The best men in the world now put the shot more than 23 metres, and the best women more than 22 metres. The Swiss **Werner Günthör** was world champion in 1987, 1991 and 1993 and won Olympic bronze in Seoul in 1988. In Switzerland the traditional **stone throwing** is also well known, for example with the Unspunnen stone. You can try the shot put at many athletics clubs as a child.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sports involving running, jumping, throwing and putting.
Circle from which the shot is put.
Angle at which the shot leaves the hand.
Technique in which you turn once around yourself before the put.

gewusst: At 7.26 kilograms, the men's shot is about as heavy as a large watermelon.
The weight of 7.26 kilograms equals exactly 16 English pounds, which explains the odd number.
In the Middle Ages soldiers pushed heavy stones or cannonballs for fun, and today's sport grew out of this.

teile.einleitung: Moore's law is an observation from computer technology: the number of transistors on a computer chip doubles roughly every two years. It is not a law of nature but a rule of thumb that held true for a surprisingly long time. It is named after Gordon Moore, one of the founders of the company Intel.
wichtigste: Moore's law says that the number of transistors on chips doubles roughly every two years.
Gordon Moore described this development in a famous article in 1965.
It describes exponential growth.
In 10 years, the number of transistors therefore grows by a factor of 32.
Dennard scaling has no longer applied since the mid-2000s.
With very small transistors, quantum effects such as electron tunnelling cause problems.
With “More than Moore”, engineers look for new ways, such as stacked chips or specialised chips.

abschnitte.text: Gordon Moore lived from 1929 to 2023 and was an American chemist. In 1968, together with Robert Noyce, he founded the company **Intel**, which is now one of the largest chip makers in the world. In 1965 he wrote an article predicting how the number of components on chips would develop. At first he assumed it would double every year; in 1975 he corrected this to about two years.

A **transistor** is a tiny electrical switch made of semiconductor material, usually silicon. It can switch current on and off and so represent the zeros and ones of a computer. The more transistors a chip has, the more it can calculate and store at the same time. Modern transistors are so small that you can only see them with an electron microscope.

Doubling means that 1 becomes 2, then 4, 8, 16 and 32. After 10 years of doubling every two years, the number is therefore 32 times as large. This **exponential growth** quickly becomes enormous. The first microprocessor, the Intel 4004 from 1971, had around 2300 transistors; according to the rule there would have been around 2.4 billion in 2011, and that roughly matched real chips.

Thanks to this development, computers became ever faster, smaller and cheaper. A mobile phone today calculates much faster than the largest computers of the 1970s. As of 2026, the largest chips contain more than a hundred billion transistors. Without this progress there would be no smartphones, no fast internet and no artificial intelligence as we know it.

For a long time, smaller transistors did not increase the power use per area; this is called **Dennard scaling**. Since the mid-2000s, this rule no longer applies, because chips would get too hot. That is why the clock speed has hardly risen since then, and several processor cores are built in instead. With structures of only a few nanometres, **quantum effects** also cause problems: electrons tunnel through barrier layers that should actually stop them.

Experts are looking for new ways to make chips more powerful anyway. Chips are stacked on top of each other, specialised chips are built for particular tasks such as artificial intelligence, or many small chips are joined together in one package. This strategy is called **More than Moore**. Research is also going into completely new ideas such as quantum computers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny electrical switch, the basic building block of every computer chip.
Growth in which an amount keeps doubling at equal intervals of time.
A material such as silicon that conducts electricity or not, depending on the conditions.
The main processing chip of a computer.

gewusst: Moore's law is more of a self-fulfilling prophecy, because the chip industry used it as a target for decades.
Modern transistors are thousands of times thinner than a human hair.
The name “Moore's law” was not thought up by Gordon Moore himself; other people later called it that.

teile.einleitung: A ruler is a flat, straight tool with a scale, used to draw straight lines and measure short lengths. It belongs in almost every pencil case. The scale shows centimetres, and in between you can see many small millimetre lines.
wichtigste: With a ruler you draw straight lines in your exercise book and measure lengths.
When measuring, you line the ruler up at zero.
The very small lines between the centimetres are millimetres.
A common school ruler is 30 centimetres long.
Many school rulers are made of plastic.
The triangular ruler with a right angle is called a set square, or in German Geodreieck.
For long distances such as the classroom a ruler is too short; for that you need a tape measure or a folding rule.

abschnitte.text: A **ruler** is a narrow, straight strip of wood or plastic with at least one perfectly straight edge. Along this edge you can draw straight lines with a pencil. A **scale** is printed along the edge, with which you can measure lengths. The most common school ruler is 30 centimetres long, but there are also short ones of 15 and long ones of 50 centimetres.

The long lines with numbers show the **centimetres**. Between two centimetres there are ten small gaps; these are the **millimetres**. The line in the middle is often a little longer and shows half a centimetre. Ten millimetres make one centimetre, and a hundred centimetres make one metre.

Place the ruler so that the **zero** is exactly at the start of the line. Careful: on many rulers the zero does not start right at the edge but a little way in. Then read off which number is at the end of the line. If a line goes from 2 to 9 centimetres, you work out 9 minus 2 and know that it is 7 centimetres long.

The **set square** (in Swiss schools usually a “Geodreieck”) is a triangular ruler with a right angle and an angle scale, which can also be used to measure angles. For longer distances you use a folding rule, which in Switzerland is often called a “Doppelmeter”, or a tape measure. Carpenters and mechanics work with steel rulers, which are very accurate and tough. You do not measure the classroom with a ruler, because it is far too short for that.

Many school rulers are made of transparent **plastic** so that you can see the line underneath. But there are also rulers made of wood, aluminium or steel. Ancient civilisations such as Egypt and Mesopotamia already had measuring rods, for example the cubit, which was based on the length of a forearm. The metre was only fixed at the end of the 18th century in France and is now used almost everywhere in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: The division into lines and numbers on a measuring device.
A unit of length; 100 centimetres are 1 metre.
A tenth of a centimetre, the smallest lines on the ruler.
A triangular ruler with a right angle and an angle scale.

gewusst: The German word for ruler, Lineal, comes from the Latin “linea”, which means line.
On some rulers one edge is slightly raised so that the ink does not smudge when drawing with a fountain pen.

teile.einleitung: Air is the invisible mixture of gases that surrounds our Earth like a shell and that we breathe. You cannot see it, but you can feel it, for example as wind. Without air there would be no life, no fire and no sound.
wichtigste: Air is a mixture of different gases.
Most of it is nitrogen, about 78 per cent.
About 21 per cent is oxygen, which humans, animals and also flames need.
The Earth's shell of air is called the atmosphere.
Air has a small weight and takes up space.
Warm air rises, cold air sinks.
On high mountains the air is thinner, which is why breathing is harder.

abschnitte.text: Dry air consists of about 78 per cent **nitrogen** and about 21 per cent **oxygen**. Just under 1 per cent is the noble gas argon. Carbon dioxide makes up only about 0.04 per cent but is very important for the climate and for plants. On top of that there is water vapour and tiny particles of dust.

If you push an empty glass upside down into water, it does not fill up. The air in the glass takes up space and does not let the water in. If you blow through a straw into a glass of water, you see **air bubbles** rising. This shows that air is a real substance, even though it is invisible.

At sea level one litre of air weighs about 1.2 grams, which is very little. But the whole column of air above us presses hard on the Earth; this is called **air pressure**. At sea level it is about 1013 hectopascals on average. Higher up there is less air above, which is why air pressure falls with height.

When air is heated, it expands and becomes lighter. That is why **warm air** rises, in a room for example to the ceiling. Hot air balloons use exactly this effect. Wind also arises because air warms up by different amounts and then forms currents that even things out.

The **atmosphere** gets thinner and thinner as you go up. On the Jungfraujoch at about 3450 metres the air pressure is only about two thirds of what it is at sea level. Every breath there contains less oxygen, which is why you get out of breath more quickly when walking. Climbers on very high summits therefore often take oxygen bottles with them.

Humans and animals breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. Plants do the opposite in **photosynthesis** and produce oxygen. A candle flame also needs oxygen; if you cover it with a glass, it soon goes out. Clean air is important for health, which is why pollutants such as fine dust are measured regularly in Swiss cities.

begriffe.erklaerung: The shell of air that surrounds the Earth.
The pressure that the weight of the air exerts on everything.
The most common gas in the air, colourless and odourless.
The gas we need for breathing and fire needs for burning.

gewusst: The air in a classroom weighs about as much as one or two children altogether.
Without air there would be no sound, which is why it is completely silent in space.
The sky is blue because air scatters blue sunlight more strongly than red.

teile.einleitung: A spoon is an eating tool used for soup, muesli or yoghurt. But a shiny metal spoon is also a little physics laboratory, because its curved sides act like two different mirrors. On the inside your reflection is upside down; on the back you see yourself small and the right way up.
wichtigste: The spoon is one of humanity's oldest eating tools.
A brightly polished metal spoon reflects best.
The inside acts like a concave mirror, the back like a convex mirror.
In the bowl of the spoon you see yourself upside down from a little distance away.
If you come very close, the image in the bowl is the right way up and becomes large.
On the back you always see yourself the right way up and smaller.
Because the spoon is curved, the reflection looks distorted.

abschnitte.text: As early as the Stone Age people used shells or carved pieces of wood as **spoons**. Later spoons were made of horn, bone, wood and metal, and rich families owned silver spoons. Today most spoons are made of rustproof **stainless steel**. There are many kinds, such as soup spoons, coffee spoons, wooden cooking spoons and ladles.

The inside of a spoon curves inwards like a bowl. A mirror like this is called a **concave mirror**. It gathers the rays of light at one point, the focal point. If you look into it from a normal distance, you therefore see yourself small and upside down. If you come very close, closer than the focal point, your image suddenly stands the right way up and becomes large.

The back of the spoon curves outwards. A mirror like this is called a **convex mirror**. It spreads the rays of light apart and shows an upright, smaller image. On the other hand you can see a larger part of the surroundings in it than in a flat mirror. Because the spoon is not flat, your nose and face look funnily distorted in both mirrors.

Convex mirrors hang, for example, at blind exits and bends as **traffic mirrors**, so that you can see a lot of the road. The wing mirrors of cars are also often slightly curved outwards. Concave mirrors are found in make-up mirrors, which magnify the face, and in torches or headlights, which concentrate the light. Large telescopes also collect the light of distant stars with concave mirrors.

For the experiment you need a clean, **shiny** metal spoon; a plastic spoon hardly reflects. Hold it at arm's length in front of your face and look into the bowl, then turn it over. Slowly move the spoon closer to your eye and watch when the image in the bowl flips. With a tablespoon and a coffee spoon you can compare how strongly the curve changes the image.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mirror that curves inwards like the inside of a spoon.
Mirror that curves outwards like the back of a spoon.
Point at which a concave mirror gathers the rays of light.
Image formed when light is thrown back by a smooth surface.

gewusst: The English word “spoon” and the German word “Span” (chip of wood) are related, because early spoons were often carved from chips of wood.
A teaspoon holds about 5 millilitres, a tablespoon about 15 millilitres.
With a large concave mirror you can concentrate sunlight so strongly that paper starts to burn.

teile.einleitung: MeteoSwiss is the national weather and climate service of Switzerland. This federal office measures the weather day and night, makes forecasts and warns the population of severe weather. Switzerland's record temperatures also come from the measurements of MeteoSwiss.
wichtigste: MeteoSwiss is the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology.
It measures the weather at many automatic stations all over Switzerland.
In Payerne MeteoSwiss regularly sends up weather balloons with measuring instruments.
With a weather model a computer calculates how the weather will develop.
MeteoSwiss warns of severe weather in 5 danger levels.
The highest officially measured temperature in Switzerland is 41.5 °C, measured in Grono in 2003.
The lowest temperature at an official station was measured in La Brévine in 1987: minus 41.8 °C.

abschnitte.text: MeteoSwiss is a **federal office** and belongs to the Federal Department of Home Affairs. Its headquarters are in Zurich, and other sites are Geneva, Locarno-Monti and Payerne. Its roots go back to the 19th century, when Switzerland set up a first nationwide network of weather stations. Today experts in weather, climate, computing and technology work together there. The forecasts appear in the MeteoSwiss app, on the internet, on the radio and on television.

abschnitte.titel: Measuring on the ground and in the air
abschnitte.text: Spread across the whole country, automatic **weather stations** measure temperature, wind, rain, humidity and sunshine. The values are sent to the head office every few minutes. Several **weather radars** on mountains detect rain and hail cells. In Payerne **weather balloons** regularly go up, carrying measuring instruments to heights of over 30 kilometres. In addition there are data from weather satellites and aircraft.

All the measurements flow into a **weather model**. A high-performance computer divides the air above Switzerland into many small cubes and calculates, according to the laws of physics, how pressure, temperature and wind change in them. Because the Alps strongly influence the weather, Switzerland needs an especially fine model. Meteorologists check the results and use them to put the forecast into words. For the next few hours a forecast is very accurate; ten days ahead it is only rough.

For thunderstorms, storms, heavy rain, snow, black ice or heat, MeteoSwiss issues **warnings**. There are 5 danger levels, from low to very high danger. The warnings appear in colour on a map in the app, on the internet and through the federal government's alert app. Fire brigades, road services and authorities can thus prepare in good time. At high levels you should follow the authorities' rules of conduct.

Switzerland's highest temperature was measured on 11 August 2003 in **Grono** in the Misox valley in the canton of Graubünden: 41.5 °C. The lowest temperature at an official station was measured on 12 January 1987 in **La Brévine** in the Jura of Neuchâtel: minus 41.8 °C. La Brévine lies in a valley in which cold air collects on clear nights, and it is therefore called the Siberia of Switzerland. MeteoSwiss also observes the **climate** over long periods. The measurements show that Switzerland has become considerably warmer since the 19th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of the weather.
A gas-filled balloon that carries measuring instruments high into the sky.
A computer program that calculates how the weather will develop.
The weather as it is on average at a place over many years.

gewusst: A weather balloon expands more and more as it rises, until it bursts high up.
Because of its cold nights, La Brévine in the Jura is called the Siberia of Switzerland.
There are more than 83 degrees between Switzerland's cold record and its heat record.

teile.einleitung: In physics a light ray is a model used to draw the path of light. It is shown as a straight line with an arrow. This simple picture is good for explaining shadows, mirrors and lenses.
wichtigste: A light ray is an imaginary model of the path of light.
In a uniform material such as air, light travels in straight lines.
Many light rays together, for example behind an aperture, are called a beam of light.
Luminous light sources such as the Sun produce their own light.
We see other objects because they reflect light into our eyes.
Light needs no material and can also travel through empty space.
When two light rays cross, they carry on undisturbed.
A laser produces a particularly narrow light ray that hardly spreads out.

abschnitte.text: Light itself is a wave that cannot be seen as a thin line. That is why physicists draw **light rays**, straight lines with an arrow in the direction of travel. The model is a simplification, like a map of the path of light. A very thin beam of light from a small aperture comes closest to the imaginary light ray.

In air, water or glass light travels in **straight lines** as long as the material is the same everywhere. That is why sharp **shadows** form behind an object. Sunbeams falling through gaps in the clouds also show nice straight lines. Only at a boundary between two materials, for example from air to water, does the ray change direction.

The Sun, a candle or a light bulb are **luminous light sources**. The Moon, a book or your bike do not shine by themselves; they only reflect light. They are called **illuminated objects**. We only see an object when light from it reaches our eye.

In clear air you can hardly see the beam of a searchlight from the side. In fog or smoke, tiny water droplets or particles send part of the light off to the side. This **scattering** brings light into our eye, and the beam becomes visible. That is how you can see light rays in a disco or in a forest.

At about 300,000 kilometres per second, light is the fastest thing there is. It needs no material and reaches us through empty **space**. Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth. Two light rays that cross do not disturb each other.

A **laser** produces a very narrow, concentrated light that hardly spreads out at all. The first working laser was built in the USA in 1960. Today lasers are found in barcode readers at the checkout, in laser pointers and in measuring devices on building sites. Because laser light is so concentrated, you must never look into it.

begriffe.erklaerung: Imaginary straight line that shows which path light takes.
Many light rays side by side, for example behind an opening.
A plate with a hole that only lets part of the light through.
When small particles send light off in many directions.
An object that gives out light itself, such as the Sun or a lamp.

gewusst: The light you see today from some stars has already been travelling for many centuries.
Scientists send laser beams to mirrors that astronauts set up on the Moon and so measure the distance to the Moon.
The straight sunbeams falling through gaps in the clouds are also called crepuscular rays.

teile.einleitung: The spectrum of light shows which colours light is made of. White sunlight contains all the colours of the rainbow, from red to violet. You can see this for yourself with a prism or on a rainy day with sunshine.
wichtigste: Light is one of the electromagnetic waves.
The light that humans can see has wavelengths of roughly 380 to 780 nanometres.
In the visible spectrum red has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest.
A spectrum in which all the colours merge without gaps is called a continuous spectrum.
Glowing gases show a line spectrum of separate coloured lines.
The Sun's spectrum contains dark lines, the Fraunhofer lines.
A spectrometer is used to split light and measure its spectrum.

abschnitte.titel: What is a spectrum of light?
abschnitte.text: Light is an **electromagnetic wave**, just like radio waves or X-rays. Every colour of light has a particular **wavelength**, which is measured in nanometres, billionths of a metre. Humans see light roughly between 380 and 780 nanometres. Red has the longest wavelength, followed by orange, yellow, green, blue and finally violet with the shortest.

If you send white light through a glass **prism**, it fans out, because each colour is bent by a different amount. In this way Isaac Newton showed in the 17th century that white light is made up of all the colours. A **rainbow** forms in a similar way, when sunlight is refracted and reflected in raindrops. You can also see shimmering colours of the spectrum on the underside of a CD.

Glowing solid bodies such as the Sun or a light bulb produce a **continuous spectrum**, in which all the colours merge without gaps. Glowing gases, on the other hand, give out only very particular colours and show a **line spectrum** of separate coloured lines. Sodium vapour, for example, glows bright yellow, as you know from old street lamps. Light with only a single wavelength, as with many lasers, is called monochromatic.

Around 1814 the German optician **Joseph von Fraunhofer** discovered hundreds of fine dark lines in the Sun's spectrum. These **Fraunhofer lines** form because gases in the Sun's atmosphere swallow particular colours. Around 1860 Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen realised that every chemical element has its very own lines, like a fingerprint. This makes it possible to find out what stars are made of without ever travelling there; the element helium was even discovered first in sunlight.

abschnitte.titel: More than the eye can see
abschnitte.text: Visible light is only a small part of the whole electromagnetic spectrum. Beyond red lies invisible **infrared**, which we feel as warmth and which William Herschel discovered around 1800. Beyond violet lies **ultraviolet**, which causes sunburn. Bees can see ultraviolet light, and some snakes can sense infrared.

abschnitte.titel: Spectra in research and everyday life
abschnitte.text: With a **spectrometer** you measure exactly which wavelengths are in a light. Astronomers use it to find out the make-up, temperature and movement of stars and galaxies. In laboratories it is used to test the purity of substances, for example in food inspection. Fireworks also use line spectra: different metal salts colour the flames red, green or blue.

begriffe.erklaerung: Distance between two wave crests; it decides the colour of the light.
Glass object that splits white light into its colours.
Spectrum made of separate coloured lines, typical of glowing gases.
Measuring device that splits light and measures its wavelengths.

gewusst: The element helium was discovered in the light of the Sun in 1868, decades before it was found on Earth.
A rainbow is really a whole circle, but from the ground you usually see only an arc.
A nanometre is so small that about 50,000 to 100,000 of them fit into the thickness of a hair.

teile.einleitung: An overtone is a quieter, higher note that sounds together with the fundamental when an instrument or a voice produces a note. We usually do not hear the overtones separately, but they give every instrument its own tone colour. That is why an A on the flute sounds different from an A on the violin.
wichtigste: Overtones have frequencies that are whole-number multiples of the fundamental.
In acoustics, a sound made of a fundamental and several overtones is called a complex tone.
The mix of overtones decides why the flute and violin sound different.
A tuning fork produces almost a pure tone without overtones.
With a fundamental of 110 hertz, the second overtone is 330 hertz.
Without keys or valves, the alphorn can only play the notes of the harmonic series.
In overtone singing from Tuva and Mongolia, the overtones can be heard as a separate melody.

abschnitte.text: A guitar string does not only vibrate as a whole, but at the same time also in halves, thirds and quarters. The vibration as a whole gives the **fundamental**. The faster partial vibrations give the **overtones**. Their frequencies are double, triple, four times and so on the frequency of the fundamental.

With a fundamental of 110 hertz, the first overtone is at 220 hertz and the second at 330 hertz. Careful: overtones and **partials** are counted differently. The fundamental is the first partial, so the first overtone is the second partial. A pure tone without overtones is rare; a **tuning fork** comes very close to it.

When a flute and a violin play the same note, the fundamental has the same frequency. What is different is the strength of the individual overtones. The flute has only a few weak overtones and sounds soft. The violin has many strong overtones and sounds brighter and richer; this mix is called **tone colour**.

The **alphorn** has neither keys nor valves. So the player can only blow the notes of the harmonic series, that is the fundamental and the overtones. Depending on how tense the lips are, the horn jumps to a higher natural note. The 11th natural note lies between two notes of our scale and sounds a little off; it is called the **alphorn fa**.

In **overtone singing**, known above all from Tuva and Mongolia, you sing a low note and use your mouth and tongue to bring out individual overtones. Then you hear two notes at once: a humming note and a whistling melody above it. On the guitar, you can play overtones as **harmonics**. If you touch the string lightly exactly in the middle and pluck it, a bright note one octave higher sounds.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lowest note of a sound; it decides the pitch.
The particular way an instrument or a voice sounds.
The notes an instrument can play without keys or valves.
A bright note produced by lightly touching a string at a particular point.

gewusst: We recognise voices on the phone mainly thanks to the overtones, which every person mixes a little differently.
In the 19th century, the physicist Hermann von Helmholtz was one of the first to explain how overtones decide tone colour.

teile.einleitung: A movable pulley is a wheel with a groove that is not fixed in place but hangs with the load on the rope. It is a simple machine with which you can lift heavy things with only half as much force. But you have to pull twice as much rope.
wichtigste: With a movable pulley the load hangs from two sections of rope.
So without friction and the weight of the pulley you need only half the force.
For a lifting height of 1 m you have to pull 2 m of rope.
The load rises only half as fast as you pull the rope.
You have to lift the weight of the pulley as well.
Combined with a fixed pulley, you can pull downwards comfortably.
Several movable and fixed pulleys together form a block and tackle.

abschnitte.text: One end of the rope is fixed at the top to a beam or hook. The rope runs under the pulley, from whose axle the load hangs, and you pull on the other end. Because **two sections of rope** now carry the load, each takes only half. So if a load of 300 N hangs on the pulley, you need only 150 N of pulling force.

What you save in force, you have to pay in distance. If the load is to rise by 1 m, both sections of rope must get 1 m shorter, so you pull 2 m of rope. This rule is called the **golden rule of mechanics**: the work, force times distance, stays the same. If you pull the rope at 0.4 m/s, the load therefore rises at only 0.2 m/s.

You can also think of the movable pulley as a **one-sided lever**. The pivot is where the fixed section of rope leaves the pulley. The load acts in the middle, at the radius, and the pulling force at the other edge, at twice the radius. According to the law of the lever you therefore need only half the force.

The pulley itself also has a weight that has to be lifted too. If the pulley weighs 20 N and the load 180 N, you need (180 N + 20 N) : 2 = 100 N. If the two sections of rope run at a steep **angle** instead of straight up, the force needed becomes greater than half the load. Friction at the axle also costs some extra force.

On its own the movable pulley has a drawback: you have to pull upwards. That is why it is often combined with a **fixed pulley**, which only changes the direction of the pull. This creates a simple block and tackle, like the ones used on building sites, on sailing ships or in workshops. Construction cranes and cable cars also contain pulley systems that work on this principle.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pulley that moves up and down together with the load.
A pulley hung in a fixed place that only changes the direction of the force.
A combination of several pulleys used to lift heavy loads.
What you save in force, you have to make up for in extra distance.

gewusst: The Greek scholar Archimedes is said to have moved a whole ship with pulleys and ropes more than 2000 years ago.
With four load-bearing sections of rope in a block and tackle, you need only a quarter of the force.
A movable pulley does not save energy; it only spreads the work over a longer distance.

teile.einleitung: A fridge is an appliance that keeps food cool so that it stays fresh for longer. It does not produce cold but pumps the heat from its inside to the outside. That is why it is often warm behind the fridge.
wichtigste: Inside the fridge it is about 5 degrees; in the freezer about minus 18 degrees.
In the cold, germs grow more slowly, which is why food keeps longer.
A fridge carries heat from the inside to the outside.
For this it needs electricity and a special refrigerant.
You can feel the heat given off at the back of the appliance.
Hot food should be allowed to cool first before it goes into the fridge.
Ice builds up in the freezer compartment over time if it is never defrosted.

abschnitte.text: Food goes off because **bacteria** and moulds grow in it. In the cold these germs multiply much more slowly, which is why milk, meat and vegetables stay fresh for longer in the fridge. A fridge is usually about 5 degrees, and a **freezer** about minus 18 degrees. At this low temperature many foods keep for months.

In a fridge a **refrigerant** flows round in a circle through pipes. Inside, it evaporates in the evaporator and takes up heat as it does so, just as sweat cools your skin when it evaporates. A **compressor** that runs on electricity squeezes the gas together and makes it hot. At the back of the appliance it turns liquid again in the condenser and gives the heat off to the kitchen air. Then the cycle starts all over again.

You should not put hot soup straight into the fridge, because it warms the fridge up and it needs a lot of electricity to get cold again. The door should only be opened briefly so that as little warm air as possible gets in. Over time a **layer of ice** builds up in the freezer compartment from the moisture in the air, so it should be defrosted now and then. There needs to be some space behind the appliance so that the warm air can escape.

A fridge is not equally cold everywhere. On the bottom glass shelf above the vegetable drawer it is usually coldest, so that is where meat and fish belong. In the door it is warmer, which suits drinks, butter and sauces. In the **vegetable drawer** the air stays moister so that lettuce and vegetables do not dry out.

In the past food was kept cool in cool cellars or with natural ice that was sawn out of lakes in winter and stored in ice houses. In Switzerland, for example, ice ponds supplied ice for breweries and butchers. In the 19th century the German engineer **Carl von Linde** built one of the first reliable refrigerating machines. Household fridges only became widespread in Switzerland in large numbers after the Second World War.

begriffe.erklaerung: Substance that circulates in the fridge and carries heat from the inside to the outside.
Pump that squeezes the refrigerant gas together.
Part inside in which the refrigerant evaporates and takes up heat.
Part at the back of the appliance that gives off the heat to the air.
Letting the ice in the freezer compartment melt and removing it.

gewusst: A fridge with its door open does not cool the kitchen; overall it actually makes it a little warmer.
The humming of a fridge comes from the compressor, which keeps switching on and off.
In the past ice was sawn out of frozen lakes in winter and kept in ice houses until summer.

teile.einleitung: A light year is not a measure of time but a distance: the distance light travels in one year. That is about 9.5 trillion kilometres. Astronomers need this huge unit to give the distances between stars and galaxies.
wichtigste: The light year is a unit of distance, not of time.
A light year is the distance light travels in one year.
That is about 9.5 trillion kilometres.
In German the light year is abbreviated Lj (in English ly).
The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light years away.
The disc of our Milky Way has a diameter of about 100,000 light years.
Anyone who looks at distant stars is looking into the past.

abschnitte.text: Light is the fastest thing there is: it travels about 300,000 kilometres in one second. A **light year** is the distance light covers in a whole year. That is about 9.46 trillion kilometres, a number with twelve zeros. Although the word “year” is in it, the light year measures a **distance** and not time.

In space the distances are so huge that kilometres become impractical. Even to the nearest star, **Proxima Centauri**, it is about 40 trillion kilometres, or about 4.2 light years. For distances within our solar system, on the other hand, people often work in light minutes: sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth. Besides the light year, experts also use the unit **parsec**, which equals about 3.26 light years.

The disc of our galaxy, the **Milky Way**, measures about 100,000 light years across. Our Sun lies about 26,000 light years from its centre. The Andromeda Galaxy, which can be seen with the naked eye as a faint smudge on dark nights, is about 2.5 million light years away. The most distant galaxies that telescopes observe today are billions of light years away.

Because light needs time on its journey, we see stars as they used to be. If a star is 10 light years away, the light we see today left it 10 years ago. The light from the Andromeda Galaxy is even about 2.5 million years old. That is why experts say that looking into the distance is always also **looking into the past**. With very large telescopes you can observe galaxies from the early days of the universe in this way.

A car driving non-stop at 100 kilometres per hour would need more than 10 million years for a single light year. Even humanity's fastest space probes would need tens of thousands of years for the journey to Proxima Centauri. The **space probe** Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the most distant human-made object, but after almost 50 years of flight it is only about one light day from the Earth. That is only a tiny fraction of a light year.

begriffe.erklaerung: Distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres.
Speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres per second.
Huge collection of billions of stars, for example the Milky Way.
Another unit of distance in astronomy, about 3.26 light years.

gewusst: In one second a ray of light could go about seven and a half times round the Earth.
Some stars we see in the sky may no longer exist, because their light has been travelling for so long.
Sunlight is about 8 minutes old when it reaches us.

teile.einleitung: Magnetism is an invisible force of nature with which magnets attract certain metals or attract and repel other magnets. More than 2000 years ago people were already amazed by stones that attracted iron. Today magnetism is found in compasses, motors and computers.
wichtigste: Magnetism is a force that comes from magnets.
The two ends of a magnet are called the north pole and the south pole.
Two like poles, for example two north poles, repel each other.
Iron, nickel and cobalt are attracted, copper and aluminium are not.
Magnetic force also works through paper.
The compass uses a magnet to show the direction.
Electricity and magnetism are closely linked; this is called electromagnetism.

abschnitte.text: **Magnetism** is one of the basic forces of nature. Magnets attract objects made of iron, nickel or cobalt. Substances that are attracted are called **ferromagnetic**. A copper coin, an aluminium spoon or a piece of wood, on the other hand, are not attracted.

Every magnet has a **north pole** and a **south pole**. If you hold two north poles or two south poles together, they repel each other. A north pole and a south pole attract each other. Remember: like poles repel, unlike poles attract.

Magnetic force also works through paper, fabric, glass or thin wood. That is why a magnet holds a note on the **fridge**. You can even move a paper clip under a table with a magnet. The thicker the layer, the weaker the effect.

The Earth itself is a giant magnet. A magnetic needle that can turn lines up with it and points roughly north. This is how the **compass** works, which was probably first invented in China. Sailors, hikers and scouts still use it to find their way today.

Electric current produces magnetism, and moving magnets produce current. This interplay is called **electromagnetism**. Electric motors, generators in power stations and loudspeakers are based on it. Hard drives also store data with tiny magnetic areas.

begriffe.erklaerung: The name for substances such as iron that are strongly attracted by magnets.
The end of a magnet that wants to point north.
A device with a magnetic needle that shows the direction.
The interplay of electricity and magnetism.

gewusst: A magnet loses its force if it is heated very strongly.
Most Swiss coins are not attracted by a magnet, because they are made of a copper and nickel mixture.
Some bacteria have tiny magnetic crystals inside them and line up with the Earth's magnetic field.

teile.einleitung: The load arm is part of every lever: it is the distance from the pivot to the point where the load acts. Together with the effort arm, it decides how much force you need to lift something. With the right ratio you can move heavy things with little force.
wichtigste: The load arm is the distance from the pivot to the point where the load acts.
The law of the lever says: force times effort arm equals load times load arm.
If the load arm is shorter than the effort arm, you save force.
In a wheelbarrow the load arm reaches from the wheel axle to the middle of the load.
A long load arm, as with a fishing rod, makes the tip move quickly and far.
In a construction crane the load arm gets longer when the trolley moves outwards.
Carrying a load close to your body shortens the load arm and protects your back.

abschnitte.text: A **lever** is a rigid object that can turn around a **pivot**. The distance from the pivot to the load is called the **load arm**, and the distance from the pivot to the point where you push or pull is called the effort arm. Strictly speaking, the distance is measured at right angles to the direction of the force. Together, both arms decide whether a lever saves force or gains distance.

A lever is balanced when force times effort arm equals load times load arm. If the effort arm is 1 m and the load arm 20 cm long, you can hold five times the force of your hand. With 300 N on an effort arm 1.2 m long you hold 900 N if the load arm measures 0.4 m. If 150 N act on an effort arm of 80 cm and the load is 600 N, the load arm is 20 cm long. The product of force and arm is called **torque**.

In a **wheelbarrow** the wheel is the pivot; the load arm reaches to the middle of the load and is shorter than the distance to the handles. That is why you can lift heavy soil easily. Nutcrackers, bottle openers and crowbars also have a short load arm. With tweezers or a fishing rod, on the other hand, the load arm is long: you need more force, but the tip moves far and fast.

On a construction crane the **trolley** with the load moves back and forth along the jib. When it moves outwards, the load arm gets longer and the torque greater. So that the crane does not tip over, it carries heavy concrete blocks as a counterweight on the other side. The law of the lever also applies to the seesaw in the playground: a light child can balance a heavy one by sitting further out.

Our body also works with levers. In the forearm the elbow joint is the pivot; the biceps is attached close to it, while the load in the hand is far away. So the load arm is much longer than the effort arm: the muscle has to pull hard, but the hand moves quickly. When lifting a box, you should keep the load close to your body. That way the load arm to your spine is shorter and your back is under less strain.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rigid bar or object that can be turned around a point.
The fixed point around which a lever turns.
Distance from the pivot to the point where the force is applied.
Force times lever arm; it shows how strongly something is turned.
Unit of force, abbreviated N.

gewusst: The Greek scientist Archimedes is said to have declared: “Give me a place to stand, and I will move the world.”
With a long crowbar a child can move a stone that they could never lift with their bare hands.

teile.einleitung: A balloon is a stretchy skin, usually made of rubber, that you fill with air or gas. At birthdays and parties it creates a festive mood, and in physics lessons it shows how gases behave. Filled with helium, it even floats upwards.
wichtigste: Most balloons are made of latex, a natural rubber, or of coated foil.
A balloon filled with helium rises because helium is lighter than air.
If you let go of a balloon without a knot, it whizzes around until the air is out.
In the cold a balloon gets a little smaller; in the warmth it expands.
If the skin is stretched too much, the balloon bursts.
Helium slowly escapes through the rubber skin, which is why the balloon goes limp after a few days.
Remains of balloons in nature are dangerous, because animals can eat them.

abschnitte.text: Most balloons are made of **latex**, the sap of the rubber tree, which is processed into stretchy rubber. Foil balloons made of coated plastic are less stretchy but hold the gas for longer. In 1824 the English scientist Michael Faraday made rubber balloons for experiments with hydrogen. Soon afterwards balloons became popular as toys.

If you blow up a balloon and let it go without tying a knot, the air rushes out of the back. As it does so, it pushes the balloon in the opposite direction, and it whizzes wildly round the room until it is empty. This principle is called **recoil**, and it also drives rockets. Because the balloon has no steering and the opening flaps about, it flies in a zigzag.

Gases expand when they get warm and contract when they cool down. That is why a balloon gets a little smaller if you put it in the fridge. If you stretch a balloon over an empty bottle and stand it in warm water, it inflates, because the air in the bottle **expands**. If you blow in too much air, the skin is stretched too much and the balloon **bursts**.

**Helium** is a gas that is much lighter than air. A balloon full of helium is therefore lighter overall than the air it pushes aside, and it is pushed upwards, like a cork in water. This effect is called **buoyancy**. But the tiny helium particles slowly slip through the rubber skin, which is why a helium balloon goes limp after a few days and sinks.

If you rub a balloon on your hair, it becomes **electrically** charged and can then stick to the wall or attract hair. Balloons released outdoors end up at some point as litter in forests, lakes or the sea. Animals can mistake the remains and strings for food, swallow them and die. That is why many Swiss municipalities and festivals now do without balloon races or use alternatives.

begriffe.erklaerung: Milky sap of the rubber tree, from which rubber is made.
Very light gas that does not burn and makes balloons rise.
Force that pushes light things upwards in air or water.
An object is pushed forwards when something rushes out backwards.

gewusst: If you breathe in helium, you briefly speak with a Mickey Mouse voice, but it is dangerous and you should not do it.
Weather services send large weather balloons up to heights of more than 30 kilometres, where they burst.
A foil balloon can hold its helium for weeks, a latex balloon often only for a day or a few days.

teile.einleitung: A short circuit happens when electric current takes a shortcut and can flow with almost no resistance. Then the current suddenly becomes very strong, wires get hot and there can even be a fire. Fuses are there to stop this from happening.
wichtigste: In a short circuit the current flows along a very short path with little resistance.
Because the resistance is so small, the current becomes very strong.
A strong current heats the wires and can start a fire.
Fuses break the circuit when there is a short circuit.
Common causes are damaged cables or water in devices.
Even small batteries can get hot in a short circuit.

abschnitte.text: Current normally flows through a device, for example a lamp. The device has a **resistance** that limits the current. In a **short circuit** the two wires touch directly, and the current goes round the device. So it takes a shortcut with almost no resistance.

The smaller the resistance, the larger the **current**. A very strong current produces a lot of heat in the wires. The plastic insulation can melt, and sparks or even a **fire** can start. That is why short circuits are a common cause of fires in houses.

Every house has a **fuse box**. In it are fuses that switch off the current if it gets too strong. In the past **wire fuses** were used, in which a thin wire melts. Today there are usually circuit breakers, which you can simply switch back on after they have tripped.

A short circuit can happen if a cable is kinked, gnawed or damaged. **Water** in a device can also create conducting connections. Sometimes the fault is in a faulty device itself. With batteries, it is enough for a metal object such as a key to touch both terminals at the same time.

Never use devices with damaged cables or plugs. Keep electrical devices away from water, especially in the bathroom. You should not carry loose batteries in your trouser pocket together with coins or keys. If a fuse keeps tripping, an **electrician** should take a look.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly a material holds back the flow of current.
A safety part that switches off the current when it gets too strong.
A plastic covering that keeps the current in the wire.
The closed path along which current can flow.

gewusst: The name short circuit comes from the current closing its circuit by a short route.
In a short circuit the current can become many times stronger than in normal use.
Birds on a power line are safe as long as they do not touch two wires at the same time.

teile.einleitung: The newton is the unit in which forces are measured. It is named after the English natural scientist Isaac Newton, who described the laws of motion. On Earth, a 100-gram bar of chocolate is pulled downwards with about 1 newton.
wichtigste: The newton, abbreviated N, is the unit of force.
It is named after Isaac Newton.
1 newton is 1 kg · m/s², the force that speeds up 1 kg by 1 m/s every second.
A mass of 100 grams has a weight of about 1 N on Earth.
Mass is measured in kilograms, weight in newtons.
A child of 40 kg has a weight of about 400 N.
Larger forces are given in kilonewtons or meganewtons.

abschnitte.text: A **newton** is the force that makes an object with a mass of 1 kilogram 1 metre per second faster every second. Written in units, that is 1 N = 1 kg · m/s². The newton belongs to the International System of Units, which is used in science all over the world. Forces are measured, for example, with a **spring balance**.

Isaac Newton lived in England from 1643 to 1727. He described how forces move objects and explained that the same gravity makes an apple fall and steers the Moon around the Earth. His three laws of motion are still the basis of mechanics today. In his honour, the unit of force was named after him.

In everyday life people often say “I weigh 40 kilos”, but the kilogram is the unit of **mass**. The force with which the Earth pulls on an object is its **weight**, and it is measured in newtons. So a child of 40 kg has a weight of about 400 N, not 40 N. A bathroom scale actually measures a force and then converts it into kilograms.

How large the weight is depends on the **gravitational field strength**. In Switzerland it is about 9.81 N/kg; for calculations, 10 N/kg is often used. At the poles it is slightly greater than at the equator, because you are closer to the centre of the Earth there and the Earth's rotation has less effect. On the Moon it is only about 1.6 N/kg, but the mass of an object stays the same everywhere.

For large forces, multiples are used: 1 kilonewton is 1000 N, so 2.5 kN is 2500 N. A meganewton is a million newtons, so 2,000,000 N is 2 MN. A car presses on the road with about 15 kN. The engines of large rockets produce thrust of many meganewtons.

Climbing ropes and karabiners show how many kilonewtons they can withstand. Engineers also calculate in newtons for bridges, cranes and lifts. In sport, people measure how many newtons are used to kick a football or push off for a jump. This makes the invisible quantity of force comparable.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that can move, slow down or change the shape of an object.
How much matter an object has, measured in kilograms.
The force with which a celestial body pulls on an object.
Tells you how many newtons of weight 1 kg has in a particular place.
A measuring device with a spring that shows forces in newtons.

gewusst: An object that weighs 50 N on Earth still has a mass of 5 kg on the Moon, but only about a sixth of the weight.
Climbing karabiners often show values such as 22 kN, which is the weight of more than two tonnes.
The symbol for the newton is a capital N, because the unit is named after a person.

teile.einleitung: A lava lamp is a light in which coloured blobs slowly rise and sink, as if lava were flowing. Behind the show are simple laws of physics about density and heat. You can easily make your own lava lamp with oil, water, food colouring and an effervescent tablet.
wichtigste: A lava lamp shows coloured blobs rising and sinking in a liquid.
Oil floats on water because it is lighter than the same amount of water.
Oil and water do not mix; even after shaking hard they separate again.
A transparent bottle is good for a homemade lava lamp.
The food colouring mixes with the water, not with the oil.
An effervescent tablet produces gas bubbles that carry coloured drops of water upwards.
The real lava lamp was invented in England in the 1960s.

abschnitte.text: A real **lava lamp** contains a glass bottle with a clear liquid and a coloured wax. In the base there is a light bulb that gives light and warmth. The wax gets warm, rises in blobs, cools down at the top and sinks down again. This creates a calm, endless play of shapes that is reminiscent of flowing lava.

What matters is **density**, how heavy a certain volume of a substance is. A substance with lower density floats on top, one with higher density sinks. When the wax gets warm, it expands and its density becomes lower than that of the liquid, so it rises. At the top it cools down, becomes denser and sinks again. This up and down caused by heat is called **convection**.

You need a transparent bottle, water, cooking oil, **food colouring** and an **effervescent tablet**. Fill the bottle about a quarter full with water and then add plenty of oil; the oil floats on top. Drip in some colouring: it sinks through the oil and mixes with the water. Now drop in a piece of effervescent tablet and watch what happens. Ask an adult to help and do it on a mat in case something foams over.

The effervescent tablet dissolves in the water and forms bubbles of **carbon dioxide**. The gas bubbles attach themselves to coloured drops of water and carry them up through the oil. At the top the bubbles burst and the gas escapes into the air. Without the gas, the drop of water is heavier than oil again and sinks down. When the tablet has completely dissolved, no more bubbles rise, and then a new piece helps.

The lava lamp was invented by the Briton **Edward Craven Walker**, who brought it on the market in 1963. He was inspired by an egg timer made of liquids that he had seen in a pub. In the 1960s and 1970s the lamp became very popular and is still regarded as a symbol of that time. A real lava lamp often needs half an hour or longer before the wax starts moving properly.

begriffe.erklaerung: How heavy a certain volume of a substance is.
Movement in a liquid or gas caused by heat.
An invisible gas that also fizzes in sparkling mineral water.
A mixture of two liquids that do not really mix.

gewusst: You should not shake a real lava lamp, otherwise the liquid turns cloudy and stays milky for a long time.
The principle of rising warm liquid works much like the currents deep in the Earth's mantle that slowly move the continents.

teile.einleitung: An air pump is a device that sucks in air and pushes it into a container such as a bike tyre or a ball. Almost every child knows the bike pump. But there is exciting physics about pressure and heat behind this simple device.
wichtigste: With a bike pump you pump air into the tyres.
The air gets into the tyre through a valve.
The pump squeezes the air together and so raises the pressure.
After a lot of pumping the pump gets warm.
A tyre that is not pumped up enough makes riding harder.
Car tyres are pumped up at the petrol station with a compressor.
Footballs and inflatable swimming toys are also filled with air pumps.

abschnitte.text: A simple air pump consists of a **cylinder** in which a piston with a seal moves. When you pull the handle out, air flows into the cylinder. When you push it in, the air is squeezed together and pushed out through a hose. A small non-return valve makes sure that the air only flows one way.

On the tyre there is a small **valve** through which air can get in but not out again. On bikes there are three common types: the Dunlop valve, the slim Presta valve and the car valve, also called the Schrader valve. That is why many pumps have a head that fits several valves. Without a valve the air would escape again straight away.

When you **squeeze** air quickly, you put work into it. Part of this turns into heat, and the air warms up. That is why the bottom part of a bike pump feels warm after a lot of pumping. There is also some friction between the piston and the cylinder.

The recommended pressure is usually marked on the side of the tyre, often in **bar**. Town bikes often ride at about 3 to 5 bar, racing bikes at much more. If the tyre is too soft, it rolls heavily and can be damaged more easily. If it is too hard, or an inflatable toy is pumped up too much, it can burst.

Besides hand pumps there are foot pumps, track pumps with a pressure gauge and electric pumps. At the petrol station and in garages a **compressor** driven by a motor is used. Large compressors also drive compressed air tools, for example on building sites. Balls such as footballs are pumped up with a needle that is pushed into the ball's valve.

Around 1650 the German scientist Otto von **Guericke** built a pump with which he sucked the air out of a container. With it he showed how strong air pressure is: two hemispheres put together with no air inside could hardly be pulled apart even by teams of horses. This famous experiment is called the Magdeburg hemispheres. So air pumps are among the first instruments of physics.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small closure that lets air through in one direction only.
The moving part in the pump that squeezes the air together.
A machine with a motor that squeezes air strongly together.
A unit of pressure; 1 bar is roughly the air pressure at sea level.

gewusst: A bike's rubber inner tube slowly loses air over time even without a hole, because the gas moves through the rubber.
Bicycle tyres filled with air were made popular by John Boyd Dunlop around 1888.
With an air pump you can not only pump air in but, if it is built the other way round, also suck it out.

teile.einleitung: The Millikan experiment is a famous experiment in which the American physicist Robert Millikan determined the smallest electric charge around 1910. To do this, he watched tiny, electrically charged oil droplets between two metal plates. The result showed that electric charge only comes in fixed, smallest portions.
wichtigste: Around 1910, Robert Millikan measured the elementary charge very precisely.
He watched charged oil droplets in an electric field between two plates.
A floating droplet shows that the electric force and the weight are equal.
Oil was chosen because it hardly evaporates, so the mass of the droplets stays the same.
Millikan worked out the radius of the droplets using Stokes' law.
All the charges he measured were whole-number multiples of the elementary charge of about 1.6 · 10^-19 coulombs.
Millikan received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1923.

abschnitte.text: Robert Andrews Millikan lived from 1868 to 1953 and was a physicist from the USA. He did research at the University of Chicago and later at the California Institute of Technology. His student **Harvey Fletcher** helped him with his famous experiment. Millikan received the **Nobel Prize** in Physics in 1923 for measuring the elementary charge and for work on the photoelectric effect.

An atomiser sprays very fine oil droplets into a small chamber. Some droplets become electrically charged by friction. They pass between two horizontal metal plates, a **parallel-plate capacitor**, which has a voltage across it. Through a microscope you can watch the lit-up droplets, which look like little stars.

A droplet is pulled down by its weight and pushed up by the **electric force**. If you set the voltage exactly right, the droplet floats still in the air. Then the weight equals the electric force, so m · g = q · U / d. An example: a droplet of 4.9 · 10^-15 kg floats at 1500 volts with the plates 5 mm apart, so it carries about 1.6 · 10^-19 coulombs.

The droplets are so small that you cannot weigh them. So Millikan let them sink without any voltage and measured how fast they fell. Using **Stokes' law** about friction in air, he could work out their radius and therefore their mass. The buoyancy in air can often be ignored, because air has a much lower density than oil.

Millikan measured a great many droplets and kept finding similar values. All the charges were whole-number multiples of one smallest charge, the **elementary charge**. Today it is known very precisely: it is about 1.602 · 10^-19 coulombs. An electron carries exactly one such negative charge.

The experiment was important proof that electricity is made up of tiny particles. With the elementary charge, scientists could also calculate the mass of an electron. Since 2019, the value of the elementary charge has been fixed in the International System of Units. The Millikan experiment is still rebuilt at many upper secondary schools today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest electric charge found freely, about 1.6 · 10^-19 coulombs.
The unit of electric charge, named after Charles-Augustin de Coulomb.
Two parallel metal plates with an electric field between them.
A formula for the friction force on a small ball moving through air or a liquid.

gewusst: One coulomb is the charge of around six quintillion electrons.
Millikan watched some droplets for hours by steering them up and down again and again with the voltage.
The droplets in the experiment are so small that you can only see them as glowing dots in a microscope.

teile.einleitung: The litre is a unit of volume, in other words of how much fits into a container. It is used above all for liquids such as water, milk or petrol. One litre is exactly as much as fits into a cube with edges 10 centimetres long.
wichtigste: The symbol for litre is l or L.
One litre is the same size as one cubic decimetre.
1 litre has 10 decilitres, 100 centilitres or 1000 millilitres.
A normal carton of milk in the shop contains 1 litre.
A full bath holds about 150 litres of water.
One litre of water weighs about 1 kilogram.
The litre was introduced in France at the end of the 18th century.

abschnitte.text: The **litre** tells you how much space a substance takes up, its **volume**. One litre equals a cube of 10 cm by 10 cm by 10 cm, which is a **cubic decimetre**. A typical milk carton or large water bottle contains exactly this much. The litre is abbreviated with a small l or, so that it is not confused with the figure 1, a capital L. The litre is not an official base unit of the international system of units, but it may be used everywhere.

For smaller amounts the litre is divided up. 1 litre has 10 **decilitres**, 100 centilitres or 1000 **millilitres**. So with one litre you can fill 5 glasses of 2 decilitres each. For large amounts there is the **hectolitre**, which has 100 litres. Two bottles of 1.5 litres each make 3 litres together.

A cup of tea holds about 2 to 3 decilitres. A cleaning bucket holds about 10 litres. A full **bath** holds about 150 litres of water, while a shower usually needs much less. A car often takes 40 to 60 litres of petrol. A person should drink about 1.5 litres a day, more in hot weather and when doing sport.

One litre of water weighs almost exactly 1 **kilogram**. That is no coincidence: when the French created the metric system, they originally defined the kilogram as the weight of one litre of water.
