Other liquids weigh different amounts; a litre of cooking oil, for example, is lighter than a litre of water. That is why oil floats on water. A litre of honey, on the other hand, is noticeably heavier.

In the past almost every region had its own measures for liquids, which made trade very complicated. In France a uniform **metric system** was introduced after the Revolution, and from 1795 it included the litre. The name comes from an old French measure, the litron. In Switzerland the metric system has applied since the 19th century. Today the litre is used almost all over the world, but in the USA people often still measure in gallons.

In Switzerland you see the litre on every drinks bottle and every milk carton. In restaurants drinks are often ordered in **decilitres**, for example 3 dl of apple spritzer or 5 dl of mineral water. When baking, milk and water are measured with a measuring jug. Petrol and heating oil are also sold in litres. Water use in the home is also counted in litres, and for large amounts in cubic metres.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much space something takes up.
A cube with edges 10 cm long, exactly the same size as 1 litre.
A tenth of a litre.
A thousandth of a litre, exactly as much as a cubic centimetre.
A container with marks for measuring liquids.

gewusst: One cubic metre of water is 1000 litres and weighs about a tonne.
The capital L as a symbol for litre was only officially allowed in 1979, to avoid confusion with the figure 1.

teile.einleitung: Newton's laws are three basic rules that describe how forces cause movement. Isaac Newton published them in 1687 in his work Principia. They explain why a ball rolls, a car brakes and a rocket flies.
wichtigste: Isaac Newton formulated the three laws of motion in 1687.
The first law is the law of inertia.
Without a resultant force, an object stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed.
The second law says that force equals mass times acceleration.
The third law is called action equals reaction.
For every force there is an equal opposing force in the opposite direction.
The unit newton equals kg·m/s².

abschnitte.text: **Isaac Newton** lived in England from 1643 to 1727. He was a physicist, mathematician and astronomer. In 1687 he published his main work, **Principia**, in which he described the three laws of motion and the law of gravitation. The unit of force, the newton, is named after him.

The **law of inertia** says that an object stays at rest or keeps moving straight ahead at a constant speed as long as no resultant force acts on it. If a bus suddenly brakes, you tip forwards because your body wants to keep going. That is why **seat belts** are so important. A rolling ball eventually stops because of friction and air resistance.

The second law links force, mass and **acceleration**: F = m · a. To accelerate a 1200 kg car at 2.5 m/s², you need 3000 N. From this comes the unit newton equals kg·m/s². If a force of 50 N acts for 4 seconds on a 10 kg object at rest, it reaches 20 m/s.

The third law is called **action equals reaction**. For every force there is an equal opposing force in the opposite direction. A **rocket** pushes gases out backwards, and they push the rocket forwards. That is why it can accelerate even in the airless vacuum of space.

In a lift, you feel the laws directly. If the lift accelerates upwards at 2 m/s², the floor pushes harder on you. For a person of 70 kg, that is around 827 N instead of about 687 N when standing still. That is why you briefly feel heavier when the lift starts going up.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tendency of an object to keep its state of motion.
How quickly the speed changes.
The sum of all the forces acting on an object.
Newton's famous book of 1687 on motion and gravity.

gewusst: According to a well-known story, a falling apple got Newton thinking about gravity.
Newton's laws were enough to fly people to the Moon in 1969.
At very high speeds close to the speed of light, you need Einstein's theory of relativity instead of Newton.

teile.einleitung: A lighthouse is a tall tower with a powerful light at the top that shows ships the way. It warns of dangerous rocks and shallows and helps sailors find their way at night. Lighthouses have existed since ancient times, and many of them are famous landmarks today.
wichtigste: A lighthouse shows ships the way and warns of dangers.
Lighthouses usually stand on the coast, on islands or at harbour entrances.
The light at night is the most important thing.
Each lighthouse flashes in its own rhythm, so sailors can tell which one it is.
The light of many lighthouses turns in a circle and so shines in all directions.
Many lighthouses are striped red and white so that they can also be seen well by day.
The Lighthouse of Alexandria was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

abschnitte.text: A **lighthouse** is a navigation mark, an aid that helps ships find their way. It stands on coasts, on rocks in the sea, on islands or at harbour entrances. Its light warns of dangerous places such as reefs and sandbanks and shows where the safe entrance is. Because the tower is so tall, its light can be seen for many kilometres, even though the Earth is curved.

So that the light shines far, it is focused with large lenses. In the 1820s the French physicist **Augustin Fresnel** invented a special lens made of many ring-shaped steps of glass, the **Fresnel lens**. It is lighter than an ordinary lens and still focuses the light very strongly. In many lighthouses the lens or the lamp turns in a circle, which is why the light shines first in one direction and then in another.

Each lighthouse has its own **light characteristic**, a particular rhythm of flashes and pauses, sometimes also its own colour. This characteristic is marked on sea charts for every lighthouse. In this way sailors can tell at night exactly which lighthouse they are looking at and where they are. By day the paintwork, for example red and white stripes, helps to tell the towers apart.

The most famous lighthouse in history stood on the island of **Pharos** off the city of **Alexandria** in Egypt. It was built in the 3rd century BC and was probably more than 100 metres tall. It was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and was later destroyed by earthquakes. Its name lives on, because in several languages the word for lighthouse still sounds like Pharos, for example “faro” in Italian.

In the past **lighthouse keepers** lived in many lighthouses with their families. Every night they had to light the lamp, top up the oil, clean the lenses and wind up the turning mechanism. Often they were alone on a lonely island for weeks. Today almost all lighthouses run automatically, and ships also find their way with satellite navigation.

There are also lighthouses on large lakes. A well-known one is the lighthouse at the harbour entrance of **Lindau** on Lake Constance, right next to the Swiss border. It is the only lighthouse in Bavaria and a popular place to visit, with a large stone lion standing opposite. For shipping on Lake Constance and the Swiss lakes there are also lights at harbour entrances and storm warning lights.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sign on the coast or in the water that helps ships to navigate.
A lighthouse's own flashing rhythm, by which it can be recognised.
Lens made of ring-shaped steps of glass that focuses light very strongly.
Person who used to look after the light in a lighthouse.

gewusst: The light of powerful lighthouses can be seen from more than 30 kilometres away.
The Fresnel lens is also used today in overhead projectors, car headlights and some magnifying glasses.
In fog many lighthouses used to give extra warning with loud foghorns.

teile.einleitung: Magnetic resonance imaging, MRI for short, is a method with which doctors obtain precise pictures of the inside of the body. It works with strong magnetic fields and radio waves instead of X-rays. With it the brain, joints and organs can be examined very precisely.
wichtigste: MRI produces pictures with magnetic fields and radio waves.
It focuses above all on hydrogen nuclei, which are found in water and fat in the body.
Clinical machines usually have a flux density of 1.5 or 3 tesla.
The superconducting magnet coils are cooled with liquid helium.
The examination is loud because gradient coils vibrate due to Lorentz forces.
Many contrast agents for MRI contain the element gadolinium.
Paul Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2003 for developing MRI.
The ETH researcher Richard R. Ernst received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1991 for methods that also serve MRI.

abschnitte.text: In **magnetic resonance imaging** you lie on a couch that moves into a tube. The tube is a giant magnet. From the measurements a computer puts together cross-sectional pictures of the body, similar to slices of a loaf of bread. Soft tissues such as the brain, muscles, ligaments and cartilage can be seen especially well on them.

There are very many **hydrogen nuclei** in the body, because we consist largely of water. These nuclei behave like tiny magnets and line up in the strong field. Radio waves briefly knock them out of step, and as they tip back they themselves send out weak radio signals. At 1.5 tesla this **Larmor frequency** is around 64 megahertz, that is in the range of FM radio stations.

A field of 1.5 tesla is about 30 000 times stronger than the Earth's magnetic field. Such fields are produced by coils of **superconducting** wire that conduct current without resistance. For this they have to be cooled with liquid **helium** to almost minus 270 degrees. The magnet is therefore always switched on, even at night.

During the measurement the machine knocks and hums very loudly. The cause is the **gradient coils**, which are switched quickly and vibrate due to Lorentz forces. Patients are therefore given ear protection or headphones. A big advantage is that MRI does not use X-rays.

The strong magnet attracts objects made of iron with great force. That is why you must not take keys, coins or hair clips into the room. Pacemakers and some implants also have to be checked beforehand. Sometimes a **contrast agent** with gadolinium is injected so that certain tissues can be seen more clearly.

The basis is nuclear magnetic resonance, for which the Zurich-born Felix Bloch received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1952. In the 1970s Paul Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield showed how to make pictures from it. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2003. The ETH chemist **Richard R. Ernst** developed measuring methods that made MRI faster and better, and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1991.

begriffe.erklaerung: Method that produces cross-sectional pictures of the inside of a body.
When something reacts especially strongly to a vibration of exactly the right frequency.
Material that conducts current completely without resistance at very low temperature.
Substance that is injected so that certain parts are easier to see in the picture.

gewusst: In the MRI room the magnet is so strong that a metal office chair carried in can fly onto the machine.
Because the machine measures radio waves, the examination room is shielded with metal so that no radio stations from outside interfere.
The method used to be called nuclear spin tomography, but the word nuclear was often confused with nuclear power.
